4cebac5d-35e1-528a-8905-bcf72d5a263b.name: Oil lamp
4cebac5d-35e1-528a-8905-bcf72d5a263b.description:
This monumental oil lamp consists of two parts, the lower a traditional candlestick and the upper a shaft with a bowl for oil.  
The splendidly calligraphed *Thuluth* inscription shows that the lamp was ordered by or for the leader of the Aq Qoyunlu Turkmen, Uzun Hasan, who ruled eastern Anatolia, Iraq, and large parts of Iran in around 1470.
keywords: Oil lamp; Thuluth; Metalwork; calligraphy; inscription

4cec7fd2-9c51-5d92-b223-cc2c061e7fc9.name: Khirbat al-Mafjar.
4cec7fd2-9c51-5d92-b223-cc2c061e7fc9.description:
Qasr Hisham (or Hisham's Palace) is considered to be one of the most beautiful and grandiose of the Umayyad *qusur* (palaces), in terms of its stucco wall decorations and mosaic floors. The palace was uncovered during the course of excavations undertaken by Robert Hamilton and Demetri Baramki during the 1930s and 40s. The complex consists of a spacious palace, public mosque, private mosque, a minaret, a fountain, a swimming pool, and a large and splendid bathhouse (*hammam*). Excavations to uncover the building took place at the north of the palace complex where a large series of rooms were discovered. These were possibly residences for those who served at the palace or commercial *caravanserai*.  
The *qasr*'s main entrance portal is located in the southeast corner leading into an open courtyard. In the courtyard many archaeological finds have been uncovered, including remains from an earthquake which struck the palace (around 130 H / 747-48). To the north of this courtyard is a swimming pool, the floor of which is paved with mosaics. A little to the west of the pool and the courtyard is the entrance to the palace interior. The entrance leads into a spacious internal courtyard that is surrounded by two storeys of rooms and halls on the south and west sides. At the centre of the arcade on the south side of the courtyard, adjacent to the base of the minaret, there is a small mosque that was designated for the use of the caliph. The public mosque is located to the north of the eastern portico where, on the south wall, there lies the recess where the *mihrab* once was, facing in the direction of Mecca. Most sections of the mosque were not roof-covered except for the area close to the mihrab, which was preceded by arcades resting on a series of columns.  
A corridor moves northward between the building of the palace and the great *hammam*. The palace *hammam* consisted of a huge square hall measuring about 30m in length, and had a mosaic floor characterised by geometric designs. This huge *hammam* hall is crowned by a dome supported by 16 piers. The *hammam* proper is preceded by a pool, while in the northern area of the *hammam* there is a series of rooms that includes the reception hall (*auditorium*), which features a mosaic floor portraying a lion pouncing on a gazelle. This panel is considered one of the most beautiful mosaics to have been discovered in the region. Next to the reception hall are the hot rooms (*caldarium*), designated for bathing, a hearth and a water closet. Canals have been uncovered on the site which brings the water from a spring at 'Ayn al-Dyuk and 'Ayn Nu'aymat, located about 8 km from the *hammam*. The canal would have provided both the *hammam* and the *qasr* with an adequate water supply.
4cec7fd2-9c51-5d92-b223-cc2c061e7fc9.short_description: This is one of the most important and grandiose of the Umayyad palaces. All the architectural and decorative arts of the Umayyad period are gathered within it. It contains one of largest and most beautiful Islamic mosaic floors to have been discovered. The palace complex has a square floor plan and was two storeys high (nothing remains except parts of the ground floor). In the middle is an open-air courtyard surrounded by porticoes, behind which are rooms. There are two mosques, one public and one private, a pool, a large bath, a throne room, a fountain, large gardens and canals bringing water from nearby springs.
4cec7fd2-9c51-5d92-b223-cc2c061e7fc9.dates: The end of hegira the 1st century / AD the first half of the eighth century.
4cec7fd2-9c51-5d92-b223-cc2c061e7fc9.address: The palace is located 2 km north of the centre of Jericho.
4cec7fd2-9c51-5d92-b223-cc2c061e7fc9.method_for_datation: The building was dated by means of archaeological excavations which took place at the site.
4cec7fd2-9c51-5d92-b223-cc2c061e7fc9.bibliography:
Creswell, K. A. C., *Early Muslim Architecture*, Volume 1, Oxford, 1969.  
Hamilton, R. W., “Who Built Khirbat al-Mafjar?”, *Levant*, No. 1, 1969, pp.61–7.  
\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_, and Grabar O., *Khirbat al-Mafjar*, Oxford, 1959.  
*Pilgrimage, Sciences and Sufism: Islamic Art in the West Bank and Gaza,* pp.144-46.
4cec7fd2-9c51-5d92-b223-cc2c061e7fc9.patrons: The qasr is associated with the Umayyad caliph, Hisham bin ‘Abd al-Malik (r. AH 105–25 / AD 724–43) and by some scholars with Caliph al-Walid bin Yazid (r. AH 125–6 / AD 743–4).
keywords: Khirbat al-Mafjar; civil architecture; mosaic; qasr; qasr of Hisham
4cec7fd2-9c51-5d92-b223-cc2c061e7fc9.author: Yusuf al-Natsheh

4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.name: Prayer rug with multiple prayer niches (fragment).
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.description:
This carpet fragment is the preserved part of a considerably larger prayer rug featuring multiple prayer niches. The carpet features a row of six red niches of various widths that are closed at the top by dark-blue arches. The sixth niche on the left-hand side is only a half-niche as the carpet was cut at this point and the border repaired. The niches are separated using fine green lines that run down to the bottom and which could be interpreted as substitute columns. The carpet’s narrow border consists of a double-edged, reciprocal pattern of alternating light-blue and yellow crenellations. The wider, less complete, border has a single row of crenellations, yellow alternating with blue.  
The particular clarity of the carpet’s design and its use of colour demonstrate the Ottoman understanding of the decorative arts and their practice. Unlike most of the other known multiple prayer-niche carpets, this one is very simple, in that nowhere is it overly decorated; however even in its simplicity, it still follows a systematic composition of ordered patterns covering the surface, as can be seen repeatedly within Ottoman art from as early as the AH 9th / AD 15th century. Its simplicity, vibrant colours and the combined overall impact it creates would definitely have appealed to middle European tastes. Followers of the Islamic faith would have prayed on multiple prayer-niche carpets placed parallel to the *qibla* wall in the mosque. Admittedly, the rows of niches on this carpet merely refer to its function or use, because, essentially, each clean surface acts as a pad on which to pray. The narrowness of each niche on the carpet hints that a believer would have required more space in which to pray than that afforded by the narrow niches on the carpet.
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.short_description: This carpet with its pattern of multiple niches is part of a once much larger rug. It was probably made for use in a mosque. It is unique because the design does not include the usual complicated patterns but instead makes a strong impact through its plain vibrant colours.
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.method_for_datation: The carpet has been dated on the grounds of its pattern, colours and knot-technique to be from the 11th / 17th century.
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.method_for_provenance: The carpet belongs to a group of Ottoman carpets that are referred to as the Ushak Group.
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.obtention: Obtained in 1961 from the O. Bernheimer Collection, Munich.

4d229eb0-4e69-5d2b-bc72-f2e57ec20ac5.name: Castle of Moura.
4d229eb0-4e69-5d2b-bc72-f2e57ec20ac5.description:
The *hisn* (castle) of Moura stands between the rivers Brenhas and Roda, whose valleys it dominates from an elevation of over 100 metres. A small settlement in the Islamic period (200 x 120 metres, approximately 2.4 hectares), its walls encircled an inner area in which there was apparently no hierarchy of spaces, in a similar way to those of Portel, Castro de Cola or Serpa, for example.  
In the Islamic period, Moura was considered by Ibn al-Faradias a 'castle of the *cora* \[administrative region\] of Beja', an assertion that demonstrates the continuation of the dependency of Moura on the ancient seat of the convents of Beja. Aside from this information, other written sources make little reference to this place.  
Other elements relating to Moura confirm continuous occupation in the Islamic period, although the dispersed nature of the remains makes systematisation difficult. As well as the presence of several towers made of *tabiyya* (dry-mud) wall, probably dating from the Almohad period, two aspects are of particular interest: on the one hand, a reference to the construction of a minaret in the middle of the AH 5th / AD 11th century, commissioned by al-Mutadid, apparently as a symbolic sign of the taking of possession of the area and at a time when the population was part of the Abbasid Taifa; on the other hand, the reference in oral tradition to the existence of a *salúquia*, a tower or part of a fortification, which is associated through Romantic legend with the name of the daughter of the supposed last *alcaide* or governor.  
The Almohad perimeter wall, which was probably built on top of a previous community-based fortification is distinctive, as is the manorial-style castle inside the fortification, with its keep dating from the end of the 15th century.  
Of the *tabiyya* walls from the AH 6th / AD 12th century which formerly encircled Moura, only one square tower remains today, in the southeast area of the fortifications, with the remains of another in the north area. The former still has on its main façade facing the Church of St John the Baptist, remnants of typical whitewash paintings in imitation of large masonry blocks. Part of a widespread campaign of military construction which was carried out throughout the Gharb region in the second half of the AH 6th / AD 12th century, the fortress of Moura seems to have been significantly fortified at that time, and this is the period to which the *tabiyya* walls which formerly surrounded the whole castle have been dated.  
The town still had an extensive Moorish quarter, largely destroyed by the construction of the walls in the 17th century. A population of market gardeners and craftsmen continued to live in this district, according to documents from the Late Middle Ages.
4d229eb0-4e69-5d2b-bc72-f2e57ec20ac5.short_description:
Moura Castle is a small settlement from the Islamic era (200 m by 120 m, approx. 2.4 ha). Its outer wall defended an inner space that appears not to have employed a hierarchical layout, similar to other examples in Portel, Castro da Cola and Serpa.  
The most important elements that have survived from Islamic times are a quadrangular turret, on whose main façade can be seen traces of lime-wash painting imitating large ashlars, and a stone commemorating the construction of a minaret in the middle of the AH 5th / AD 11th century.
4d229eb0-4e69-5d2b-bc72-f2e57ec20ac5.method_for_datation: The main basis for dating the wall – the only clearly identifiable element – is its typological parallel with other walls of *tabiyya* still existing in the Gharb al-Andalus. The chronology of these is contemporary with the building campaigns of the Almohad period carried out throughout the region in the second half of the 6th / 12th century.
4d229eb0-4e69-5d2b-bc72-f2e57ec20ac5.bibliography: Macias, S., “Moura na Baixa Idade Média: Elementos Históricos e Arqueológicos”, *Arqueologia Medieval*, no. 2, Porto, 1993, pp.127–57.
keywords: Moura; Almohads; hisn; tabiyya; Gharb al-Andalus; al-Faradi; al-Mutadid; military architecture
4d229eb0-4e69-5d2b-bc72-f2e57ec20ac5.author: Santiago Macias

4d56acb6-f968-5add-bfc8-034bceab6cd0.name: Glass weight.
4d56acb6-f968-5add-bfc8-034bceab6cd0.description:
A glass weight produced in Egypt between the AH 2nd and 9th / AD 8th and 15th centuries, which would have been used to check the weights of prototype gold, silver, and copper coins. A gold *dinar* would typically weigh 4.25 g and a silver *dirham* would have weighed 2.97 g. Metal coins were hand-minted and it was, therefore, difficult to ensure the exact accuracy of the weight; tampering with the weight of hand-minted coins was also a problem. Glass weights such as this one were developed to monitor the accuracy of metal coinage, and were used by the sellers to make sure that the correct vale of metal was being paid in return for the goods being purchased. The Arabic texts stamped on these weights usually bore the name of the ruler or official who ordered their issue and were usually re-issued every time the ruler or official changed office. This particular example is orange in colour and has a stamped Arabic inscription on one side (still to be deciphered), while the back is flat and plain.  
  
These glass weights testify to Fustat's position as one of the richest cities of the Middle East during the Fatimid period (AH 296–566 / AD 909–1171). A busy port, the markets of Fustat traded a wide variety of goods that arrived from all over the world, from places as far away as China. Fustat was also an important manufacturing centre, producing fine ceramics, glassware, steel and copper products, soap, sugar, textiles and paper.
4d56acb6-f968-5add-bfc8-034bceab6cd0.short_description: This glass weight was made in AH 5th- / AD 11th-century Egypt. Merchants and shopkeepers used such weights to check the weight of gold or silver coins, making sure that they were of the right weight and nobody had tampered with their precious metal. They were marked with the same designs as on the coins.
4d56acb6-f968-5add-bfc8-034bceab6cd0.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
4d56acb6-f968-5add-bfc8-034bceab6cd0.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: many comparable examples have been found in Fustat, Egypt, which have been dated to the Fatimid period after deciphering the scripts stamped on them.
4d56acb6-f968-5add-bfc8-034bceab6cd0.obtention: Donated to Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum in 1929.

4d7b079a-e0d0-5069-8f8b-a7c650770aed.name: Collection of mystical stories
4d7b079a-e0d0-5069-8f8b-a7c650770aed.description:
This manuscript is a collection of 39 mystical stories, poems and treatises written in Persian, Turkish and Arabic. Whilst there are no miniature paintings accompanying the written text of the manuscript, each chapter does however open with an intricately illuminated *unwan* (chapter heading).  
The contents of the manuscript include, among other things, *tafsir* (exegesis on the Qur’an), stories about mysticism, *qasida* poetry (an Arabic form of poetry, similar to the ode) and philosophical treatises on the Christian gospel.  
Whilst an exact date is known (1123 AH or 1711 AD) because it was clearly recorded in the collophon of the manuscript, a precise place of origin is absent in the written record.
4d7b079a-e0d0-5069-8f8b-a7c650770aed.method_for_datation: A precise date can be inferred with relative certainty because the last chapter of the manuscript closes with the words; "finished in the year 1123".
4d7b079a-e0d0-5069-8f8b-a7c650770aed.obtention: The manuscript was brought into the collection by Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall.
4d7b079a-e0d0-5069-8f8b-a7c650770aed.bibliography: Flügel, Gustav, *Die arabischen, persischen und türkischen Handschriften der Kaiserlich-Königlichen Hofbibliothek zu Wien*, vol. 3, Vienna: Verlag der K. K. Hof- und Staatsdruckerei, 1867: 489-501.
4d7b079a-e0d0-5069-8f8b-a7c650770aed.binding_desc: The manuscript is half-bound in red leather with ornamental gilding on the spine upon which the title of the manuscript is impressed in golden letters, reading "neun und dreyssig mystische Abhandlungen" ("thirty-nine mystical treatises"). The material used for the boards of the book itself is cypress wood. This binding was custom made for Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall.
materials: Ink on paper. Calligraphic *nasta‘liq* script of 27 lines per page.
keywords: manuscript; tafsir; qasida
4d7b079a-e0d0-5069-8f8b-a7c650770aed.author: Leonie Fernsebner

4d95a12b-05ca-5d85-bfaf-474830773927.name: Monkeys taunting a lion
4d95a12b-05ca-5d85-bfaf-474830773927.description: This single-page drawing of Monkeys Taunting a Lion is on a folio from a dispersed album. Ruled off in a pale blue frame decorated with golden trees, flowers, birds, and insects and trimmed down to a narrow frame ornamentation, the drawing is outlined in black and has line detail with some light grey shading. The subject of this drawing is not determined by a narrative text. However, it may have been inspired by an animal fable such as *Kalila wa Dimna* (Kalila and Dimna), which has a long tradition in Iran.\[1\] The artist was also likely influenced by the influx of Chinese styles, patterns, and motifs in the early 15th century.\[2\] The vogue for Chinese drawing and painting may have been the inspiration for this drawing, similar to the wild landscape with the struggling animals and dragon.
4d95a12b-05ca-5d85-bfaf-474830773927.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection

4da4dffd-186e-54fb-aa72-d606f46820ba.name: Screen in passageway of the Paço dos Infantes.
4da4dffd-186e-54fb-aa72-d606f46820ba.description:
The arrangement in the museum today was based on a design made in 1894, with the screen still *in situ*, by the artist Rosa Mendes Junior, the original of which is in the museum.  
This screen came from the south wall of the passageway which linked the ducal palace of Beja to the monastery of Nossa Senhora da Conceição, above the Viela dos Infantes alleyway,and has been reconstructed with great accuracy, although only some of the materials are original. Great care was taken in the reconstruction to rebuild one of the sections (the one furthest to the left of the onlooker) entirely using original pieces.  
The whole piece is made up of six small pillars made of brick, octagonal in section, which have grooves on two of their faces into which the pieces of terracotta are fitted. These pieces, three in each of four sections and seven in the other, are framed to give the whole screen a sense of consistency and to ensure less visibility and greater seclusion to any person in the passageway, with compact bricks in the lower part and upper part up to the ogee arches at the top which join the pillars to one another. Above these arches, the cornice is decorated with a scheme of arches grouped in threes (with greater emphasis given to the central one) and linked by a small dentil, imitating a Lombardy frieze. The overhang of the double pitched roof which covered the passageway is reconstructed above the cornice.  
Two of the sets of terracotta panels have quatrefoils, with the foils spiralling out from a central eye (like the sgraffito work of the S. Brás chapel at Évora, dating from around 1485), and in one of these groups, the one in the central section, the eye and the plant designs form openings to provide the interior of the passageway with natural light. The same happens with all the panels of the other three sections: two are ornamented with very stylised plant motifs and one (the one furthest to the onlooker's right) with seven sections on top of one another decorated with intersecting pointed arches.
4da4dffd-186e-54fb-aa72-d606f46820ba.short_description: This screen is all that remains of the palace that the Duke of Beja (future King Manuel I) commissioned around AH 890 / AD 1485. It consists of six small octagonal pillars made of brick and fitted with terracotta pieces. The passageway was demolished in 1895 and restored in 1927.
4da4dffd-186e-54fb-aa72-d606f46820ba.initial_owner: Duke and Duchess of Beja, Dom Fernando and Dona Brites, (infante and infanta). The screen gave the duchess direct yet secluded access to the upper choir of the Monastery of Nossa Senhora da Conceição.
4da4dffd-186e-54fb-aa72-d606f46820ba.dimensions: Height 322 cm, length 363 cm, depth 22.8 cm.
4da4dffd-186e-54fb-aa72-d606f46820ba.method_for_datation: As the nuns were relocated to this monastery in 1475, the passageway cannot predate that year. Master builder João de Arruda was working at the palace in 1485, which means that it is possible that his campaign of work included the building of the passageway. When the palace was demolished in 1895, architectural pieces were salvaged which match this screen in stylistic terms. The infanta, Dona Brites, died in 1506, and it is unlikely that she would have commissioned the building of the passageway near the time of her death.
4da4dffd-186e-54fb-aa72-d606f46820ba.method_for_provenance: There is a photograph and drawing of the passageway *in situ*. There are records of the dismantling and conservation of the materials which were salvaged from the passageway itself, some of which were used for the fairly rigorous reconstruction – the decorated bricks of the panels, clay bricks of the flooring, cyma mouldings \[type of cornice mouldings\], shafts, etc.
4da4dffd-186e-54fb-aa72-d606f46820ba.obtention: The passageway was demolished in 1895 and some of its materials were collected in the former Town Hall. The screen was reconstructed in 1927 in the museum, where it is housed today, which is the former monastery of Nossa Senhora da Conceição.

materials: Brick (in the supporting and opaque areas); terracotta (in the sections with ornamentation and openwork).
keywords: openwork screen; Mudéjar; duke and duchess of Beja; João de Arruda; palatial architecture; plant motif decoration; geometric decoration

4dac9cf9-671a-53db-afe9-db1a23d3b6cf.name: Preparation of Medicine. Folio from Manuscript of an Arabic Translation of 'De Materia Medica' of Dioscorides
4dac9cf9-671a-53db-afe9-db1a23d3b6cf.description: This is a single leaf from a manuscript copied in AH 621 / AD 1224 in Baghdad by Abdallah ibn al-Fadl, a well-known calligrapher, for a long time believed to be the author of the miniatures. "De Materia Medica" a treatise by Dioscorides, a Greek doctor, was very popular in the Middle Ages. The Khanenko Museum keeps a folio that depicts a process of medicine-making. Extremely trustworthy and artistically convincing is the manner used by the medieval artist in rendering ethnic features of personages, their gestures, clothing and various details of everyday life.
4dac9cf9-671a-53db-afe9-db1a23d3b6cf.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by V. Krachkovskaya (1926, origin), publication of H. Buchthal (1942, accurate date).
4dac9cf9-671a-53db-afe9-db1a23d3b6cf.method_for_provenance: Publication of Vera Krachkovskaya (1927): the Khanenkos' collection, publication of Hugo Buchthal (1942): former Fredrik Robert Martin's collection.
4dac9cf9-671a-53db-afe9-db1a23d3b6cf.obtention: Purchased by Bohdan and Varvara Khanenko in Paris, 1914, from Fredrik Robert Martin's collection. Donated by Varvara Khanenko in 1918, nationalised by Bolshevik regime in 1919.

4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.name: Bottle.
4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.description: A pear-shaped bottle made of stone-paste with a tall elegant neck and flaring mouth. The body of the vessel is covered in a spiral pattern of tightly coiled floral stems, painted in cobalt-blue and turquoise. The same floral scrolls run horizontally around the neck. Placed throughout the design are diamond-shaped medallions. The break between the design on the neck and body may have been intended to make room for a gold mount. The distinctive spiral pattern can also be found on Ottoman manuscript illuminations, particularly as a background for the *tughra*, the sultan's official monogram. The shape of this bottle echoes a common Venetian glass form. Its exact function is unknown.
4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.short_description: An elegant ceramic bottle with blue and turquoise underglaze. While the shape may have derived from Venetian glass, the spiral pattern recalls Italian *tondino* ceramic dishes. There are also parallels between the tightly coiled floral stems and Ottoman manuscript illumination.
4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.type: Stone paste blue and turquoise painting
4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.method_for_datation: This bottle can be dated to about 936 / 1530 due to its design which is similar to that of a cut-down bottle in the British Museum, with the same spiral pattern, bearing the date 935 (1529).
4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.method_for_provenance: This type of spiral decoration is known as 'Golden Horn' ware, so called because of the number of sherds decorated in this style that were dug up at Sirkeci on the southern shore of the Golden Horn estuary in Istanbul. However, this bottle was probably made in Iznik, the main centre of production for ceramics in Ottoman Turkey in the 10th / 16th century.
4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.obtention: Part of the John Henderson bequest to the British Museum in 1878.
4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.bibliography:

Rogers, J. M., and Ward, R., *Suleyman the Magnificent*, London, 1988, p.195, cat. no. 136.
materials: Stone-paste with blue and turquoise painting under the glaze.
keywords: Venetian glass; Italian influence
4dca8e78-1b75-504e-8688-364ab7e1d7f0.author: Emily Shovelton

4dcb82b4-7bfd-5da7-932f-7b81314a4d12.name: Mausoleum (*qubba*) of Taynabak al-Hasani.
4dcb82b4-7bfd-5da7-932f-7b81314a4d12.description:
Al-Taynabiyya is located in the Maydan al-Fawqani quarter (meaning the upper parade ground) to the south of Damascus. Maydans were originally open fields on the periphery of the city used for exercise and military training, which became settled with the expansion of pilgrim and merchant traffic in southern Damascus, a fact attested to by the medieval historian Ibn Asakir (d. AH 571 / AD 1176) who notes that the first settlements in the Maydan suburb took place during the Zangid period. Thus this section of the trade and pilgrim route, which heads to the holy cities of the Hijaz via the fertile Hauran Plains of southern Syria, began to be absorbed into the urban fabric of Damascus.  
As the area was considered auspicious, many *emir*s, including Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi (Saladin), desired to be buried there in order to receive the blessings and prayers of passing pilgrims. During the Mamluk period in the AH 8th / AD 14th century, urban development was rapid and the quantity of religious, social and economic constructions, such as mosques, *hammam*s, grain markets, and *khan*s, saw a marked increase. The most characteristic type of building to be found on both sides of the Maydan's main artery were the mausoleums (*qubba*); their polychrome façades and painted cupolas offered the suburb a distinctively colourful and picturesque character. Al-Qubba Al-Taynabiyya is one of more than 20 mausoleums to have been built by the Mamluks.  
The outer façade of the domed Al-Qubba al-Taynabiyya faces east. The monument is symmetrical in layout and constructed out of black-and-white alternating stone, in a style known as a*blaq*. The entrance, situated in the centre of the façade, is part of an elaborate niche that has a fluted mussel-shaped half-dome ceiling surmounted by a *muqarnas* arch. The niche is topped by a flat, protruding upper section. Beneath the *muqarnas* is an intricate square containing a Mamluk blazon composed of three parts: an empty upper section, a goblet in the middle section, a smaller goblet in the lower section and, between two lozenges, there is a a napkin motif. The goblet, signifying the cupbearer, is one of the most frequently used symbols in Mamluk heraldry, particularly since Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun's time (who ruled three times: AH 693–4 / AD 1293–4; AH 698–708 / AD 1299–1309; AH 709–41 / AD 1310–41), followed by the napkin, symbolising the table master. In this context it is difficult to identify any particular officer and often the use of a composite blazon can be interpreted as a generic status symbol. Above the two windows on each side of the entrance niche are rosettes of interlaced stone incrustations. The monument has two domed chambers: the southern one is a prayer hall, while the northern one houses the *qubba*, where the wife of the founder was buried in AH 798 / AD 1396, and later Taynabak himself in AH 802 / AD 1400.
4dcb82b4-7bfd-5da7-932f-7b81314a4d12.short_description: During the AH 8th / AD 14th century the Maydan area, an open field originally used for military training and located along the pilgrim route to the south of Damascus, began to develop as an extension to the city's urban fabric. It became increasingly attractive as a location for mausoleums and religious institutions, which would auspiciously receive blessings and prayers from passing pilgrims. Over 20 Mamluk buildings, distinctive because of their striped *ablaq* facades, elaborate entrance niches and red domes, are located on this road, the mausoleum of Amir Taynabak being just one of them.
4dcb82b4-7bfd-5da7-932f-7b81314a4d12.method_for_datation: The monument was dated by its portal inscription.

4dd47636-3e12-5dc6-a5e7-714bce7a0020.name: Canopy with lotus roundels
4dd47636-3e12-5dc6-a5e7-714bce7a0020.description:
A spectacular example of Indian silk weaving, this textile has possibly the widest loom-width of any known samite. A textile such as this, with a width in excess of 3 metres, would have stretched the effort and expense of drawloom weaving to their limits. Apart from the extreme technical difficulty of weaving a samite of this scale, the very high quality of yarns, dyes and workmanship suggest that it could have been woven only in the controlled production environment of a royal workshop.  
A textile of this size would have been used as a canopy or ceiling cloth for a congregation hall or chapel at one of Tibet’s Buddhist establishments. However, this particular example, with its abstract roundels, could have served equally well as the ceiling of a royal tent at any Indian court.
4dd47636-3e12-5dc6-a5e7-714bce7a0020.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art
4dd47636-3e12-5dc6-a5e7-714bce7a0020.method_for_datation: Date and provenance are based on stylistic and technical grounds.
4dd47636-3e12-5dc6-a5e7-714bce7a0020.bibliography: Jain, R., in *Textiles, Carpets and Costumes*, London: The Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art, volume 14, Part Two. \[In preparation / forthcoming\]
keywords: India; Mughal; silk; textile

4de66610-5115-59fb-9ce1-0f567da6ad1d.name: Convent of the Conception of St Francis.
4de66610-5115-59fb-9ce1-0f567da6ad1d.description:
Built on land belonging to the Galiana Palaces, work on this convent was carried out in two stages, the first between the 13th and 15th centuries and the second in the early 16th century. The complexity of the building accounts for the protracted period of time taken to complete it. The lower cloister basically accounts for the surviving structures from the first period, with its tombstones decorated with plasterwork that is a foundation for the study of early Gothic Mudéjar decoration in Toledo, and a reference for subsequent funerary sculpture. Of the numerous tombs, the one for Lupus Fernandi in the east wing stands out as one of the most exquisite of its type in Toledo. It takes the shape of a stilted engrailed arch crowned with a frieze of honeycomb and plaster work with digitate and ring leaflets, an Arabic inscription and intertwined motifs that are repeated in the intrados with 8- and 16-lazo knotwork. Running from left to right there are two protomes (upper bodies) of lions. The text about the deceased is an antecedent of the thinking that would become widespread in the late middle ages on the subject of mortality.  
The first convent church, probably erected in the 14th century, would have consisted of a central nave and two side naves with chapels. There is little left of the old chancel dedicated to St Catalina, which probably dated back to the first half of the 15th century and was covered with a Gothic egg-and-dart motif brick vault, or of the chapel of St Jeronimo, built by the merchant Gonzalo López de la Fuente and decorated in 1422, whose Manises-tiled plinth has been lost but whose vault covered with glazed clay and fired clay has survived. The tower and some of the brick arches are also Mudéjar from the time of the Franciscans, as are the arches and plasterwork of the sacristy, now located inside a chapel on the right-hand side of the church.  
Alterations made since the convent was handed over to the nuns of the Conception changed the original form profoundly. The most noteworthy Morisco-Renaissance work includes the plasterwork and tiles of several of the apertures in the lower cloister, the construction and decoration of the upper cloister and the decoration of several of the apertures in the Courtyard of the Aljibes (pools). Other buildings from the 16th century were already being built in the Renaissance style.
4de66610-5115-59fb-9ce1-0f567da6ad1d.short_description: This convent, whose outer walls follow the typical Toledan model of masonry with rows of bricks, still contains the most original Mudéjar vault: a hemisphere decorated with tiles (*alboaire*), in this case blue and gold. Its structure, also made of ceramic, forms an interlacing pattern now difficult to make out.
4de66610-5115-59fb-9ce1-0f567da6ad1d.method_for_datation: A tombstone, possibly made for Gonzalo Esteva, suggests that the first building was inhabited by 1280. In addition to this tombstone, cited by Amador de los Ríos (see Bibliography) the walls of the cloister contain those of the mayor Per Juanes (d. 1297), Arias Ferrades de Galliçia (d. 1304), Lupus Fernandi (d. 1312) and Johan Alfonso (d. 1345). The chapel of St Jeronimo, now walled in, has a vault with Manises tiles made by the craftsman Alfonso Fernández in 1422.

Amador de los Ríos, R., *Monumentos Arquitectónicos de España: Toledo*, Madrid, 1905, pp.353–77.  
Franco Mata, á., “Convento de la Concepción Franciscana”, *Arquitecturas de Toledo*, Vol. I: *Del Romano al Gótico*,Toledo, 1992, pp.481–7.  
Martínez Caviró, B., *Conventos de Toledo*, Madrid, 1990, pp.256–85.  
Martínez Caviró, B., *Mudéjar Toledano. Palacios y Conventos*, Madrid, 1980, pp.43–96.
4de66610-5115-59fb-9ce1-0f567da6ad1d.history: The Franciscans erected the first building, which must have been inhabitable before 1280. It was extended at the time of Queen María de Molina (*c*. 1265–1321) and in 1501 the order moved to San Juan de los Reyes. Queen Isabel I of Castile (r. 1474–1504) gave the convent to the women's community of the Conception, founded by St Beatriz de Silva (1424–91) along with the neighbouring convent of Santa Fe. It was founded in 1489 under the same dedication, but was subject to Cistercian rule. After the death of the founder and in light of problems caused by this dual obedience, they combined under the rule of the Seraphic St Francis in 1511.
keywords: Convent of the Conception of St Francis; Toledo; Mudéjar, plasterwork; protome; vault; knotwork; Manises tiles; glazed clay

4df720fc-29e6-59ab-9430-1945b274992e.name: Pair of earrings.
4df720fc-29e6-59ab-9430-1945b274992e.description:
The Fatimid period is distinguished by the development of precisely executed objects with high levels of decorative concentration. This is evident in wood, metal, and gold objects from the period.  
This pair of earrings is made from a gold web that is hollow from the inside. Each individual earring is in the form of a bird carrying in its beak a small gold ball. The loop provided for hanging the earring from the ear of the wearer connects the head of the bird with the rear of its body, making the arch of the bird's back straddle the earlobe.  
The earrings were made from gold wire carefully soldered together and accentuated with a few gold granules. The granule technique creates a light and hollow whole that is both aesthetically and practically pleasing. This technique was also used to create spherical or bi-conical beads that were then strung together into necklaces and other kinds of jewellery.
4df720fc-29e6-59ab-9430-1945b274992e.short_description: This small but meticulously executed pair of gold earrings is a prime example of dexterity in the technique of filigree. Birds were a favoured ornamental motif and the filigree technique maintained the lightness of the subject without compromising their opulence.
4df720fc-29e6-59ab-9430-1945b274992e.dimensions: Length (at longest point) 3.5 cm, depth (at deepest point) 1.21 cm.
4df720fc-29e6-59ab-9430-1945b274992e.method_for_datation: The production of this type of hollow, woven gold object was well known in the Fatimid period, specifically in the first half of the 5th / 11th century.
4df720fc-29e6-59ab-9430-1945b274992e.method_for_provenance: Although purchased in Raqqa, the method of production described above was associated with multiple sites in Egypt and Syria, such as Cairo and Aleppo. It is difficult to determine, therefore, a definitive provenance.

Seipel, W., *Schätze der Kalifen: Islamische Kunst zur Fatimidenzeit*, Wien, 1998, pp.119–20; fig. 76.
keywords: Earring; gold, woven; Aleppo; Cairo; Raqqa; bird
4df720fc-29e6-59ab-9430-1945b274992e.author: Mona al-Moadin

4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.name: Dish.
4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.description: A flat, circular brass tray with perpendicular walls. Minutely detailed silver inlay covers the base over a hatched ground. This is one of the finest examples of Mahmud al-Kurdi's work, combining intricate detail with a bold overall design. Radiating from a central octagon are pairs of crescents alternating with four oval-shaped medallions. The crescents and medallions float in a dense arabesque design, while even tighter arabesques fill the medallions themselves and the central octagon. A striking effect is created by the crescents that are inlaid with a solid strip of silver against a swirling arabesque background. The signature of Mahmud al-Kurdi appears in the four roundels that sit between the pairs of crescents. Al-Kurdi's work is part of a group of metalwork known as 'Veneto-Saracenic'; a style that is characterised by dense patterning, peculiarly European shapes and which often bears a coat of arms. It is probable that this tray was produced specifically for the European market and that it was for everyday use in a domestic setting.
4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.short_description: This brass tray is one of the finest examples of the work of master metalworker Mahmud al-Kurdi, with finely detailed inlaid decoration. One of a group of objects known as ‘Veneto-Saracenic’, often featuring dense patterning, and sometimes adapted to European shapes with European coats of arms.
4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.dates: Second half of hegira 9th century / AD 15th century.
4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.method_for_datation: The tendency towards more intricate patterns without figurative decoration is typical of 9th- / 15th-century metalwork in Mamluk Egypt and Syria, and also in Iran.
4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.method_for_provenance: The provenance of 'Veneto-Saracenic' work is still debated by scholars. In the 19th century it was thought that these pieces were produced in Venice by Muslim craftsmen. However, given the stylistic connections between 'Veneto-Saracenic' and Mamluk inlaid metalwork, it seems more likely that this tray, along with other objects in this style, were made in either Syria or Egypt where there were workshops that produced specific forms to suit the European taste.
4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.obtention: Bequeathed to the British Museum by John Henderson in 1878.
4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.bibliography:
Auld, S., Renaissance Venice, Islam and Mahmud the Kurd, London, 2004, pp. 219–20, cat. no. 5.1, (reproduced on the front cover).  
  
Ward, R. Islamic Metalwork, London, 1993, pp.116–7, plate 93.
materials: Brass engraved and inlaid with silver.
keywords: Trade; geometric decoration; daily life
4e024b5f-c870-54a0-abfe-e793ed34deb4.author: Emily Shovelton

4e4e72ee-c59e-5dac-bbc4-668eefd07742.name: Madrasa al-Zahiriyya.
4e4e72ee-c59e-5dac-bbc4-668eefd07742.description:
Sultan al-Sacid Baraka Khan, the son of the Mamluk Sultan al-Zahir Baybars, built a mausoleum (*qubba*) for his father north of the Umayyad Mosque and nearly face to face with the noteworthy Ayyubid monument, al-Madrasa al-‘Adiliyya. Although Baybars had expressed a wish to be buried in the village of Daraya near Damascus, his son chose the Umayyad Mosque vicinity where several former rulers were already buried, such as the Ayyubid ruler al-Kamil Muhammad (r. AH 635 / AD 1238), and his brother al-Ashraf Musa (r. AH 626 / AD 1229).  
The *qubba* is attached to a *madrasa* which was added at a later time. The *qubba* has a square ground plan, each side measuring 13.52 m, surmounted by two octagonal tambours with a pair of pointed-arch windows on every side of the upper drum and similarly styled windows on alternating sides of the lower drum. The domed construction shows a clear reference to the building in front of which it was built: the Madrasa al-‘Adiliyya completed by the Ayyubid Sultan al-‘Adil Sayf al-Din (r. Damascus AH 592–615 / AD 1196–1218).  
The upper part of the *qubba*'s outer wall is decorated with a round window, surrounded by a shallow, carved interlace pattern and two four-lobed cartouches. This is a new detail in damascene architectural ornament deduced from late Ayyubid marble decorations in Aleppo (see for example the Madrasa al-Sultaniyya (AH 620 / AD 1223)) and it relates to the décor on the main gate of the Mosque of al-Zahir Baybars in Cairo (built AH 665–7 / AD 1267–9).  
The entire outer-wall layer of the building is made of smooth and finely fitted limestone blocks. The 4.0-m wide portal niche includes three lines of inscription and is surmounted by a particularly rich *muqarnas* arch with a fluted mussel-shaped half-dome ceiling. Through the portal one enters the courtyard with the *qubba* entrance to the right. The lower section of the inner *qubba* walls are decorated with 3-m high inlaid marble panels, topped by a floral relief border with a vine (*karma*) frieze. Above the *karma* frieze, a 1.5-m high glass mosaic panel completes the wall decoration, showing a landscape with floral and architectural elements reminiscent of the Umayyad Mosque mosaics. By referring to the décor of the prestigious Umayyad Mosque, Baybars superseded earlier architectural heydays, not only in his political undertakings and monumental building commissions, but clearly also visible in his choice of decorative elements.  
Although the mosaics and the marble panels of the interior are ascribed to AH 680 / AD 1281 according to the portal inscription, it is probable that these ruined adornments of Sultan Baybars were reproduced accurately by his son. Some scholars have also suggested the employment of the same architect for the sake of an accurate redecoration.  
Similar glass mosaics and *karma* frieze decorations are found in the *madrasa* and *qubba* of Qalawun in Cairo, possibly indicating that Sultan al-Mansur Qalawun employed the same workshop as that used for the Madrasa Zahiriyya for his architectural projects in Cairo.
4e4e72ee-c59e-5dac-bbc4-668eefd07742.short_description: To honour his father, the highly esteemed warrior and first Mamluk Sultan al-Zahir Baybars, Sultan Sa‘id Baraka Khan erected a mausoleum next to the venerated Umayyad Mosque. The mausoleum is built as part of a *madrasa* and follows the common mausoleum layout, a square room with a red-painted dome on top of octagonal tambours. Internal decorations include marble panels, a carved vine frieze and glass mosaics, all of which show immediate inspiration from the Umayyad Mosque and show resemblance to the mausoleum of Qalawun, suggesting that this sultan employed the same workshop.
4e4e72ee-c59e-5dac-bbc4-668eefd07742.method_for_datation: The building inscription contains the signature of the architect. A later inscription, added by Sultan Qalawun, refers to the founder Baraka Khan's funeral in 680 (1281), and is certainly related to a later decorative phase and completion of the whole complex.

4e4e72ee-c59e-5dac-bbc4-668eefd07742.architects: Ibrahim ibn Ghana’im al-Muhandis who, a decade before, had built the Qasr al-Ablaq in Damascus for Sultan al-Zahir Baybars.

4eddb93b-3a9e-5dab-9508-a1c433de3f4b.name: Bottle vase
4eddb93b-3a9e-5dab-9508-a1c433de3f4b.description: In the second half of the eighteenth century the neighbourhood of Tophane in Istanbul saw the establishment of the pipe makers’ guild. Most of the then existing sixty workshops produced a wide variety of objects such as coffee cups, writing sets, goblets, decanters, carafes, trays, etc. The high-quality red pottery manufactured here was often decorated with silver and gold highlights. Some of the dark brown vessels, such as the present one, had silver-inlaid decoration. The surface of this long-neck bottle vase is divided into sixteen vertical compartments filled with silver-inlaid vegetal and floral motifs. Incised vertical grooves bordered by rows of stamped circular motifs separate the compartments. The stamped motifs as well as the precious silver inlays recall the elaborate decoration of metal vessels and jewels.
4eddb93b-3a9e-5dab-9508-a1c433de3f4b.holder: The National Museum of Art of Romania
4eddb93b-3a9e-5dab-9508-a1c433de3f4b.method_for_datation: Stylistic comparison with Tophane wares from the Medelhavsmuseet in Stockholm donated to the Museum after the 1873 Vienna World Fair.
4eddb93b-3a9e-5dab-9508-a1c433de3f4b.obtention: Transferred in 1949 from the National Museum Carol I in Bucharest.
4eddb93b-3a9e-5dab-9508-a1c433de3f4b.bibliography: Dunca, M., *Islamic Art at the National Museum of Art of Romania*, Bucharest: National Museum of Art of Romania, 2015: 108, no. 49.
materials: Earthenware, dark brown slip, silver inlays
4eddb93b-3a9e-5dab-9508-a1c433de3f4b.author: Mircea Dunca

4ee050c8-f860-5f8e-afca-7d0c987f64b7.name: Fragment of a dish
4ee050c8-f860-5f8e-afca-7d0c987f64b7.description: Fragment of a ceramic dish featuring a musician playing the lute (*\`ud*), surrounded by a jar and ewers with flowers and leaves. The musician’s garment is adorned with palmettes and his sleeves bear *tiraz* bands. Fatimid ceramics, such as this, often depict scenes from courtly life and provide valuable information on the painting tradition of the period.
keywords: Dish; Fatimid; Tiraz; Earthenware

4ef96a03-7d8c-53f4-abe0-2c7f030b251f.name: Dish.
4ef96a03-7d8c-53f4-abe0-2c7f030b251f.description: A white dish with a foliate rim, painted under the glaze with a floral composition. Blue tulips, some with red dots and red rosettes sprout from emerald-green stems which grow out of a blue-and-green 'shrub' at the bottom of the composition. The outer rim of the dish is filled with tightly coiled black spirals surrounded with blue and enlivened here and there with green, a pattern descended from the Chinese wave-and-rock pattern. The freely designed, quasi-naturalistic floral spray relates this dish to a number of similar wares thought to date from the early years of the reign of Sultan Murad III (AH 982–1003 / AD 1574–95).
4ef96a03-7d8c-53f4-abe0-2c7f030b251f.short_description: A white dish decorated with freely rendered floral motifs, including tulips and rosebuds, in the brilliant colours associated with the peak of the Ottoman ceramic industry at Iznik.
4ef96a03-7d8c-53f4-abe0-2c7f030b251f.method_for_datation: Comparison with similar objects of the period.
4ef96a03-7d8c-53f4-abe0-2c7f030b251f.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.
4ef96a03-7d8c-53f4-abe0-2c7f030b251f.bibliography: Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., *Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey*, Istanbul/London, 1989, pp.246–7.
keywords: floral decoration
4ef96a03-7d8c-53f4-abe0-2c7f030b251f.author: Barry Wood

4efddfdd-e8a3-5895-9f9c-d7247e51a06f.name: Portrait of an unknown scholar
4efddfdd-e8a3-5895-9f9c-d7247e51a06f.description:
This portrait depicts a calligrapher or scholar, wearing a white turban and with a red beard dyed with henna. Crouched in the corner of a simple room, lost in thought, he holds the mouthpiece of his water pipe. To his left, on top of a chest, a few personal objects include a pair of spectacles, a silver pocket watch, pencil cases, a book and a small glass vase with a bunch-flowered narcissus (*Narcissus tazetta*).  
  
We know almost nothing about the painter, Mirza Aqa, mentioned in the poem accompanying this portrait. The qualities of this work are due in particular to the pictorial technique used by the painter. The faithful, almost rough rendering of the face gives the figure a strong, penetrating presence. The play of perspective, light and shadow, and the realism shown by the painter can be found in other contemporary Qajar painters.
4efddfdd-e8a3-5895-9f9c-d7247e51a06f.method_for_datation: By comparison with similar dated works.
4efddfdd-e8a3-5895-9f9c-d7247e51a06f.method_for_provenance: By comparison with stylistically similar works.
4efddfdd-e8a3-5895-9f9c-d7247e51a06f.bibliography: Langer, Axel, “Portrait d’un érudit, ” in Gwenaëlle Fellinger (ed), *L’Empire des roses. Chefs-d’oeuvres de l’art persan du XIXe siècle*, exh. cat., Ghent and Lens: Éditions Snoeck and Louvre Lens, 2018: 244-245.
materials: Opaque watercolour and ink on paper
4efddfdd-e8a3-5895-9f9c-d7247e51a06f.author: Axel Langer

4f4aebf4-ad51-596f-8d75-02d79f90d769.name: Sphinx
4f4aebf4-ad51-596f-8d75-02d79f90d769.description: This sphinx was found in Rafiqa, Raqqa’s twin city, in 1924 together with the cock in the David Collection and the figure of a horseman in Syria’s National Museum. As ceramic sculptures, they are unique not only in Syria, but also in the rest of the Islamic world. They are fountain figures, and all have pipes to carry water up to the figures’ heads.
4f4aebf4-ad51-596f-8d75-02d79f90d769.dates: Hegira 2nd half of the 6th century / AD 2nd half of the 12th century
materials: Cast, modelled, and carved fritware painted in an opaque white and a turquoise glaze
keywords: Syria; Fritware; zangids; imaginary animal; zoomirphic imagery

4fd82ac8-dbcf-5a74-b304-99a394f55745.name: Djama’a ‘Ali Bitchine.
4fd82ac8-dbcf-5a74-b304-99a394f55745.description:
This is one of the Ottoman period's first mosques. It was built after AH 1032 / AD 1622 by 'Ali Bitchine, an Italian renegade who was originally called Picenino. In 1843, it underwent several transformations in order to adapt it to its new role, having been turned into a Catholic establishment under the name of Notre-Dame des Victoires by the colonial authorities.  
The mosque was built over rooms that were partially buried underground and over shops that opened out onto Bab al-Oued street, thus evening out the difference of levels that existed between the courtyard and Bab al-Oued street. The prayer hall is a large square area, covered by a dome, surrounded by a gallery on three sides (eastern, northern and southern) and by a double gallery on the western side (which today is partially destroyed). These galleries were covered by over a dozen small cupolas. The double gallery leads out onto a courtyard. The *mihrab* is built through a series of corbels onto the eastern wall and opens out onto the prayer room through a semi-circular arch. The large upper part of the square-based minaret, located in the northeastern corner, is missing, having been demolished in 1860. 'Ayn al-Shar'a (street fountain) flowed at the foot of the minaret, on Bab al-Oued street.  
The large dome has been underpinned: the columns that originally supported it were fixed into stone blocks, which in turn were replaced by concrete columns. Both the building's spaces and its volume portray characteristic Ottoman influence.
4fd82ac8-dbcf-5a74-b304-99a394f55745.short_description: This mosque, which bears the name of its patron, is one of the first of the Ottoman period. The square prayer room is covered with a cupola and surrounded by single galleries on the east, north and south sides and a double gallery on the west side leading to a courtyard, all crowned with cupolas. The corbelled *mihrab* looks out on to the room through a horseshoe arch. The square-plan minaret rises from the northeastern corner. The mosque has been modified on several occasions.
4fd82ac8-dbcf-5a74-b304-99a394f55745.method_for_datation: Citing Delvoux, G. Marçais, in *L'architecture musulmane d'Occident*, gives AD 1622 (AH 1032) as the date.

Bourouiba, R., *Apports de l'Algérie à l'architecture arabo-islamique*, Algiers, 1986.  
Cresti, F., *Contributions à l'histoire d'Alger,* Rome, 1993.  
Dokali, R., *Les mosquées de la période turque à Alger,* Algiers, 1974.  
Marçais, G., *L'architecture musulmane d'Occident*, Paris, 1954.

keywords: Religious architecture; commerce; water; corbel; Ottomans; Algiers
4fd82ac8-dbcf-5a74-b304-99a394f55745.author: Ali Lafer

4ff776a6-3eb5-5f3e-935c-a64b779f2d12.name: Arabian *qānūn*
4ff776a6-3eb5-5f3e-935c-a64b779f2d12.description: Trapezoid-shaped soundbox made of black painted wood, decorated with three gilt roses with foliage; as is typical for this instrument, the lower part is covered with parchment. The bridge rests on four feet and holds treble-chord gut strings (originally there were 19) attached to wooden pegs.
4ff776a6-3eb5-5f3e-935c-a64b779f2d12.obtention: The item belonged to the collection of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Este
4ff776a6-3eb5-5f3e-935c-a64b779f2d12.bibliography: Schlosser, Julius, *Die Sammlung alter Musikinstrumente, Beschreibendes Verzeichnis*, Vienna: Schroll, 1920.
keywords: Musical instruments; wooden decorations; floral motifs; floral decoration; arabesque; travel; musical instrument; Near East
4ff776a6-3eb5-5f3e-935c-a64b779f2d12.author: Beatrix Darmstädter

501785a0-9d3d-5517-9bcf-01c3e0ae7519.name: Bowl
501785a0-9d3d-5517-9bcf-01c3e0ae7519.description: This bowl has a central high boss and gadrooned sides. Vessels of this shape, harking back to antique libation bowls, were used in the Islamic world in the hammam or as magic bowls. The magic healing properties of this particular bowl are betrayed by the undeciphered symbols on the rim. Qur’anic verses ornament the frieze under the rim and the sides of the boss, while on its flattened top is inscribed, within a six-pointed star, the name of Allah.
keywords: Ottoman bath culture; Quranic inscriptions; Magical bowl

5025fcbf-006f-56e7-9dd7-22c514b328bd.name: Ceiling.
5025fcbf-006f-56e7-9dd7-22c514b328bd.description:
Remnant of a Mudéjar ceiling, with *alfarje* work (an Iberian decorative style), made from chestnut wood. It is profusely decorated, with pointed and intersecting lacework, forming eight-pointed and sixteen-pointed stars. The complexity of the central motif, widely known on *azulejos* (glazed tiles), gives this composition a very dynamic appearance. The exuberance of this motif was enhanced by its polychromy, and some vestiges of its gilding are still visible.  
The date of its production is known (1477) and it is also known that it was part of the campaign of work undertaken by the Count Bishop of Coimbra, João Galvão (1460–81), in his cathedral.
5025fcbf-006f-56e7-9dd7-22c514b328bd.short_description: Ceiling fragment from the upper choir of the Old Cathedral in Coimbra from AH 882 / AD 1477. It is profusely decorated with broken and interlacing knots, forming eight- and sixteen-pointed stars. Its varied colouring, some traces of which have survived, enhance the exuberance of the piece.
5025fcbf-006f-56e7-9dd7-22c514b328bd.method_for_datation: By written documentation (see Bibliography: *Notas. Museu Machado de Castro* and Vasconcelos, *Sé-Velha de Coimbra*).
5025fcbf-006f-56e7-9dd7-22c514b328bd.method_for_provenance: Documentary evidence – there is an account stating that the inscription of the date was visible on the frieze of the choir (see Bibliography: *Notas. Museu Machado de Castro*).
5025fcbf-006f-56e7-9dd7-22c514b328bd.provenance: Chancel of the Sé Velha cathedral of Coimbra.
5025fcbf-006f-56e7-9dd7-22c514b328bd.obtention: Taken down from the chancel of the Sé Velha cathedral in 1894, the ceiling was then moved to the Episcopal Palace, and put up in one of the rooms there. Given that the Museum now occupies this building, its incorporation into the museum is considered a transfer.

5032bffe-ba78-553b-bd60-df9e0091fb80.name: Dish
5032bffe-ba78-553b-bd60-df9e0091fb80.description: In Turkey, underglaze-painted pottery, produced for the Ottoman court and wealthy patrons, is renowned for its unique style of motifs and colours, once again widely admired in Europe. Mostly fashioned into dishes, bowls and drinking vessels, these Iznik wares were another major influence on Western ceramic production. This Iznik dish with composite floral motifs is painted in underglaze cobalt blue, sage green, manganese and outlined in black is dated AD c. 1540.
5032bffe-ba78-553b-bd60-df9e0091fb80.bibliography: *Islamic Arts Museum Malaysia*, Volume 2, Kuala Lumpur: IAMM Publications, 2009: 155.

507c8e53-6414-5d53-af15-cbb3861a2b67.name: Plate
507c8e53-6414-5d53-af15-cbb3861a2b67.description: During the last third of the 16th century, a type of floral decoration emerged in Iznik ceramics known as “bouquets with bent flowers”. Blue tulips, red carnations and a blue blossom spray nestle in asymmetrical arrangement around the plate. The graphic quality in the rendering of the blossom spray is admirably enhanced against the white background. Stylized wave motifs in the border pattern have almost lost touch with their Chinese source.
507c8e53-6414-5d53-af15-cbb3861a2b67.bibliography: Noever, Peter (ed), *Global:Lab: Kunst als Botschaft. Asien und Europa 1500-1700, Exh. cat. Museum of Applied Arts Vienna*, Ostfildern: Hatje Cantz, 2009.
materials: Quartz frit ceramic, decoration: underglaze painting and so-called tomato red
keywords: Ceramic; floral decoration; Iznik style
507c8e53-6414-5d53-af15-cbb3861a2b67.author: Mio Wakita-Elis

50900128-bb54-580c-9129-d9d24be9c5ef.name: Ten folios from the *Shahnamah* of Firdawsi made for Shah Tahmasp I
50900128-bb54-580c-9129-d9d24be9c5ef.description:
The ten folios come the *Shahnamah* made for the Safavid ruler, Shah Tahmasp I (r. 1524–1576). One of the finest illustrated Persian manuscript ever made, it has been referred to as the ‘Houghton’ *Shahnamah* after the collector who broke it up in New York in the 1970s. It is of large format, on fine gold-sprinkled paper, and with 258 illustrations. The format is independently conceived for each painting and must have involved constant consultation between scribes, painters and marginators. Folio 516, which in the Khalili Collection, is the only folio in the manuscript to bear a date.  
The manuscript was given by Shah Tahmasp to the Ottoman Sultan Selim II at the time of the latter’s accession in 1566. By 1903, the manuscript was in the possession of Edmond de Rothschild. It changed hands once again in the 1960s, when its then owner, Arthur Houghton Jr, began to disperse it. Today, some 140 of its paintings are in museums and collections throughout the world. The rest of the manuscript – the binding, the text block and 118 paintings – have been in the Contemporary Art Museum in Tehran since 1994.

5107fe4b-1985-514c-8253-6146fb963e56.name: Incense burner
5107fe4b-1985-514c-8253-6146fb963e56.description: The incense burner has a cylindrical body topped by a half-dome cover partially opened at the front. The lower portion is supported by four feet resembling animal legs and is divided into four panels by pairs of vertical grooves. The dome is also divided into two zones through the same pattern. The decorative repertoire, engraved in the body of the object and perforated in the upper dome to allow smoke to escape features animal figures and benediction inscriptions within vertical cartouches and medallions. It is a decorative style widespread in the medieval Islamic world, particularly in the 11th and 12th centuries.  The object could also be hung, as shown by the elongated ring with a small figure of a bird that stands at its top. The half-dome shape of the incense burner is inspired by architectural models and belongs to a widespread style in eastern Iran from the 10th to the 13th century.  Most of the known incense burners show only three feet. The object presented here is one of the few examples to have four. Using perfumed essences and aromatic substances to perfume rooms and for personal cosmetics is well documented in all Islamic territories during the Middle Ages through written sources and by various objects (burning essences, dispersants for perfumed waters, containers, etc.), made of different materials. Most often used in sovereigns’ palaces or in urban aristocracy residences, these objects were also used in religious buildings, usual in the Christian church. Since the first centuries of the Islamic era, incense became a very important trade branch. Great varieties of oils and perfumed essences, aromatic woods and herbs were available in special markets (Suq al-'Attariyin) in the main cities. Islamic craftsmanship therefore developed a production sector specialised in providing the tools necessary to meet this specific demand. Metal incense burners, in particular, are among the most valuable objects of Islamic artistic production.

5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.name: ‘Miletus ware’ bowls.
5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.description:
Inv. no. 3161: A bowl, the centre of which is framed by a circular band. Within it, dark-blue triangles are painted on a white ground. The points of the triangles meet, creating hexagons in the white space between them. These hexagons have dark-blue circles at their centres. The border is decorated with wave-and-rock motifs.  
  
Inv. no. 3174: A bowl; on a white ground, within dark-blue frames, stylised palmettes emerge from stalks, their centres filled with spirals. In the border, interlaced white motifs appear on a dark-blue ground. The outside is decorated with green spiralling tendrils.
5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.short_description: These two ceramic bowls have red paste, white slip and blue-and-white decoration. They are early examples of a ceramic group known as 'Miletus ware', which as a result of excavations at Iznik tile kilns is now known to have been produced at Iznik.
5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.dimensions: Inv. no. 3161: Height 14 cm, diameter 27 cm; Inv. no. 3174: Height 14 cm, diameter 34 cm.
5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.method_for_datation: As a result of the archaeological excavations at the Iznik kilns, many objects were found related to production of ceramics. These finds showed that ceramics variously classified as 'Miletus', 'Rhodian', and so forth were actually produced in Iznik, and they make it possible to establish a single classification and dating system for such wares.
5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.method_for_provenance: The bowls were found during the course of archaeological excavations at the Iznik kilns.
5124bb70-6aff-5029-9ff0-37a4fe33e513.obtention: The bowls were found during archaeological excavations at Iznik and brought to the Museum on 10 February 1967.

keywords: Ceramics; Iznik

512a98e0-b879-5c4f-8280-321140a92bdf.name: Alaaddin Mosque.
512a98e0-b879-5c4f-8280-321140a92bdf.description:
Built on an ancient mound, the mosque is named after the Sultan Alaaddin Keykubad I, who completed it. Its present state presents a distorted layout. To the north of the prayer hall is a wide courtyard. The western part of the south (*qibla*) wall is thicker than the eastern part. The eastern part of the prayer hall has seven aisles separated by six rows of columns that are different from one another because most of them are spolia. Both the western and eastern areas of the prayer hall have columns that are connected by pointed arches and both areas are covered with a flat roof. Where the rows of columns join the eastern wall there are wide engaged piers. The western part of the mosque has an even more irregular layout because columns were added to the west of the bay in front of the *mihrab*, as was the case in the eastern part, where the irregularity of the piers also points to repairs at various times.  
Traces of brick arches observed in the east and west walls in a north–south direction give the impression that these walls were formed by closing off arches. The present lateral lines of arches sometimes end at piers or sometimes in the middle of arches on the west and east. This is considered to be an indication that the eastern part, i.e. the original mosque, had aisles running perpendicular to the *qibla* wall.  
There are two portals at the north end of the mosque. The pointed arch of the eastern portal is surmounted by a knot-work motif in bi-coloured marble. This façade and the columned niches on it were built during the reign of Alaaddin Keykubad I. The wooden *minbar*, executed using the *kündekari* technique, and the *mihrab* decorated in tile mosaic, are noteworthy, for they reflect the fine taste and workmanship of the Seljuq period.  
There are two monumental tombs in the courtyard. The decagonal one was built during the reign of Kılıçarslan II. The (incomplete) octagonal one was probably built during the reign of İzzeddin Keykavus I.  
The structure was originally built as a mosque and is still used as a place of worship today.
512a98e0-b879-5c4f-8280-321140a92bdf.short_description: Alaaddin Mosque is built on an ancient mound known today as Alaaddin Hill. The two parts of the prayer hall point to important alterations in the history of the structure. Decorations on the northern façade and northern portal display Mamluk influence while the tile mosaics on the transition zone of the cupola before the *mihrab* and those on the *mihrab* bear characteristics of the AH 7th / AD 13th century.
512a98e0-b879-5c4f-8280-321140a92bdf.dates: Construction began during the reign of Sultan Mesud [Mas’ud] I (hegira 510 / AD 1116) and was completed during the reign of Sultan Alaaddin Keykubad [‘Ala al-Din Kay Qubadh] I (hegira 635 / AD 1237).
512a98e0-b879-5c4f-8280-321140a92bdf.method_for_datation: The structure is dated on the basis of its architectural properties and the repair inscriptions. There are several inscriptions in the mosque, especially on the courtyard walls. In these inscriptions, four Seljuq sultans are named: Mesud I (r. 510–50 / 1116–55); Kılıçarslan II (r. 550–88 / 1155–92); İzzeddin Keykavus I (r. 607–17 / 1210–20) and Alaaddin Keykubad I (r. 617–34 / 1220–37). Construction of the mosque was by order of Mesud I and it was added to and altered at various times. The tiles of the domed bay before the *mihrab* were made by Kerimeddin Erdişah in 617 / 1220, probably during the reign of İzzeddin Keykavus I or Alaaddin Keykubad I.

512cb99c-ea37-501f-9c8b-da383856d20e.name: Moulded bowl with *kufic* inscription
512cb99c-ea37-501f-9c8b-da383856d20e.description: This moulded, facetted bowl of fritware shows a large benedictory *kufic* inscription enhanced by rabbits, birds and a large crowned sphinx. Cobalt blue streaks accentuate the decoration in the well and around the outside. The delicate body material was intended to imitate Chinese porcelain. The bowl’s shape may imitate a contemporary metal vessel.
512cb99c-ea37-501f-9c8b-da383856d20e.dates: Hegira late 6th century / AD late 12th century
keywords: Bowl; kufic; inscription; calligraphy; fritware; ceramic; animal decoration; bird; imaginary animal

514a81db-7510-53f7-ac77-3b802711bb9f.name: Bottle for perfumes or ointments
514a81db-7510-53f7-ac77-3b802711bb9f.description: This green glass bottle has iridescent turquoise and pink patterning due to a phenomenon of alteration of the original material. Typical of the Islamic medieval style, the bottle’s elongated pear-shape is used for objects intended to contain ointments or liquid perfumes. However, no direct comparisons have been made between this bottle and other examples intended for the same use. Islamic glass from the Middle Ages was highly appreciated in Asia, Europe and the Mediterranean for its high level of technical and artistic qualities. As one of the most productive sectors of trade, glass was both a luxury good exemplifying the technical, formal and decorative innovations of the Islamic masters, and a practical object created to contain oils, perfumes and liquids of all kinds. For its modest workmanship, the bottle examined here falls into the latter category for everyday use.

5150b05e-b2e8-5539-a394-8b94a7f2c963.name: Castle of Aljezur.
5150b05e-b2e8-5539-a394-8b94a7f2c963.description: A fortification sited on the top of a hill close to the banks of the river of Aljezur, formerly navigable to the sea and close to the land route connecting with the region of Baixo Alentejo, surrounded by a maritime lagoon in a valley of well-irrigated fertile land. The Castle of Aljezur occupies an area of 57 x 54 metres. The structure has a polygonal plan, with a gateway facing north, defended by a semi-circular bastion. In its perimeter wall there is a second square tower, which seems to have been added at a later period to the wall's construction. The fortification was built from schist, a stone corresponding to the geological substratum of the region. Inside the castle there is a cistern of indeterminate date.
5150b05e-b2e8-5539-a394-8b94a7f2c963.short_description: An Almohad-era fortress located on the top of a hill overlooking the Aljezur River, once navigable to the sea, that runs beside the overland route to the Baixo Alentejo region. The site is surrounded by a lagoon within a valley of well-irrigated, fertile land. The castle has a polygonal plan with a north-facing gateway defended by a semi-circular bastion. The fortress was built of schist stone, a material available in abundance in the region. There is a cistern of uncertain date within the castle.
5150b05e-b2e8-5539-a394-8b94a7f2c963.dates: Hegira second half of 6th–first half of 7th century / AD second half of 12th–first half of 13th century.
5150b05e-b2e8-5539-a394-8b94a7f2c963.method_for_datation: The ceramic materials found in archaeological excavations and associated with the fortification are the main source of dating information. The hemispherical vessels enamelled in white, a honey-brown-coloured glazed bottle, basins and water pots made from light-coloured paste with stamped decorations and tall pots with incisions, have parallels with those from the levels of the 12th and 13th centuries from the Castle of Silves. Vessels with carination with honey-coloured glazed surfaces were also found in Almohad levels at Silves and Mértola.

51757aaf-3959-52b5-9501-f542549914de.name: ‘Keff’ or hand-palm amulet.
51757aaf-3959-52b5-9501-f542549914de.description:
A small, moulded glass 'keff' hand, which would have been threaded with many others like it to make a chain or necklace; it may also have been sewn on to a garment or a headdress. The main function of the keff is to protect the wearer against the 'evil eye' by stopping the damage that evil thoughts and deeds can do to the wearer. This hand is made of coloured glass, which has been cast into a mould. The loop has been made by twisting the base of the hand (the wrist area) on itself; the loop is at the front of the hand in the palm area, and once threaded, the fingers of the hand would point down.  
  
The keff pre-dates Islam and has been fully incorporated into Islamic popular culture, used widely as a protective charm throughout the Middle East and North Africa. Although the keff is particularly prevalent on jewellery it also appears on paper charms and talismans, on textiles and embroidery, and on vernacular architecture.
51757aaf-3959-52b5-9501-f542549914de.short_description: In popular Islamic cultures of the Middle East, small glass amulets such as this one would have been used both as decoration and for protection. The main function of the *keff* is to protect the wearer against the 'evil eye' by stopping the damage that evil thoughts and deeds can do to the wearer.
51757aaf-3959-52b5-9501-f542549914de.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums.
51757aaf-3959-52b5-9501-f542549914de.dates: Hegira, late 13th–early 14th century / AD late 19th–early 20th century.
51757aaf-3959-52b5-9501-f542549914de.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: many similar examples made of the same colour glass and of the same size exist and they have been dated to the Ottoman period and attributed in provenance to Hebron in Palestine.
51757aaf-3959-52b5-9501-f542549914de.method_for_provenance: Many similar examples exist attributed in provenance to Hebron in Palestine.

517b9478-f631-507d-9c9f-4381e1f51b61.name: Textile Panel
517b9478-f631-507d-9c9f-4381e1f51b61.description: Most of the textiles that survive from Fatimid Egypt, mainly fragments, were made or reused as burial shrouds and were preserved on account of the dryness of the Egyptian climate. This comparatively large panel may therefore derive from a funerary context; to compensate for areas of loss, it appears to have been pieced together in modern times from four parts of the same cloth, suggesting the original panel was once much longer. Its materials (bleached linen and silk), tapestry-weave technique, and bands of geometric decoration all mark it as a product of the Fatimid period. There are several bands of inscription that can be read as a repetition of “Help from Allah,” but because it lacks a royal or historical inscription, this cloth was likely made for a humbler clientele rather than for the ruling elite. However, it is otherwise very similar in style and manufacture to the so-called Cadouin Shroud (Abbey of Cadouin, France), inscribed in the name of the caliph al-Musta‘lī (r. Hegira 487-495/ AD 1094–1101).
517b9478-f631-507d-9c9f-4381e1f51b61.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
517b9478-f631-507d-9c9f-4381e1f51b61.dates: Hegira late 5th century / AD late 11th-early 12th century
517b9478-f631-507d-9c9f-4381e1f51b61.method_for_datation: Although it lacks an historical inscription, it is similar to the so-called Cadouin Shroud, inscribed in the name of the Fatimid caliph al-Musta‘lī (Hegira 487-495 / AD 1094–1101).
517b9478-f631-507d-9c9f-4381e1f51b61.method_for_provenance: The materials, tapestry-weave technique, and bands of geometric decoration mark it as a product of the Fatimid Egypt.
517b9478-f631-507d-9c9f-4381e1f51b61.obtention: Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mallon (1884-1975, and 1890-1968, respectively), New York, until 1947 (sold to); LACMA, through the Hearst Foundation Fund.

517f2c6d-9b8c-5c89-b704-834aeb01c0f0.name: Tiraz
517f2c6d-9b8c-5c89-b704-834aeb01c0f0.description: Textiles from the first centuries of the Islamic era survive mainly in the form of fragments, including *tiraz*, with their characteristic embroidered or woven inscriptions supplying the name and titles of the ruler. Such cloth was produced in state factories and was the exclusive preserve of the caliph. This piece belongs to the Tulunid period (Hegira 254–292 / AD 868–905) in Egypt, where most of the surviving *tiraz* were discovered. It is one of the largest such examples; however, the inscription is too fragmentary to be read.
517f2c6d-9b8c-5c89-b704-834aeb01c0f0.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
517f2c6d-9b8c-5c89-b704-834aeb01c0f0.dates: Hegira second half of the 3rd century–4th century / AD second half of the 9th century–10th century
517f2c6d-9b8c-5c89-b704-834aeb01c0f0.method_for_datation: The linen is undyed while the wool wefts are mustard, olive green and black, which are all typical of the Tulunid period. The letters comprising the *kufic* text are consonant with Tulunid architectural inscriptions as for example the wood inscribed panels from the mosque of Ibn Tulun, in Fustat, completed in Hegira 265 / AD 879.
517f2c6d-9b8c-5c89-b704-834aeb01c0f0.method_for_provenance: Most surviving *tiraz* come from Egypt, in this instance perhaps from a workshop of the Nile Delta.
517f2c6d-9b8c-5c89-b704-834aeb01c0f0.obtention: Collection of Maan Z. Madina (1926-2013), New York, until 2002 (sold to); LACMA, The Madina Collection of Islamic Art, gift of Camilla Chandler Frost.
