9b5d3d0d-e554-56aa-a4ef-440d5f3ce35d.name: Calligraphy mounted as album page
9b5d3d0d-e554-56aa-a4ef-440d5f3ce35d.description:
The page with calligraphy and a floral border originally belonged to one of the albums compiled for the Mughal ruler Shahjahan (r. 1627-1658). The border consists of two overlapping tendrils with reduced foliage and a few stylised flower heads (peonies, lotuses and rosettes). With their golden contour lines and colours which allude to enamel, they are reminiscent of the pietra dura inlay work characteristic of the Shahjahan period. The tendril is enlivened by pairs of naturalistically rendered birds. It is this interplay of stylisation and naturalism that is important for the aesthetic appeal and visual pleasure.  
  
The four-line calligraphy is the work of Mir ʿAli Haravi. Born in Herat in 1476, he became a pupil of Sultan ʿAli Mashhadi after his basic education. After the capture of Herat in 1528 by the Uzbeks, Mir ʿAli Haravi, who had achieved renown, was brought to Bukhara, where he worked until his death in 1556.  
  
Among Mir ʿAli Haravi's great admirers was Shah Tahmasp's nephew Sultan Ibrahim Mirza (1540-1577), who owned several albums of the master scribe's calligraphy. Subsequently, the other great collector was Shahjahan and it is quite conceivable that some of his own Mir ʿAli calligraphies had formally been in the possession of Ibrahim Mirza.
9b5d3d0d-e554-56aa-a4ef-440d5f3ce35d.initial_owner: Around 1987 Hashem Khorovani, Geneva, 1987-2004: art market, London
9b5d3d0d-e554-56aa-a4ef-440d5f3ce35d.method_for_datation: The border is typicall for albums that once belonged to the Mughal ruler, Shajahan. Their dating was established by various scholars in the past decades.

9b7dcb90-c55f-53d3-9cfa-d242f27958bc.name: Yusuf and Zulaykha of Jami'
9b7dcb90-c55f-53d3-9cfa-d242f27958bc.description: Chapter 12 of the Qur’an tells the well-known story of the life of the prophet Yusuf (Joseph). In the fifteenth century, the story of Yusuf’s encounter with Zulaykha (the wife of Potiphar) was retold and expanded, in verse, by the renowned Persian poet Jami’. The story is an allegory of the mystical search for union with the divine, with Zulaykha representing the longing of the imperfect human sole for the divine perfection of God, which is in turn represented by the figure of Yusuf. In the illustrations to the manuscript, produced about a century and a half after the poet’s death in AD 1492, Yusuf's status as a prophet is indicated by the flaming halo surrounding his head. The manuscript opens with an illuminated heading.
materials: Coloured pigments and gold on paper
keywords: illustration; miniature painting; calligraphy; script; illumination; floral decoration; arabesque; allegory

9b8ab3ff-1008-5ce8-b032-994aad3a8bf4.name: Fountain basin.
9b8ab3ff-1008-5ce8-b032-994aad3a8bf4.description: Oblong basin in grey marble. A sculpted decorative element consisting of two poly-lobed arches that end in serpentine motifs can be found at both ends of the cavity. The four cornerstones of the basin's edge are adorned with four full medallions. The cavity of this fountain consists of a hollow with a bordering edge. One of the two sides features an orifice that was once connected to piping. The basin's exterior form becomes narrower towards its base.
9b8ab3ff-1008-5ce8-b032-994aad3a8bf4.short_description: This rectangular basin is decorated with sculptures consisting of two poly-lobed arches finished with snake motifs. There are four full medallions in the four spandrels around the basin. This basin was probably used to provide water to the Palace of the Sea (Dar al-Bahr).

9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.name: Basin
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.description:
This basin was discovered in pieces at the end of the 19th century in the centre of Seville. Restoration work has reconstructed the bands of inscriptions, as well as the decoration on three of its sides.  
The front is decorated with three tri-lobed arches, framed by alfiz (frame) panels supported on columns. Each arch contains a plant sprouting leaves, palmettes, pinecones and intertwining stems. The space between the arch and the alfiz panel shows the same type of decoration, and the whole thing is framed by an inscribed strip.  
The right-hand side shows a space divided vertically into three parts. The central area is undecorated, probably to allow space for the water to come out, and the other two sides show similar scenes: eagles, seizing deer with their talons, bear two lions face to face on their outspread wings, while beneath them two griffins facing each other complete the scene. This iconography, of Sassanid origin, refers to power, abundance and eternity.  
Only the inscribed band is preserved from the third side, a strip with ducks and fishes, and, underneath it, the remains of a lion attacking a deer.  
We know from the inscription that this basin was commissioned for the royal palace of al-Zahira on the orders of al-Mansur, prime minister and favourite of Hisham II, who was still a child when he became Caliph in AH 366 / AD 976, following the death of his father al-Hakam II. The unstoppable rise to power of al-Mansur started shortly after the accession of Hisham II. With the intention of establishing a parallel dynasty to the legal Umayyad one, al-Mansur built a palatine city called Madinat al-Zahira. This new city, rival to Madinat al-Zahra, was in the eastern part of Córdoba, but limited material remains have survived to the present day. The city was burnt to the ground in AH 399 / AD 1009.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.short_description: Emulating the Umayyad caliphs who built Madinat al-Zahra, the hajib of Córdoba al-Mansur built the palatine city of Madinat al-Zahira, and he commissioned this ablutions basin for it, as stated on the inscription. Animal-shaped spouts would have emerged from the attached side pillars, of which only traces have survived.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.dimensions: Height 68 cm, width 150 cm, depth 77 cm.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.method_for_datation: The inscription in *kufic* lettering says: '…Almanzor Abi Amir Muhammad ben Abi Amir and glory to God. \[This was\] ordered to be made for the royal palace of al-Zahira and was finished with the help and assistance of God under the direction of the great Amiri Fata in the year seven seventy and three hundred'. Consequently, the basin has been dated to 377 / 988.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.method_for_provenance: There are two other basins attributable to the same period and place, one of which can be found in the Alhambra Museum, Grenada, and the other in Marrakesh (Morocco). This latter was made for ‘Abd al-Malik, son of Al-Mansur. The three pieces have similar decorations of eastern origin on one of their sides.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.provenance: The missing royal palace of Madinat al-Zahira (Córdoba), Spain.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.obtention: The basin arrived at the National Archaeological Museum in stages. The two most important parts, the front and part of one of the sides, were bought on 22 November 1882. Another fragment arrived in 1923. Finally, on 30 July 1930, the last piece arrived from the Provincial Archaeological Museum of Seville.

9b960e40-8e8e-58fe-bdb1-3947c5bce14d.name: Textile fragment with white ground with the Virgin Mary and the Christ Child, surrounded by angels, tulips, roses and honeysuckle
9b960e40-8e8e-58fe-bdb1-3947c5bce14d.description: The image on the textile is of Our Lady of Victories (*Nikopoia*); she is holding the Christ Child, who has his arms outstretched in a gesture of the Crucifixion. Fabrics with Christian motifs were woven in the Ottoman Empire for liturgical vestments of the Orthodox liturgy and exported, Russia being an example. The Christian motif is framed by plants of Ottoman origin, such s the tulip and the honeysuckle.

9b989b53-9b7d-5857-8fea-c5edf077c94a.name: Marriage contract
9b989b53-9b7d-5857-8fea-c5edf077c94a.description: Many verbal agreements guide the Muslims in their daily lives. By writing down these transactions, the words are safely recorded, preserved and thus made accessible to the rest of the world. Elegant calligraphy, the illumination of folios and aesthetic layout of documents were considered essential when producing a legal contract that bound two people in marriage. This marriage certificate between Al-Husayn II ibn Mahmud and Fatima bint Abdullah is dated AH Jumada al-Awwal 1240 (AD December 1824). The certificate is richly decorated with gouache heightened with gold on vellum, and inscribed with Maghribi script. Four large headings on the certificate were inscribed with *naskhi* script.
materials: Gouache heightened with gold on vellum

9b9b293c-0f7f-5225-8785-1a295c4c8c6a.name: Incense burner.
9b9b293c-0f7f-5225-8785-1a295c4c8c6a.description:
This spherically shaped incense burner has a very varied composition. The lid takes the form of a fretted dome, decorated with interlacing foliage elements and surmounted by an open rosette encrusted with coral. The lower half, in which the incense is placed, features the same ornamentation. The two halves are attached to one another via a hinge and a small chain, from which hangs a ball of coral. The entire piece rests on a round base at an angle, on gentle volutes encrusted in coral and decorated with stylised vegetal elements that alternate with damascened surfaces that stick out.  
The aromas of incense or of amber, burning inside on hot charcoal, escaped through the perforated lid.  
Used inside both homes and mosques during religious festivities, the incense burner contributed a pleasant aroma to the surrounding environment.
9b9b293c-0f7f-5225-8785-1a295c4c8c6a.short_description: Perfume burner with an openwork, domed lid crowned with a coral-encrusted rosette and attached to the lower part, where the incense was placed, by a hinge and a small chain suspending a ball of coral. On the base, the stylised plant decoration alternates with damascened areas.

9b9d46dd-31d6-5cf2-9ae5-d6821a180e85.name: Crucible / Melting Pot
9b9d46dd-31d6-5cf2-9ae5-d6821a180e85.description: This crucible is of special interest because of its decoration. The overall shape is like a bowl or a small cauldron. Around its rim is a simple zig-zag ornament, which seems to be fairly worn off. The inside is smooth but on the outside, the base is slightly drawn-in and then splayed to form the foot. Noteworthy is its overly long spout. In the back and on the sides are three rather large flanges with carved decoration. They are tear-shaped with two bird heads on each side growing out of it. Their eyes, and wings only in the back, are illustrated through carvings. The side ones show the knot of Solomon in the middle, whereas the one in the back features a blossom. Each flange tip has a small bump at its sharp end. It could be a variety of the so-called Khorasan-type, as it includes similar pieces with elaborate flanges on three sides.  Another similar piece is presented by Geza Fehérvári but described as a lamp.

9b9d46dd-31d6-5cf2-9ae5-d6821a180e85.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and through comparison

9bbd09d8-43b6-522d-b0ae-19223921613e.name: Batha Palace.
9bbd09d8-43b6-522d-b0ae-19223921613e.description:
Sultan Hasan I had this palace constructed and used it as a guest house for distinguish visitors and guests.  
Between 1912 and 1916, it was home to the services of the general residence of the French Protectorate, before they were transferred to the new capital Rabat. It was then converted into a museum of local art before becoming the present-day Batha Museum, a museum of ethnography and a cultural centre.  
The palace, a genuinely regal building, is imposing because of the space it occupies, the height of its walls and the beauty of its gardens (*ryad*). The wide main entrance, which extends into a double zigzag hallway, leads visitors to a wide expanse divided between two large buildings and a large garden. The garden, in the Andalusian style, occupies 58 per cent of the total area of the palace. Its size bears witness to the fact that the palace was used for pleasure and as a summer residence.  
The rectangular garden is enclosed to the east and to the west by a raised courtyard. An east–west avenue and a north–south avenue, both paved with herringbone bricks, divide it into four parts of equal size, each planted with trees and flowers. A fountain stands in the centre of the garden and gives it a sense of equilibrium.  
Along the north and south sides of the garden there are two galleries that give a good view of the flowerbeds. The porticoes of the galleries rest on 28 painted wooden columns. The ceilings are richly decorated with floral and geometric motifs outlined on the wood. Copper lamps of different shapes, reminiscent of the Orient, embellish the galleries.  
The east and west courtyards of the palace are rectangular and paved with marble tiles separated by *zellij* (small tiles) bands. Each courtyard is decorated with a pool linked to two polygonal basins. To the east, the courtyard is surrounded by a gallery behind which there are rooms of unequal dimensions that were used for storage. The west courtyard is surrounded on three sides by a gallery that leads to a number of very large rooms, decorated with *zellij* and covered with richly sculpted wooden ceilings.
9bbd09d8-43b6-522d-b0ae-19223921613e.short_description:
This royal palace stands to the west of Fez *medina*, in the Marinid expansion Fez-Jdid, near the Bujlud gardens. Started towards the end of the AH 13th / AD 19th century and completed during the reign of Sultan Mulay 'Abd al-'Aziz, it was used to accommodate the sultan's most illustrious guests.  
Later occupied by the services to the residence of the Protectorate, then converted into a museum of indigenous art in 1916, the palace consists of two buildings separated by a beautiful *riyad* (interior garden). Now restored, it is still used as a museum and hosts cultural events.
9bbd09d8-43b6-522d-b0ae-19223921613e.method_for_datation: Al-Naciri's *Istiqsa* and all historical sources date the start of the work to the reign of Sultan Mulay al-Hasan I, and its completion to the reign of Sultan Mulay 'Abd Al-'Aziz.

keywords: Palace; zellij.

9bbd279c-caa6-5b81-867d-5d87688d25b6.name: Dish with anthropomorphic moon.
9bbd279c-caa6-5b81-867d-5d87688d25b6.description: Dish with slanted sides and a ring-base. The decoration, painted in a typical red lustre, as was common in later Hispano-Moorish products, consists of a large rhomboid motif containing a circle whose profile, accentuated by a slight groove, serve to link the brim and the side of the dish. In the spaces between the rhombus and circle there are 'feathered triangles' made up of a series of thick, opposed, parallel lines, producing an effect similar to stylised leaves. The brim, the edge of which is closed with a think band of solid lustre, depicts typical leafy shoots with a central element that appears to be a large round fruit (possibly a pomegranate). The leaves are rendered with a characteristic series of curved parallel lines that evoke the idea of metal springs. Practically identical plant shoots (missing only the central fruit) are repeated in the decoration of the base of the dish where, beside a popular anthropomorphic moon motif, two characteristic 'grotesque lions' confront one another.
9bbd279c-caa6-5b81-867d-5d87688d25b6.short_description: This plate is attributable to late Hispano-Moorish production by virtue of its typical red-lustre decoration, which consists of geometric shapes and an anthropomorphic moon flanked by grotesque lions.
9bbd279c-caa6-5b81-867d-5d87688d25b6.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
9bbd279c-caa6-5b81-867d-5d87688d25b6.method_for_provenance: This type of decoration is fairly common in Valencian products from the first half of the 11th / 17th century and is used without significant alterations on a range of different objects (dishes, long-neck vases, handled jars, jugs).

9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.name: Persian miniature painting mounted as individual painting
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.alternate_name: Shepers and nobles greeting a prince and princess on horseback
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.description:
The miniature was executed with opaque watercolours and can most probably be attributed to the Safavid artist Muhammad Qasim. The rural scene is dominated by a princely couple on horseback being greeted by six men of different ages accompanied by four women. There are great stylistic and compositional parallels to the so-called Windsor-*Shahnama*, which was completed in 1648 and has been in the possession of the English Crown since 1839. It is suggested that the miniature was originally intended as an illustration for this manuscript of the *Book of Kings*.  
  
The border, richly decorated with arabesques, is quite probably the work of the Qajari illuminator Razi Taliqani. Such a conclusion has been drawn as it bares striking similarities to several comparable works by the artist that came onto the market in Paris and London at the end of the 19th/beginning of the 20th century. Such a proliferation of his work in Europe are the fruits born by his collaboration with Sidney Churchill (1862-1921) in the second half of the 1880s. As a civil servant of the British Empire, Churchill was then working in Iran. The mounting on thick cardboard speaks against its use as part of an album (pers. *muraqqaʿ*), which is corroborated by remnants of brownish paper on the reverse: a technique that was typically used to cover the back side of small Western picture frames, normally used for graphic art or photographs.
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.dates: Hegira mid-11th century / AD mid-17th century (miniature); Hegira late 13th century / AD late 19th century (border)
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.method_for_datation: By comparision with similar dated works, esp. the so-called Windsor *Shahnama* of 1648 and its partly signed illustrations as well as similarly framed objects from collections in Paris and London.
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.method_for_provenance: The object bears a stamp with the initials JR of the previous owner. There are similar objects with comparable borders in public collections in Paris and London which have been published and whose history is known.
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.obtention: Purchased with funds of the Rietberg-Kreis
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.bibliography: Carey, Moya, *Persian Art: Collecting the Arts of Iran for the V&A*, London: V&A Publishing, 2017.
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.artist: Attributed to Muhammad Qasim, died Hegira 1070 / AD 1659/60 (miniature); attributed to Razi Taliqani (border). Muhammad Qasim, active Hegira 1036-1070 / AD 1627-1659/60; Razi Taliqani, active Hegira before 1295-after 1327 / AD before 1878-after 1908/09.
materials: Opaque watercolour and gold on paper
9bc17d75-b39a-5d67-9e00-8637ff14285a.author: Axel Langer

9bc4738a-149f-58cd-8ef4-babead8e025c.name: Planispheric Astrolabe
9bc4738a-149f-58cd-8ef4-babead8e025c.description:
A planispheric astrolabe with a flat brass disk, a triangular projection at the top (*kursi*), and two suspension rings. Six plates sit inside it, held in place with an openwork star map (*ankabut*), which is fastened to the ruler on the verso with a horse that projects outward. This astrolabe is exact in scientific detail and contains the requisite inscriptions and tables without superfluity. The front of the instrument contains a movable star chart or rete (*ankabut* in Arabic), with 42 leaves pointing to the stars and with a smaller off-center circle representing the elliptic. Behind the rete is placed a brass disk inscribed with circles of equal altitude for a particular observer. Thirty nested circles, beginning with the horizon and reaching the point of the zenith, indicate circles of equal altitude on the sky, each three degrees higher than the one outside it. Additional arcs on the plate divide the sky in azimuth, and below the horizon parts of still more circles display the equal and unequal hours used for time reckoning.  
Because a plate applies to a particular latitude only, a variety of plates are generally provided; an unusually large number, six plates, each inscribed on both sides, are included with this astrolabe. Five of the plates serve for the following pairs of latitudes: 18 and 20 degrees; 22 and 24 degrees; 28 and 30 degrees; 32 and 34 degrees; 36 and 38 degrees (the designer omitted 26 degrees because no major town in the Middle East falls near this latitude). The plates for the latitudes of Persia (32, 34 and 36 degrees) have particularly elaborate decorations surrounding the inscriptions. The sixth plate contains on one side a typical "tablet of horizons" and on the other a grid of ecliptic coordinates.  
Underneath all the plates, in the so-called "womb" of the astrolabe, is a gazetteer containing the longitudes and latitudes of 46 towns; in addition it lists the azimuth of Mecca, and for the innermost series also the direction to Mecca.  
A moveable index for measuring the altitudes of the sun or stars, called an alidade, is fastened on the back side of the instrument; on this astrolabe the alidade is not decorated and is either unfinished or, more likely, a later replacement. Similarly, the "horse" that holds the alidade and plates in place is also a replacement. On the upper part of the back side, within the decorative bracket called the "*kursi*," a hole has been drilled for a magnetic compass, which is now missing.  
The entire back surface of the astrolabe combines calligraphy with a compact assortment of astronomical graphs and tables. The finely calibrated upper left quadrant gives sines and cosines, whereas the rectangular "shadow box" below the center yields tangents. The almost vertical arcs in the upper right quadrant show the seasonal height of the noon-day sun for various latitudes, and the nearly horizontal arcs give the seasonal height of the sun when it is in the azimuth of Mecca as seen from seven cities: Tus, Yazd, Isfahan, Qazvin, Basra, Baghdad and Shiraz. Semicircular tables on the lower quadrants consist of the decorated names of the zodiacal signs, flanked on the inside by the astrological "faces" and lunar mansions and on the outside by the astrological "limits" and the list of planets ruling each of the limits. Within this shadow box is a 4 x 10 grid of symbols exhibiting the astrological triplicities of zodiacal signs as well as the planetary lords of the signs by day and by night.
9bc4738a-149f-58cd-8ef4-babead8e025c.method_for_datation: Scholarly review and/or comparison to similar objects from the period.
9bc4738a-149f-58cd-8ef4-babead8e025c.method_for_provenance: Astrolabes were used for astronomical and mathematical calculations. This one is signed by two famous astrolabe makers who worked both together and separately in the Iranian city of Isfahan.
keywords: Astrolabe; Metalwork; Brass; Isfahan; Iran; Asia; Persian

9bcbd3de-c7a4-5e77-8084-66ab743c25b3.name: Large Persian basin
9bcbd3de-c7a4-5e77-8084-66ab743c25b3.description: This large onion-shaped basin was probably made in the early 16th century in Safavid Persia. It features the signature of the artist Shazi, “Amal-I shazi”, together with an inscription comprising parts of a poem by the poet Helali and verses by Halaki Herati, a less well-known poet from Herat, suggesting that the basin was produced at Herat, which was then part of Persia.
9bcbd3de-c7a4-5e77-8084-66ab743c25b3.method_for_datation: Arthistorical and historical analysis, archival and inventory research
9bcbd3de-c7a4-5e77-8084-66ab743c25b3.method_for_provenance: Listed in the AD 1875 inventory of the Münz- und Antikenkabinett
9bcbd3de-c7a4-5e77-8084-66ab743c25b3.obtention: From the k.k. Münz- und Antikenkabinett
9bcbd3de-c7a4-5e77-8084-66ab743c25b3.bibliography: Leitner-Böchzelt, Susanne and Pfaffenbichler, Matthias (eds), *Die Welt des Orients. Kunst und Kultur des Islam*, Leoben: Stadtgemeinde Leoben, 2006.
keywords: Furnishing; metalwork; Shazi; Safawid art; court life; Persian poetry; Helali; Herat; epigraphic decoration; inscription

9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.name: Door wings and a knocker.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.description:
Both of the wooden wings belonging to the door of the Ulu Cami (Great Mosque) in Cizre were clad in sheets of bronze and then decorated with brass strips and plates attached with iron nails. The border band has a decoration of quatrefoils fitted using round-headed nails. Each wing has three medallions, each with a 12-pointed star in the centre. The areas in between are filled with half-medallions that make up two half- and two full-medallions along the join when the wings are shut. The spaces in between the medallions and the geometric motifs are filled with metal plates decorated with arabesque-palmette motifs in openwork. Traces of pigment suggest that the background of these motifs was originally painted in red and blue to make them stand out more boldly. The half- and quarter-medallions along the outer edges of the door wings imply that the composition extends to infinity. Near the centre of the door wings are two loops for mounting the knockers, one of which is now on display in Copenhagen. The cast bronze knocker still on the door is formed of two symmetrical dragons that are engraved and which join at the centre with a lion's head. The dragons, have pointed ears, almond eyes and wings; their scaly bodies loop around in a spiral to form knots, and their tails join and end in eagle's heads.  
  
On the upper portion of the door wings is an inscription frieze with cast bronze letters. As some letters are missing, the inscription cannot be read in full. The legible part reads: 'May Allah give power to Abul Kasım Mahmud Sanjar Shah, our lord'. The person mentioned is the atabeg of Cizre, Mahmud Sanjar Shah, who ruled from AH 605–39 / AD 1208–41.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.short_description: Magnificent portals of monumental mosques symbolise the gates of Paradise. The naming of the sultan, geometric decoration symbolising infinity on the door-wings and the dragon and lion motifs on the doorknockers are an expression not only of the divine power of God but also of the power of the sultan.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.initial_owner: Mahmud Sanjar Shah (AH 605–639 / AD 1208-1241), atabeg of Cizre, from the Artuqid dynasty.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.dimensions: Door wings: each, height 300 cm, width 112 cm (224 cm in total); knocker: height 27.5 cm; width 24 cm, depth 3 cm.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.method_for_datation: The patron was the atabeg of Cizre, Mahmud Sanjar Shah, who ruled from 605–639 / 1208–41. It is likely that the knockers were produced together with the wings for the door of the Ulu Cami (Great Mosque) in Cizre, itself built in 550 / 1155.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.method_for_provenance: The door wings and knockers were specially prepared for the door of the Ulu Cami (Great Mosque) in Cizre. Thus, it is highly likely that they were produced in Cizre or in southeastern Anatolia.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.obtention: The door wings and knocker were transferred to the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts from the Mardin Museum in 1976.
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.bibliography:
ölçer, N. *et al*, *Museum of Turkish and Islamic Art*, Istanbul, 2002, pp.95–7.  
  
Roxburgh, D. J. (ed), *Turks: A Journey of a Thousand Years, 600–1600*, London, 2005, pp.399–400.
materials: Door wings: wood (walnut and poplar), metal (bronze and brass), openwork; knocker: cast and engraved bronze.
keywords: Figurative decoration; geometric decoration; vegetal decoration
9beb3626-1910-5e59-a90a-ae27e1cb3c8d.author: Alev Özay

9bf8a3f3-f2b5-587e-9b91-0d1241828349.name: Spherical bottle.
9bf8a3f3-f2b5-587e-9b91-0d1241828349.description:
A spherical bottle made of thick, grey-yellow glass with a short opening. Its body is completely covered with decoration that has been cut and deeply engraved into its surface. The decoration consists of a main frieze in which medallions with peacocks and with plant-motifs alternate. Minor side friezes adorn the body. The bottle’s stopper, with which its short opening would have been closed, appears to be missing.  
The bottle’s carefully incised patterns, along with the stylisation of the peacocks and of the ornamentation, find a parallel in the exceptional rock-crystal receptacles that were made in Egypt during the Fatimid era, and which were brought over to Europe after the dissolution of Fatimid treasures. It is therefore possible that this spherical bottle was made by a workshop in Egypt that possessed the knowledge of how to work with, and decorate, rock-crystal. The bottle’s quality suggests that the person who commissioned its making was a member of the court. Its form is similar to that of spherical ceramic vessels known as a ‘sphero-conical vessels’. There is no available information regarding its past use, but, given its workmanship, it must have contained something equally precious.
9bf8a3f3-f2b5-587e-9b91-0d1241828349.short_description: This unique bottle of thick glass is adorned with a deeply cut frieze in which triangles with ornamental patterns alternate with birds in medallions. Fatimid Egypt was famous for its glass and especially rock-crystal vessels, which were highly esteemed in Europe where many survived in treasuries.
9bf8a3f3-f2b5-587e-9b91-0d1241828349.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
9bf8a3f3-f2b5-587e-9b91-0d1241828349.method_for_datation: Dating the object with accuracy is very difficult as few close parallels exist. Only a general date can be offered to place it within the Fatimid period.
9bf8a3f3-f2b5-587e-9b91-0d1241828349.method_for_provenance: Stylistic comparison to polished glasswork from the excavations in Fustat, Cairo’s old town, as well as the particular colouring of the glass, suggest that the object probably came from Egypt. Only new research or new findings will add further information.
9bf8a3f3-f2b5-587e-9b91-0d1241828349.bibliography:

Kröger, J., “From Fustat to Nishapur: Questions about Fatimid Cut Glass”, in *L’Egypte Fatimide: Son Art et Son Histoire* (ed. M. Barrucand), Paris, 1999, pp.219–32.

9c0d7e7b-502c-5d62-8588-ba4d3901df58.name: Camel figurine
9c0d7e7b-502c-5d62-8588-ba4d3901df58.description: The pottery of Dhofar is, like the region itself, quite distinct from the rest of the country in terms of form, producer and technique. Dhofari pottery can be broadly divided between Salalah ware and the combined ware of the coastal villages of Taqah and Mirbat. The key differences noted are the type of clay used and the featured stylistic forms. The simple terracotta camel figures made in the coastal villages of Dhofar bear a resemblance to pre-Islamic forms. However, modern potters attach neither spiritual nor religious significance to their use of ancient forms. Beyond their use as decorative objects, spiritual and religious significance has long since been lost in time.
keywords: Figurine; Camel; Terracota; Dhofar

9c229c05-ca31-5b40-81ef-a242c176e646.name: Staghorn animal composite
9c229c05-ca31-5b40-81ef-a242c176e646.description: This rare stag horn sculpture would have been used during royal processions. It acted as a counterweight on the lace fabric used to carry a sword or a powder horn. It was produced during the Mughal period. Animals with gold-inlaid eyes are carved on its surface. The animals in the centre carving are felines, bears or *nilgais* (blue bulls). This horn is an outstanding example of the Indo-Islamic style of figurative representation. The stylised animal motifs are probably derived from book designs.
9c229c05-ca31-5b40-81ef-a242c176e646.bibliography: *Stiftung für die Hamburger Kunstsammlungen: Erwerbungen 2013-2014*, Hamburg: Stiftung für die Hamburger Kunstsammlungen, 2015.
keywords: Mughal; horn

9c3ba099-689c-55c4-bac9-756e88089561.name: Mosque and Madrasa of Amir Sarghatmish.
9c3ba099-689c-55c4-bac9-756e88089561.description:
This building contains a mosque, *madrasa* and a mausoleum. The *madrasa* was designated to teach the Hanafi School of *fiqh* – one of the four *Sunni* schools – and became a refuge for Hanafi Ulama, especially the Persians among them. Historians mention, in fact, that the patron, Amir Sarghatmish, was very close to Persian scholars and revered them to the point of excess.  
The principle (northwestern) façade of the building overlooks the street. A dome tops the mausoleum on the southern end of the façade. This dome was built in the manner of Samarkand (Persian) domes, as it is of an elongated bulbous shape, with a high drum, built from brick. It is composed of an outer shell and an inner one. The southern façade is composed of a portal within a recess, which is crowned by an arch, and topped by a semi-circular domed ceiling, below which are *muqarnas*. This entrance is reminiscent of the portal into Madrasa al-Tashtamuriyya (built AH 782 / AD 1381) in the city of Jerusalem. On the left of the entrance is a slender minaret built of stone whose height measures 40 m, and which consists of three stories crowned by a carved dome. The second, octagonal, storey is decorated with an inlaid casing of red and white stone that is arranged in a geometric pattern made up of zigzag lines that assume the form of a linked chain of V-shaped letters. Minarets of this period are distinguishable by this particular decorative style, a further example of which may be seen in the minarets of the Mosque and the Khanqah of Amir Shaykhu which are located close to this building.  
The design of the building follows the plan of cruciform, or cross-shaped, *madrasa*s. The floor-plan consists of four *iwan*s, arranged around an open courtyard, in the middle of which is a fountain. The *qibla iwan* (southeastern) is composed of singular architectural ornamental components. There is a dome with a high drum that covers the central section of the *iwan* and which, although it is lower, resembles the dome of the mausoleum. The dome in the *qibla iwan* is older than that in the mausoleum and is said to be the oldest dome on top of a *madrasa mihrab* extant in Egypt. It collapsed and was restored in 1940 to its original form. On the walls on the two sides of the *mihrab*, there are still remnants of revetment composed of marble panels containing the blazon and titles of the Amir Sarghatmish. There is another panel that contains leafy decoration and clusters of grapes and vine leaves. Nine panels of wall revetment from the *qibla iwan* were transferred to the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo.  
There are clear Persian influences in the building, exemplified in the shapes of the domes, the decoration on the wall revetment of the *qibla iwan*, and of course the known interest of the building's sponsor in Persian arts and culture, along with his high regard for Persian people. These observations allow the assumption that the architect of this building was a Persian.
9c3ba099-689c-55c4-bac9-756e88089561.short_description: This monument is situated beside Ibn Tulun Mosque. The site once stood within the Tulunid city of Qata'i. The building comprises a mosque, a mausoleum and a *madrasa* to teach the Hanafi school of jurisprudence. Persian influences are evident in the mausoleum dome, which is bulb-shaped with a long neck, and in the ornamental components of the *qibla iwan*.
9c3ba099-689c-55c4-bac9-756e88089561.address: The monument is located on Saliba Street, in the Sayyida Zaynab district. It is adhered to the northwestern extension (*ziyada*) of the Mosque of Ibn Tulun.
9c3ba099-689c-55c4-bac9-756e88089561.method_for_datation: The building was dated based on an inscription band located at either side of the portal, which includes the name of the sponsor and the date of construction.
9c3ba099-689c-55c4-bac9-756e88089561.bibliography:

Creswell, K. A. C., *Muslim Architecture of Egypt*, Vol. II, Oxford, 1960.  
Al-Maqrizi, *Al-mawā'iz wa'l-i'tibār bi-dhikr al-khiţaţ wa'l-āthār \[Exhortations and Contemplation of the Recollection of Plans and Monuments*\], 2 Vols, Cairo, 1853.  
Salem, al-Sayyed Mahmoud Abd al-Aziz, *al-Ma'din al-Masriya – Nazra 'Amma 'an aslaha wa tatawuriha mundu al-fath al-'arabi hatta al-fath al-Othmani \[The Egyptian Minaret – A General View of its Origin and Development from the Arab Conquest until the Ottoman Conquest*\], Cairo, 1959.

9c626e5e-abec-533c-b33a-b1bcd38e5849.name: Coin Inscribed with Declaration of Faith
9c626e5e-abec-533c-b33a-b1bcd38e5849.description:
The Declaration of Faith is one of the five pillars of Islam and provides a foundation for all other Islamic beliefs and practices. In translation, it usually reads, "There is no God but Allah and Muhammed is His Messenger".’ This message was often conveyed on coins such as the one shown in this exhibit.  
  
In the centuries before the arrival of Islam, 200 BC-651AD, many rulers, dynasties and powers issued coins that circulated in Oman and the Arabian Gulf. Coins made in Oman 133-906 AH / 751 - 1500 AD also demonstrated a means of displaying power, status and independence. Local rulers issued their own currency from as early as 174 AH / 791 AD.  
  
Followers of Ibadism (a branch of Islam) established an Imamate (a unique governing system based on electing a person known for his knowledge and piety) in Oman in 132 AH / 749 AD. The Ibadi imams issued their own silver coins, many of which were found in a hoard discovered in 1422 AH / 2002 AD in the Wilayet of Buhla. The coins carry the mint name "Uman", and the names of the Ibadi rulers " al-khalil bin Shadhan" and " Rashid bin Said".  
  
The Wajihids, a local dynasty led by Yusuf bin Wajih, a former Abbasaid governor based in Oman, took control of the northern coastal regions of Oman during the 4th century AH / 10 century AD, developing the town of Sohar into a major centre of international commerce and producing their own currency. Coins issued by the Wajihids kept the standard Abbasid inscription, with the name of their local governor added below the inscription on the reverse.  
  
Trade in southern Arabia centred on the Yemen port of Aden, from where many Ayyubid dinars made their way to Oman. Meanwhile, the kings of Hormuz (in modern- day Oman and Iran) competed for trade along the coast of Iran. Small gold and silver Hormuzi coins became the most important currency in Oman during this period.
9c626e5e-abec-533c-b33a-b1bcd38e5849.obtention: Ministry of Heritage and Culture Collection
9c626e5e-abec-533c-b33a-b1bcd38e5849.artist: Issued by Nasr bin Ahmed Samani
keywords: Coins; Currency; Numismatics; Abbasid; Hurmuz

9c700bb2-5d48-5ba0-9ba7-87bc128ebc4e.name: Capital.
9c700bb2-5d48-5ba0-9ba7-87bc128ebc4e.description:
The decoration on the acanthus capital clearly demonstrates that the capital is based on examples from Antiquity. It has two wreaths of leaves and four volutes that run diagonally. Over the volutes lies the abacus, the top slab of the capital. The volutes end in four-petalled blossoms. Acanthus leaves cover the protruding volutes. The leaves terminate under the abacus and appear to be holding it up. On top of the abacus one can see an architectural design that was obviously drawn using square and compasses. An inscription, encircling the abacus, refers to the capital’s artists, patron and builders.  
This explicit reference to the craftsmen and builders involved in the building is exceptional for buildings of this period. Abd al-Rahman III (AH 300–50 / AD 912–61) is referred to in the inscription: ‘In the name of God, a blessing from God for the leader of the believers. May God endow Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad with a long life’. Later it declares: ‘\[This forms part of what\] he commissioned to be executed under the direction of his slave Shunaif, made by Fath, the marble specialist’. Shunaif was the foreman, and Fath was identified for the first time in an inscription on a building in AH 318 / AD 930. He had originally been a slave in the court of the caliphs and was not of Arab descent. As is testified by numerous building inscriptions, Fath worked over decades on various Caliphate buildings in Andalusia. His name is also associated with the enlargement of the great mosque in Córdoba and the castle complex of Madinat al-Zahra. It is not possible to determine whether this capital comes from one of these architectural complexes. However, it has been determined that the foreman Shunaif worked on the Salon Rico, the reception hall of Madinat al-Zahra in AH 342–3 / AD 953–4. Abd al-Rahman had declared himself Caliph of the western Islamic world in AH 317 / AD 929.  
Acanthus capitals were also symbols of wealth and of immortality, ever since their use from the 5th century BC in Ancient Greece. The acanthus thistle, with its opulent and thick, well-defined leaf margins was therefore a popular decorative form also employed in the Greek provinces such as Spain.
9c700bb2-5d48-5ba0-9ba7-87bc128ebc4e.short_description: Marble capitals with ornament influenced by the Classical period were used in the palaces of the Umayyad rulers in al-Andalus. Although some capitals have inscriptions it is exceptional to find the names of the patron, the overseer and the marble-worker who chiselled the capital out of a marble block.
9c700bb2-5d48-5ba0-9ba7-87bc128ebc4e.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
9c700bb2-5d48-5ba0-9ba7-87bc128ebc4e.dates: Hegira mid-4th century / AD mid-10th century (AH 300–50 / AD 912–61).
9c700bb2-5d48-5ba0-9ba7-87bc128ebc4e.dimensions: Height 33 cm, diameter of the abacus 31 cm.
9c700bb2-5d48-5ba0-9ba7-87bc128ebc4e.method_for_datation: The object has been dated to between 300 and 350 / 912 and 961 through the inscription dedicated to the Caliph Abd al-Rahman III and citing the name of Fath the craftsman.
9c700bb2-5d48-5ba0-9ba7-87bc128ebc4e.method_for_provenance: The provenance from the Caliphate of Córdoba, Spain has been securely established through the inscription citing to Caliph Abd al-Rahman III.
9c700bb2-5d48-5ba0-9ba7-87bc128ebc4e.obtention: From a gallery in New York.

9c9255a5-9a88-5f13-953c-48f2830112c9.name: Ottoman official document containing the *Tughra*
9c9255a5-9a88-5f13-953c-48f2830112c9.description: The Ottoman Sultan's certificate presents an expressive, secular form of calligraphy. It is crowned by the ornate, triangular seal of the Sultan, the *tughra*. Here, it is the *tughra* of Sultan Mahmud I (1730-1754). The lines are written narrowly in gold, black and, red ink and each one is written in an upward curve to prevent the possibility of forgery. Official, ornamentally decorated documents, such as this one, would hang in offices or private houses and served as status symbols.
9c9255a5-9a88-5f13-953c-48f2830112c9.method_for_datation: Inscription mentions Sultan Mahmud I (1730-1754) and date Hegira 1150 / AD 1737.
keywords: Calligraphy

9c99c966-ce63-54c0-ab28-822914e17003.name: Madrasa al-Jaqmaqiyya.
9c99c966-ce63-54c0-ab28-822914e17003.description:
The Madrasa al-Jaqmaqiyya was built opposite the north entrance to the Umayyad Mosque, by order of the then Governor of Damascus, Sayf al-Din Jaqmaq al-Arghunshawi. It was constructed on the foundations of the former school for orphans, the Maktab al-Nasir Hasan, founded in AH 762 / AD 1361, and was completed and turned into a convent in AH 769 / AD 1367. The building re-used decorative elements of the previous monument that was destroyed by Timur's attack on Damascus in AH 803 / AD 1401. Jaqmaq enlarged the former building southward by constructing a *turbe* (mausoleum) and re-instating a *maktab* (orphanage). He also added windows to the north façade.  
The *madrasa* has a rectangular plan measuring 20 m x 17.5 m. It has a two-aisled room with a covered square courtyard. Like the Taurizi Mosque in Damascus (built AH 823–6 / AD 1420–3), and the Mausoleum of al-Ashraf Barsbay in Cairo (completed AH 828 / AD 1425), it is an example of a mosque with a covered courtyard, in contrast to the formerly common *riwaq*\-type mosque that followed the example of the Umayyad Mosque of Damascus. The covered courtyard became typical of Mamluk *madrasas* in Syria.  
During the Mamluk period, the major cities of Aleppo and Damascus adopted features of imperial architecture developed in Cairo, although in each city these were adapted in different ways and developed into a characteristic style. The *madrasa*s outer walls are decorated in black-and-white stone alternating in rows, a decorative technique known as *ablaq*, and a typical architectural feature of Damascene architecture. The high niche with elaborate masonry, seen also on the façade, is exceptional and represents a very early example belonging to the first construction phase of AH 762 / AD 1361. This feature was skilfully developed and attributed to many buildings in Aleppo and occurs frequently from the beginning of the AH 9th / AD 15th century seen also, for example, in the Utrush Mosque.  
An elaborate *muqarnas* niche with polychrome stone ornamentation decorates the eastern facade of the mausoleum where the founder, Sayf al-Din Jaqmaq al-Arghunshawi (d. AH 824 / AD 1421) is buried.  
The building was restored following bomb damage in the 1940s. Today the building accommodates the Museum of Arabic Calligraphy.
9c99c966-ce63-54c0-ab28-822914e17003.short_description: The *madrasa* was built by the Mamluk governor of Damascus, Sayf al-Din Jaqmaq al-Arghunshawi (r. AH 821–3 / AD 1418–20), serving as his mausoleum. Its layout is typical of Syrian *madrasas* in the Mamluk period: a central covered courtyard flanked by two aisles. The façade also features Mamluk decorative elements: pronounced *ablaq* stripes topped by a *muqarnas* portal and huge bands of calligraphic inscriptions, similar to Ayyubid *madrasa* facades but more elaborate. An elaborate high niche on its eastern facade, a feature common in Mamluk Aleppo, reveals reciprocal influences between the two cities.
9c99c966-ce63-54c0-ab28-822914e17003.address: Opposite the north entrance to the Umayyad Mosque, Damascus, Syria.
9c99c966-ce63-54c0-ab28-822914e17003.method_for_datation: According to the inscription above the entrance of the building, the *madrasa* was founded in the year 810 (1407–8), during the reign of Sultan Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, by the Governor, Sayf al-Din Jaqmaq al-Arghunshawi. There is also a re-foundation date inscription of 822 (1421–2).

9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.name: Wooden beam.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.description:
A wooden beam taken from the Dome of the Rock during restoration works of the 1960s. The beam is made from cedarwood, likely to have been imported from Lebanon. It contains an epigraphic inscription written in Fatimid foliated *kufic* script. The inscription is placed inside a rectangular frame that begins and ends with a tapered niche, and which is adorned with decoration carved in relief. It includes the name of the craftsman who made it and participated in the restoration works in the Dome of the Rock during the Fatimid period in the reign of Caliph al-Zahir bi-Amrillah (r. AH 411–27 / AD 1021–36). It is likely that this craftsman undertook the decoration of other artefacts inside the Dome of the Rock. The inscription beginning with the *Basmala*, reads: “In the Name of God, the Most Beneficent, the Most Merciful. The Work of 'Abd al-Baqi bin al-Hasan bin Ismai'l al-Dimashqi. May God support him”. Despite our lack of knowledge about this craftsman, the fact that his name contains the title “al-Dimashqi” indicates that there was a continual flow of craftsmen from Damascus into Jerusalem during the Fatimid period. Damascus was (and is still) famous for its wood-carving, and Jerusalem was supplied with a steady stream of skilled Damascene craftsmen to work on the construction of the Dome of the Rock at the end of the AH 1st /AD 7th century.  
The beam does not contain any other decoration. It has fortuitously preserved its splendour without damage, which confirms the skill of its workmanship in the treatment of the wood before it was mounted at the Dome of the Rock.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.short_description: This beam from the Dome of the Rock was made from cedarwood that was probably imported from Lebanon. The beam bears an inscription in Fatimid foliated *kufic* script within a rectangular frame that begins and ends with a tapered recess. It is decorated and the text is carved in relief. The piece records the carver who made it in the time of Caliph al-Zahir.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.dimensions: Length 183 cm, width 18.5 cm, depth 20 cm.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.method_for_datation: The beam was dated by way of reliable knowledge concerning the areas that underwent restoration in the Dome of the Rock during the Fatimid period. In addition, the Fatimid script used in the epigraphic inscription is a reliable distinguishing mark.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.method_for_provenance: It is not known whether this beam was crafted in Jerusalem or at another site. Usually, however, the piece would be carved and constructed on site. It is likely, therefore, that it was carved in Jerusalem, while the cedarwood was imported from Lebanon. The craftsman was probably from Damascus, as is evident from the inscription.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.obtention: According to the registers of the Islamic Museum, the piece was transferred from the Dome of the Rock to the Museum in 1960.
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.bibliography: Hamilton, R. W., *The Structural History of al-Aqsa Mosque: A Record of Archaeological Cleaning from the Repairs of 1938–42,* London, 1949.
keywords: Wood; carving; cedar; kufic script; wooden beam
9cc9092e-917f-5963-aa95-2f593ab99290.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh

9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.name: Pendant.
9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.description: A gold crescent-shaped pendant with enamel work. Two bands of delicate gold filigree work surround a panel of cloisonné enamel with a symmetrical design of two birds arranged on either side of a tree. The pendant may have been hung with strings of pearls from the three loops along the bottom. The enamel inset imitates Byzantine designs. Gold jewellery from Byzantium was known in Fatimid Egypt originating either from Byzantine craftsmen who immigrated to Egypt or through diplomatic gifts sent by Byzantine rulers. In 1046 the Fatimid Caliph al-Mustansir (r.1036–94) received a large gift from the Emperor of Byzantium which included hundreds of gold vessels, brocade and gold-embroidered turbans. This exchange of diplomatic gifts is recorded in The Book of Treasures and Gifts, by Ibn Zubayr, written just before the destruction and dispersal of the Fatimid treasury in 1062.
9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.short_description: Gold jewellery with delicate filigree work was popular during the Fatimid period. Some pieces, such as this pendant, also feature enamel work derived from Byzantine designs. The Fatimid treasury is known to have accumulated a vast hoard of gold objects that included jewellery.
9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.method_for_datation: The pendant resembles other gold jewellery from the Fatimid era; generally small in size and often decorated with filigree work, cloisonné enamel, or niello. From the mid-11th century figurative elements began to appear, such as birds. The dating of Fatimid jewellery has been derived from excavations in a number of sites, including that at Fustat in Cairo.
9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.method_for_provenance: The Fatimids were renowned for their rich splendid jewellery. Most of the workmanship would have taken place in Egypt, the political centre of the Fatimid dynasty.
9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.obtention: Purchased by the British Museum in 1981.
9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.bibliography:

keywords: Figurative decoration; jewellery

9ce61178-e421-548d-99f8-805b537a5ef8.name: Column capital.
9ce61178-e421-548d-99f8-805b537a5ef8.description:
A marble column capital, which is typical of the capitals associated with the Mamluk period, especially the second half of it. This style of column capital endured for a long time during the Ottoman epoch in Palestine. The capital is elongated in form and consists of rows of *muqarnas* that diminish to the point of almost disappearing. In this way the capital makes the transition from one level to the next, and one extension to the other, in a flowing manner rather than in a sudden leap as in many other forms of capital. The capital exhibited here is characterised by its simplicity, elegance and the intricacy of its design, not to mention the technical difficulties its execution must have posed.  
The capital begins as a cylinder and is of the same diameter as the pillar on which it would rest. The cylindrical form narrows by degrees, facilitating the transition to a multi-sided column, and within which is an inscription in *naskhi* script. The inscription is difficult to read because it is damaged, as well as having a proliferation of gilding and colours, but perhaps it is a quote from the Qur'an. Each side forms the beginning of a *muqarnas*, diminished, simple and progressive. Each elevation of the *muqarnas* increases its size to end at the apex of the capital. The capital widens without any transitional decoration except with facets of marble that reach a square ledge above the capital. Traces of gilding remain on the capital, which may indicate to us that it was affixed to one of the *mihrab*s of the mosque, as many of the *mihrab*s were gilded.
9ce61178-e421-548d-99f8-805b537a5ef8.short_description: This elongated marble capital alludes to the prevailing style of capitals during the Mamluk period. It is decorated by a rows of muqarnas that diminish to the point of almost disappearing. This gives a beautiful fluency in the transition between levels and from one extent to the next without forcing a sudden leap. The capital contains inscriptions that are difficult to read.
9ce61178-e421-548d-99f8-805b537a5ef8.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
9ce61178-e421-548d-99f8-805b537a5ef8.dimensions: Height 36 cm, base 33 cm x 33 cm.
9ce61178-e421-548d-99f8-805b537a5ef8.method_for_datation: Dating of the capital was possible by comparing it with similar ones; the manufacturing technique and form of *muqarnas* used bears a resemblance to capitals that are still *in situ* in a number of Mamluk buildings in Jerusalem.
9ce61178-e421-548d-99f8-805b537a5ef8.obtention: It is not known exactly how the Museum acquired this column capital, but it is likely that it was brought from a Mamluk building within the environs of the Haram al-Sharif.

9d00287d-1b75-52cd-aaf2-a362c89a4645.name: Footed dish or *tazze*.
9d00287d-1b75-52cd-aaf2-a362c89a4645.description: A circular stone-paste (fritware) dish with a shallow well, curved sides (*cavetto*), an everted scalloped rim and a low, circular foot-ring. The well is filled with a naturalistic arrangement of flowing flower stalks, rising from a tuft of green leaves. The flowers include red carnations, red roses, blue tulips, with red dotted detailing, and blue hyacinths, all of which are executed in order to exploit the shape of the well. The scalloped rim carries a wave border in blue and black. The underside is decorated with ten floral motifs disposed at regular intervals, consisting of an alternating pattern of five blue flower-heads with green centres, and five bouquets of three blue tulips.
9d00287d-1b75-52cd-aaf2-a362c89a4645.short_description: Ottoman Iznik was most famous for the production of brilliant polychrome wares revealing an exuberant naturalism which was influenced to a considerable extent by the innovative drawings of the leading Ottoman court designer Kara Memi. The best pieces were executed between AH 956 and 982 / AD 1550 and 1575.
9d00287d-1b75-52cd-aaf2-a362c89a4645.method_for_datation: This dish belongs to a group of Iznik wares characterised by a naturalism that was influenced by the innovative drawings of the leading Ottoman court designer Kara Memi and datable to between 956–82 / 1550–75.
9d00287d-1b75-52cd-aaf2-a362c89a4645.method_for_provenance: Dishes of this naturalistic, floral decorative style are known to have been produced in Iznik during the second half of the 10th / 16th century.
9d00287d-1b75-52cd-aaf2-a362c89a4645.obtention: Bought from J. M. Whitehead, London in 1883.
9d00287d-1b75-52cd-aaf2-a362c89a4645.bibliography: Atasoy, N., and Raby, J., *Iznik: The Pottery of Ottoman Turkey*, London, 1989, pp.222–30, fig. 397 (for a related piece and discussion of this type from Iznik).
materials: Stone-paste (fritware) with a blue, green and black underglaze, and bole-red underglaze-slip, over which a clear glaze.
keywords: Iznik; stone-paste (fritware); Kara Memi; hyacinths
9d00287d-1b75-52cd-aaf2-a362c89a4645.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis

9d02de34-15a1-5e36-948f-bfe9b4a617e0.name: Hasa Fortress.
9d02de34-15a1-5e36-948f-bfe9b4a617e0.description:
An important station on the pilgrimage route in southern Jordan, Hasa lies about 150 km south of Amman, west of the Hijaz railway. The main components of the site are: a square fortress (24 m x 24 m); a water reservoir (23 m x 23 m); a bridge across Wadi al-Hasa and a section of paved road.  
The fortress was built of limestone and basalt. The maximum surviving height is about 10 m. The perimeter walls are provided with small undecorated slit windows at two levels. Machicolations (projecting windows, measuring 2.5 m x 1.5 m) are preserved on the west, south and east walls. The entrance, which has a scroll decoration above it, was placed in the middle of the northern wall; it consists of a shallow arched porch and a vaulted passageway. The gate complex leads to a square courtyard measuring 12.5 m x 12.5 m with a rectangular structure at the centre to shelter a 20-m deep well.  
On the ground floor nine rooms were organised around a courtyard. Four of the rooms were *iwan*s with slightly pointed vaults. The remaining five were barrel-vaulted rooms with the one adjacent to the south wall of the fortress being the longest (22 m x 4 m).  
Two staircases leading up to the first floor were placed on the sides of the entrance of the south room. On the first floor the rooms are preserved only along the southern wall of the fortress. This side is occupied by seven rooms with barrel-vaulted roofs. The room in the centre was probably the mosque.  
Part of the second floor above the mosque is preserved but no complete structure can be identified.
9d02de34-15a1-5e36-948f-bfe9b4a617e0.short_description: Hasa, about 150 km south of Amman, is an important station on the pilgrimage route. The main components of the site are: a fortress from the time of Sultan Mustafa II (AH 1170–87 / AD 1757–74); a reservoir; a bridge built by Aydinli Abdullah Pasha, Governor of Damascus (r. AH 1142–5 / AD 1730–3); and a paved road. The fortress perimeter walls, built of limestone and basalt, have slit windows at two levels; projecting windows are preserved on three walls. The entrance has a scroll decoration above. It leads to a courtyard with a rectangular structure at the centre to shelter a 20-m deep well.
9d02de34-15a1-5e36-948f-bfe9b4a617e0.dates: The bridge dates to Hegira 1140 / AD 1730s; the fortress to the time of Sultan Mustafa II (AH 1170–87 / AD 1757–74).
9d02de34-15a1-5e36-948f-bfe9b4a617e0.method_for_datation: Mehmed Edib (1926) attributes the bridge at al-Hasa to Aydinli Abdullah Pasha the governor of Damascus (r. 1142–5 / 1730–3), while archaeologists Jaussen and Savignac (1909) on the basis of an Arabic verse inscription, suggest that the fortress and the bridge were built by Sultan Mustafa II (1170–87 / 1757–74).

9d0fa2dd-7af5-5431-b7d1-d0b10e4e74c1.name: Qur΄an section
9d0fa2dd-7af5-5431-b7d1-d0b10e4e74c1.description: The manuscript on paper has 47 folios, each with five lines of *naskhi* script in black ink. There are rosettes between verses and every fifth verse there is a larger roundel in the margin. The morocco binding is original to the manuscript.
keywords: Manuscript; naskhi; calligraphy; Qur΄an; religious manuscript

9d2deaea-eeb3-5b49-bc73-3dda66bf24ef.name: Four basalt reliefs.
9d2deaea-eeb3-5b49-bc73-3dda66bf24ef.description: Four Basalt reliefs that are fine illustrations of the 'minor arts' and which borrow their themes from the classical world prior to the Islamic conquest: a hunting dog; a griffon; a Pegasus and an amphora decorated with flowers. Such images find their parallels not only in earlier Byzantine mosaic church floors and in contemporary mosaics of the AH 1st–2nd / AD 7th–8th centuries, but earlier than that, in the periods from which they originate: the Greek, Roman and Sassanid. The skill used to make these carvings has given them a lively, even playful, appearance. It seems that these reliefs, along with others still *in situ* at Qasr al-Azraq, formed an arch over a viewing platform where spectators would sit to watch the water sports played out in the water reservoirs near Qasr al-Azraq.
9d2deaea-eeb3-5b49-bc73-3dda66bf24ef.short_description: Four basalt reliefs from an arch over a viewing platform where spectators would watch the water sports played out in the water reservoirs near Qasr al-Azraq. Probably Umayyad, the images depicted have late Byzantine and Umayyad parallels but they originate in the Greek, Roman and Sassanid periods.
9d2deaea-eeb3-5b49-bc73-3dda66bf24ef.holder: Museum of Jordanian Heritage, Yarmouk University.
9d2deaea-eeb3-5b49-bc73-3dda66bf24ef.dates: Thought to be hegira 2nd century / AD first half of the 8th century.
9d2deaea-eeb3-5b49-bc73-3dda66bf24ef.dimensions: a: Height 13 cm, width 46 cm, depth 18 cm; b: Height 41.5 cm, width 47.5 cm, depth 19 cm; c: Height 34 cm, width 45 cm, depth 13 cm; d: Height 52 cm, width 58.5 cm, depth 17.5 cm.
9d2deaea-eeb3-5b49-bc73-3dda66bf24ef.method_for_datation: The date of production for these reliefs is uncertain, but stylistic analysis of the griffon identifies it as an image used decoratively in other Umayyad palaces: Khirbat al-Mafjar in Jericho, Qasr al-Hayr al-Gharbi in Syria, al-Mushatta and al-Hallabat in Jordan, and this may give vital clues to the accurate dating of these objects. The same thing could be said about the Pegasus which is a Sassanid decorative element but also represented in Umayyad palaces. Historical sources also mention that al-Walid ibn Yazid (or Walid II, d. 126/ 744) spent time at Qasr al-Azraq.
9d2deaea-eeb3-5b49-bc73-3dda66bf24ef.method_for_provenance: The reliefs were found in a one of the water reservoirs near Qasr al-Azraq in 1983.
9d2deaea-eeb3-5b49-bc73-3dda66bf24ef.obtention: The reliefs were recovered in the course of reed clearance in the water reservoirs near Qasr al-Azraq in 1983. They were then put on loan to the Museum of Jordanian Heritage from the Department of Antiquities in 1988.

9d4974ab-f811-5127-ae3d-e1895f9c8e80.name: *Hirz* (Necklace) with Qur’an Case
9d4974ab-f811-5127-ae3d-e1895f9c8e80.description: A fascination with the possibilities of design within a rectangular format is evident in the myriad interpretations of the *hirz* (necklace) Qur’an case. Squares, rectangles, diamonds and incremental components of triangles are all in widespread use as elements of Omani design. Simple patterns formed by straight, intersecting lines are most easily executed and therefore predominate on the hardest materials – stone, bone, metals and hardwood. In woodwork, angular designs are often faceted, a technique which enhances visual interest through the interplay of light and shadow.
9d4974ab-f811-5127-ae3d-e1895f9c8e80.obtention: Museum of the Ministry of Heritage and Culture
keywords: Hirz; Necklace; Jewellery; Qur'an

9d54bf76-910a-5ef1-bcfd-bc844a35cd59.name: Danan Synagogue (Slat Rabbi Shelomo Danan).
9d54bf76-910a-5ef1-bcfd-bc844a35cd59.description:
In order to establish his authority over the country, Mulay Rashid, the founder of the 'Alawid dynasty (AH 1075–83 / AD 1664–72) had to fight against the Marabut brotherhoods, in particular the Dilai, whose *zawiya* was located near to the town of Khenifra in the Middle Atlas on the land of the Ait Ishaq, where a significant Jewish community lived.  
In AH 1076 / AD 1666, Mulay Rashid took Fez from the Dilai and decided to make it his capital. He undertook the revitalisation of the town by restoring it and repopulating it. To do so, he moved in elements of the Arab Cheraga tribe from eastern Morocco, whom he enlisted in his army, and he brought a large part of the Jewish community of Ait Ishaq to relaunch economic activity in the town and take on certain administrative functions. This migration involved the expansion of the Jewish Quarter (*mellah*) and it resulted in the construction of a new synagogue.  
This new temple, erected by Mimon Bussidan around AH 1091 / AD 1680, owes its name to Rabbi Shelomo Danan (1847–1928) who officiated there at the beginning of the 20th century.  
The building originally consisted of three naves backing on to the rampart of the *mellah*, which constitutes its eastern wall and is home to the huge *hekhal*, the cabinet where the Torah scrolls are kept.  
A fourth nave, with a lower ceiling and an *azara* (women's gallery), was added subsequently.  
Later still, the synagogue was endowed with a *teba* (altar) raised up on steps, which included an elegant wooden lectern and a wrought-iron balustrade overlooking the prayer room.  
The entrance, originally located in the enclosure wall, was blocked up at the time of the construction of the fourth nave, and henceforth access was gained from the opposite side through a very plain door, a square hallway that leads to the *teba* and the fourth nave.  
Restoration work undertaken at the end of the 20th century brought to light a *mikvé* (ritual bath) beneath the synagogue, from which a trapdoor leads to an underground water course. The faithful would go there during the festival of Rosh Hashanah to 'to shake off their sins in the water'. This *mikvé*, which was initially located outside the synagogue, was bricked in to enable the construction of the fourth nave.  
The building's load-bearing walls are made of full bricks and lime mortar, with the exception of the eastern wall which is part of the adobe enclosure wall.  
The octagonal pillars are made of full bricks and the floors are covered with green and white rectangular earthenware tiles set in a herringbone pattern.  
The interior decoration is focused around the Torah cabinets, with the upper part being surrounded by a large band of sculpted plaster painted with geometric motifs, and the lower part with a band of ceramic marquetry in white and blue that reaches the floor via a high step that runs all round the room.  
The synagogue is no longer used as a place of worship and, being classified as an historic monument, it is open to the public.
9d54bf76-910a-5ef1-bcfd-bc844a35cd59.short_description:
To kickstart the economy and reinforce the government, the 'Alawid Mulay Rashid moved a part of the Middle Atlas Jewish community to Fez, which he had recently conquered. A new synagogue was erected in the extended Jewish quarter.  
The original three naves were later complemented by an altar with a wooden lectern, an iron balustrade, and a fourth nave with a women's gallery. There is a ritual bath in the basement. In the prayer room, the painted plasterwork and ceramic inlays of the Torah cabinets are the main decorative elements.  
The synagogue is no longer sacred and is now open to the public.
9d54bf76-910a-5ef1-bcfd-bc844a35cd59.method_for_datation: Information provided by Simon Lévy, General Secretary of the Foundation of Judeo-Moroccan Cultural Heritage.
9d54bf76-910a-5ef1-bcfd-bc844a35cd59.bibliography: *La Synagogue Danan restaurée*, Foundation of Judeo-Moroccan Cultural Heritage, Casablanca, undated.
9d54bf76-910a-5ef1-bcfd-bc844a35cd59.patrons: Mimon Bussidan, well-known Jew originally from Zawiyat Aït Ishaq (Middle Atlas).
keywords: Religious building; tolerance; bricks; zellij; sculpted plaster

9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.name: Jar with lid.
9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.description:
The spherical jar stands on a high foot and has a cylindrical rimless neck with a flat lid with a knob. The body is covered inside and outside with an opaque, pale turquoise-coloured tin glaze. In the lower part the glaze is not thick enough so that the reddish colouring of the body shines through the glaze. The abstract decoration of the jar is mainly composed of a series of vertical stripes alternating with dotted lines, called 'millipedes', around the neck and a scale pattern filled with stylised half-carnations on the spherical section of the jar. The foot-ring is undecorated. The colours used are a deep limonite yellow, two gradations of brown, a light one of iron oxide and a dark one of manganese, and cobalt-blue and copper green. The use of brown, yellow, blue and green as full, unmixed tones is the characteristic colour scheme of Moroccan polychrome faience. Faience is the type of decoration: after a first firing the potters put on the opaque tin glaze on the earthenware vessel; the mineral pigments used for the polychrome decoration were applied over the dried glaze; in a second firing glaze and pigments melted together.  
The small and large red dots irregularly spread over the whole outside surface of jar and lid are a striking feature. It is a paste with a base of red lead applied over the glaze by fingertip. After drying, the paste appears like red wax. However, this kind of decoration was not executed by the potters themselves. It was done by the faience traders, at first to cover the traces of the firing tripods on plates and later on all kinds of pottery vessels.  
Faience was an urban ceramic in Morocco whose most important centre of production was Fez. The objects made by the faience potters were mostly functional and for everyday use. This pot was possibly used for storing fat or yeast. Unlike other examples of this kind of stock pot, however, this one does not have the usual two handles.
9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.short_description: Jar on a high foot and with a flat lid with knob. The decoration is composed of vertical stripes alternating with dotted lines and stylised half-carnations. The colour scheme is characteristic of Moroccan polychrome faience. This pot might have been used for storing fat or yeast.
9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.dimensions: Height approx. 21.3 cm, diameter of rim 10.5 cm.
9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.method_for_datation: Dating is difficult. There are only a few dated faiences and the same forms and patterns were used throughout various periods. The red dots were probably common from the end of the 12th / 18th century.
9dd54e6a-3ac7-5825-b7ce-cc73c549cb45.method_for_provenance: On the basis of the pattern, the technique and the colour scheme.

9de82036-a221-545b-84e8-7f91036b9036.name: Dish.
9de82036-a221-545b-84e8-7f91036b9036.description: A circular stone-paste (fritware) dish with a shallow well, broad, everted rim and a low, circular foot-ring. The well is decorated with seven bouquets, comprising one at the centre, surrounded by six others. The flowers are naively drawn and the pigments overall very pure: red, green and blue with black. The rim has a white, cusped zigzag band, reserved against a green ground; a narrow blue line accentuates the zigzag patterning and contrasts with the white and green.
9de82036-a221-545b-84e8-7f91036b9036.short_description: Towards the end of the late AH 10th century / AD 16th century the artistic quality of Iznik wares began to decline. Raw materials were less refined, colour schemes duller and designs simpler. Dishes with simple floral bouquets were made between the AH late 10th / AD last quarter of the 16th century.
9de82036-a221-545b-84e8-7f91036b9036.dates: Hegira, late 10th century / AD late 16th century.
9de82036-a221-545b-84e8-7f91036b9036.method_for_datation: Dishes with similar floral designs have been attributed to the late 10th / late 16th century.
9de82036-a221-545b-84e8-7f91036b9036.method_for_provenance: Ceramics of this type are known to have been produced in Iznik during the late 10th / late 16th century.
9de82036-a221-545b-84e8-7f91036b9036.obtention: A gift from Miss Beatrice Danford, Newton St. Boswells, in 1953.

9df9ad1d-8d86-536f-b9dc-b840825f1265.name: Parish Church.
9df9ad1d-8d86-536f-b9dc-b840825f1265.description:
The parish church of the village of Dois Portos in Alta Estremadura, to the north of Lisbon, near the Atlantic, is one of the few churches in this vast region which still has a Mudéjar ceiling. Its architectural structure dates entirely from the 16th century, from the time when the early Renaissance was becoming established, and it even has elements, such as the capitals of the aisles, which indicate a master builder who had worked with the great royal architect João de Castilho, in Lisbon and at Tomar. This would lead to its being dated to the 1530s.  
These ceilings were to be found more or less all over the country, and this one might be included in a group influenced by Sintra and Lisbon. It was a fashion which became established in court circles during the early reign of Dom Manuel I (r. 1495–1521), reaching its climax in the construction of the National Palace in Sintra. But it was not confined to there, since the application of glazed tiles (*azulejos*) from Seville was widespread, and appeared in an infinite number of churches and palaces, to give them an 'Andalusian air', as was the construction of other features in the same tradition, such as the projecting battlements and windows with surmounted arches, visible in a very ruined palace at Azóia, in the convent of Madre de Deus de Xabregas in Lisbon and in the Convent of Varatojo, on the outskirts of Torres Vedras.  
The most striking aspect of the parish church of Dois Portos is the simultaneous use of two styles which are apparently contradictory: the classical capitals, symbolic of a stylistic movement which championed the architecture of the ancient world, and the ceiling of polychrome and gilded tracery, evocative of a very different style, clearly opposed to that recommended by the champions of the art of Greco-Roman Antiquity.
9df9ad1d-8d86-536f-b9dc-b840825f1265.short_description:
The parish church of Dois Portas in the Alta Extremadura region, to the north of Lisbon and near the Atlantic, is one of the few in this vast area to have retained its Mudéjar ceiling.  
The most striking aspect of the church is the simultaneous use of two apparently contradictory systems: classical capitals, symbolic elements of architecture of the ancient world, and a multicoloured, gilded ceiling with interlacing designs, evocative of another world, clearly opposed to the one defended by the advocates of the art of Greek and Roman Antiquity.
9df9ad1d-8d86-536f-b9dc-b840825f1265.method_for_datation: On the basis of stylistic analysis.
9df9ad1d-8d86-536f-b9dc-b840825f1265.bibliography: Dias, P., “Arquitectura Mudéjar Portuguesa: Tentativa de Sistematização”, *Mare Liberum*, no. 8, Lisbon, 1994, p. 67.
keywords: parish church; Dois Portos; Mudéjar; early Renaissance; Dom Manuel I; projecting battlements; surmounted arch; tracery ceiling
9df9ad1d-8d86-536f-b9dc-b840825f1265.author: Pedro Dias

9e027897-a1bc-5a18-981c-ff0bd612de0a.name: Mortar
9e027897-a1bc-5a18-981c-ff0bd612de0a.description:
This object is an octagonal-shaped bronze mortar. A *kufic* inscription runs along the rim while a relief of lions’ heads, birds, and ribbons adorns the base. The main body is decorated with raised teardrop-shaped studs and there is a handle for steadying the mortar while preparing ingredients.  
Given its octagonal shape, low base, and matching everted lips separated from the body by mouldings, the mortar was probably made in Iran between the 12th and 13th century. A similar object in Victoria and Albert Museum resembles this mortar in both size and design.
9e027897-a1bc-5a18-981c-ff0bd612de0a.method_for_datation: By comparison with similar objects, e. g. Sweden Medelhavsmuseet (BEK 1958.06); Victoria & Albert;  Museum for Islamic Art, Berlin; Lindenmuseum, Stuttgart;  The Metropolitan Museum of Art (07.208).
