b8456794-0ef9-5329-826d-f6575b715bad.name: Incense Burner
b8456794-0ef9-5329-826d-f6575b715bad.description:
This is a hollow cast incense burner in the shape of a bird with silver inlay, perforated details and an opening on the top of the tail. Inlay and openwork can be found on the whole surface.  
The eyes are elevated and inlaid, a comb is placed at the back of the head and scrolls highlight the crest. Ornament compartments with spiralling tendrils surround the polygonal neck, followed by geometric medallions which are perforated at the throat. Below that is a compartment with pacing animals in front of spiralling tendrils, followed by a drop-shaped medallion with geometric scrolls. This design is repeated in every perforated medallion. The lower chest is highlighted by a cup-like medallion and blossoms. The top of the tail is open and forms a slope. A large inscription frames the inner half of the wings. It consists of elongated letters that end in small heads. A perforated medallion highlights the centre; a tendril-scroll ornaments the wingtips.

b8adbf3d-fcfa-509c-ac13-b2d0c7288418.name: Tankard.
b8adbf3d-fcfa-509c-ac13-b2d0c7288418.description: A tall, stone-paste (fritware) tankard of cylindrical shape with a flat angular handle with curved projections at the top and bottom. The tankard is decorated with an undulating succession of tall red tulips and blue-green so-called *saz* leaves that alternate with smaller red and blue flowers. All the flora springs from a decorative band around the lower body, enhanced by blue and red detailing. This decorative band is repeated around the lip. The handle shows crude abstract detailing. This type of tankard first appears in Ottoman ceramics in the AH late 10th / AD mid–late 16th century and was widely exported. Metal prototypes of this type are known from the Balkans. Leather or wood models may also have contributed to the development of this ceramic type.
b8adbf3d-fcfa-509c-ac13-b2d0c7288418.short_description: This type of tankard first appears in Ottoman ceramics in the AH 10th / AD 16th century and was widely exported subsequently. Metal prototypes of this type are known from the Balkans. Leather or wood models may also have contributed to the development of this type in ceramics.
b8adbf3d-fcfa-509c-ac13-b2d0c7288418.dates: Hegira, late 10th century / AD mid–late 16th century.
b8adbf3d-fcfa-509c-ac13-b2d0c7288418.method_for_datation: Iznik tankards with this particular type of decoration have been attributed to the late 10th / mid–late 16th century.

b8c3263e-bcad-57f1-85f6-7e684aea8d52.name: Cistern.
b8c3263e-bcad-57f1-85f6-7e684aea8d52.description:
A water tank or cistern, circular in cross-section, almost 20 m deep (the depth reached with cleaning and excavation, but thought to be much greater) and 3 m in diameter at the mouth. As 2 to 3 metres of water can always be seen it is possible that the construction is linked to phreatic (underground) waters.  
It is a very rare work of hydraulics, built of local stone – Silves red sandstone – giving it a high quality of construction. Architecturally it is a fine example of technical craftsmanship and functionality: a vaulted spiral staircase descends alongside it for 16 metres in a gallery to the lower level.  
The entire staircase, consisting of four flights, is roofed by a magnificent segmented tunnel vault. Three windows, with semi-circular-shaped vaults, form the link between the gallery of the staircase and the well, allowing access to the water at the different levels of filling, and also provide the gallery with ventilation and natural light.  
This monument was built at the end of the AH 6th / AD 12th century or the beginning of the AH 7th / AD 13th century, close to the inner surface of the wall which runs around the *medina* (town) and which was rebuilt at the same time. In this area the wall is wider and has a watchtower built against the outside.  
Undoubtedly these three structures (wall, watchtower and cistern), built at the same time, functioned as a defensive, structural and architectural whole.  
The function of this monumental cistern was probably to supply water to most of the lower part of the town, namely the *hammam* (public baths) which was very close, some 100 m away.  
The cistern was filled in with earth and rubbish and its function abandoned with the arrival of the Christians at the end of the AH 7th / AD 13th century. It was only rediscovered in 1979, when reconstruction and repaving work was begun in that area. The archaeological excavations which followed brought to light not only the magnificent structure itself but also an extraordinary haul of ceramics, with pieces dating from the AH 3rd–4th / AD 9th–10th centuries to the AH 11th / AD 17th century, now on display in the Silves Municipal Archaeology Museum.  
The cistern is today part of the Silves Municipal Archaeology Museum, where it plays a central role, with the whole permanent exhibition arranged around it.  
This unique example of a cistern linked to phreatic waters has been classified as a National Monument since 1990.
b8c3263e-bcad-57f1-85f6-7e684aea8d52.short_description: This Almohad water tank or cistern was fed from the Silves water table. A vaulted spiral staircase descends into a gallery to a depth of 16 metres. The entire four-flight staircase is covered by a segmented barrel vault. Three windows with semi-circular vaults link the stairwell to the well, giving access to the water as well as naturally lighting and ventilating the gallery. The cistern is now the centrepiece of the Municipal Museum of Archaeology around which the other exhibits are arranged.
b8c3263e-bcad-57f1-85f6-7e684aea8d52.dates: Hegira second half of 6th–first half of 7th century / AD second half of 12th–first half of 13th century.
b8c3263e-bcad-57f1-85f6-7e684aea8d52.method_for_datation: From the style, construction and architecture of the structure. There are documentary records of the existence of a cistern close to the *hammam*.

b8c40522-1727-5d7d-b72d-d30eb8d6a67e.name: Four choir stalls.
b8c40522-1727-5d7d-b72d-d30eb8d6a67e.description:
Monumental choir stalls from the convent of Santa Clara. The four stalls held by the National Archaeological Museum are part of a set originally made up of 50, with the 46 remaining stalls now at the San Diego Mission in the United States.  
The wooden structure and the painted decoration are particularly noteworthy. The construction is made in such a way as to reduce the use of nailed elements to a minimum. The usual range of colours has been used, with a predominance of pinks, dark red, green-black, white and yellow-green applied on a strong base of white primer, producing a visually astounding result.  
The architectonic aspect of the work, with its octagonal columns, curved lobed arches and a roof with corbels and *tabicas* (small boards), give it a grandiose character. It is the oldest example of tall choir stalls in Spain having been made around 1353, the same year that María de Padilla, the lover of King Peter I of Castile, founded the monastery, as proclaimed by the shields with rampant lions and fire shovels, Maria de Padilla's emblem.
b8c40522-1727-5d7d-b72d-d30eb8d6a67e.short_description: These four stalls give an idea of the original monumentality of the complete set of 50 stalls from the Convent of Santa Clara de Astudillo in Palencia. It has an architectural structure and its parts are simply assembled. The decoration is dominated by brightly coloured plant arabesques.
b8c40522-1727-5d7d-b72d-d30eb8d6a67e.dimensions: Height 290 cm, width 285 cm, depth 100 cm.
b8c40522-1727-5d7d-b72d-d30eb8d6a67e.method_for_datation: Surviving historical documentation dates it between 1353 and 1357.
b8c40522-1727-5d7d-b72d-d30eb8d6a67e.method_for_provenance: The stalls were in their original location until 1932.
b8c40522-1727-5d7d-b72d-d30eb8d6a67e.provenance: Convent of Santa Clara de Astudillo, Palencia, Spain.
b8c40522-1727-5d7d-b72d-d30eb8d6a67e.obtention: The stalls were donated to the National Archaeological Museum on 1 August 1932 by Apolinar Sánchez Villalba in order to obtain permission to export the 46 remaining stalls to the United States.

b8c52c07-1db7-5b7e-a968-695ff14489a0.name: Ceramic bowl.
b8c52c07-1db7-5b7e-a968-695ff14489a0.description: Glazed bowl with vertical rounded rim, circular mouth, body shaped as inverted truncated cone with low carination and base with diagonal foot-ring. Covered with honey-coloured monochrome glaze and decorated in *cuerda seca* with white, green and honey colours separated by lines of manganese. The central theme is the word '*baraka'* written in *kufic* characters, surrounded by a frieze of palmette leaves which runs around the rim of the bowl. The object has been restored.
b8c52c07-1db7-5b7e-a968-695ff14489a0.short_description: Bowl decorated entirely using *cuerda seca* from the Almoravid or Almohad periods. The central motif is the word ‘*baraka*’ written in *kufic* characters and surrounded by a frieze of palmettes that runs around the brim of the bowl. Similar pieces have been found around the western Mediterranean.
b8c52c07-1db7-5b7e-a968-695ff14489a0.dimensions: Height 8 cm, diameter (of mouth) 25 cm, diameter (of base) 10.3 cm.
b8c52c07-1db7-5b7e-a968-695ff14489a0.method_for_datation: The stratigraphic context in which the object was found was very disordered, which led to its being dated to the 6th / 12th century by comparison with objects of similar form, decorative technique and theme, in particular from Almería and Málaga.
b8c52c07-1db7-5b7e-a968-695ff14489a0.method_for_provenance: The abundance of this type of ceramic in Málaga, in which very similar calligraphy is found, and Almería (Spain) where kilns have been found in which objects with this type of decoration were made, has led researchers to attribute its production to these localities.
b8c52c07-1db7-5b7e-a968-695ff14489a0.obtention: Found in the archaeological excavations carried out by the Campo Arqueológico de Mértola in the citadel of the Castle of Mértola.

Torres, C. and Macias, S. (eds.), *O Portugal Islâmico*, Lisbon, 1998, p.93.

b8ecf061-5f47-5eb8-bd73-a5714784eff0.name: Plate.
b8ecf061-5f47-5eb8-bd73-a5714784eff0.description:
A ceramic plate decorated with geometric designs in yellow pigment on a brown background and under a transparent glaze.  
  
The inner surface is divided into four zones, each pair corresponding with each other. One pair consists of curved triangles filled with crossed lines forming, net-like, small indented squares; the other two zones show crisscrossed curved lines which form an arrow–head design.
b8ecf061-5f47-5eb8-bd73-a5714784eff0.short_description: Ceramic plate from Tall Hisban, decorated with geometric designs in yellow pigment on a brown background and under a transparent glaze. The inner surface is divided into four zones, forming two pairs of crisscrossed curved designs.
b8ecf061-5f47-5eb8-bd73-a5714784eff0.dimensions: Height 8.8 cm, diameter 30.3 cm, diameter (of base) 10.7cm.
b8ecf061-5f47-5eb8-bd73-a5714784eff0.method_for_datation: The plate was dated by its stratigraphic context in the archaeological excavation.
b8ecf061-5f47-5eb8-bd73-a5714784eff0.method_for_provenance: The plate was recovered from Tall Hisban during an archaeological excavation.
b8ecf061-5f47-5eb8-bd73-a5714784eff0.obtention: The plate was recovered during the course of an archaeological excavation carried out at Tall Hisban in 1993.

b9121ce3-b4a5-5b98-93ab-b74dd4c75a5e.name: Arch.
b9121ce3-b4a5-5b98-93ab-b74dd4c75a5e.description: This arch was part of the arcade of the southern portico of the Aljafería Palace in Saragossa. The whole consists of a 13-lobed arch supporting a series of small hollow arches formed by the crossing of other larger arches, which are also poly-lobed. The upper part is decorated with plant arabesques interrupted by four small scalloped cupolas. It is completed by a large arch that appears to be supported on columns, with their shafts and capitals. In this arch we can see how certain structural elements (arches, columns or small cupolas) are used as purely decorative elements, a common practice in the art of the Taifa kingdoms. The fretwork in these arcades, created by a series of arches that multiply harmoniously, produces an effect of light and shade. It is an art that places more importance on visual impact than on the materials or even the architecture. The artistic forms of this period follow the caliphal tendencies of the Great Mosque of Córdoba, but in the Taifa kingdom of Saragossa there is a special tendency towards more elaborate designs, which would later be adopted in various Andalusian and Mudéjar buildings.
b9121ce3-b4a5-5b98-93ab-b74dd4c75a5e.short_description: The south side of the Aljafería courtyard was decorated with an arched portico similar to this one, built for effect and for decoration and with no real structural function. It was inspired by the intertwining arcades of the Great Mosque of Córdoba, but its complexity makes it singularly baroque in style.
b9121ce3-b4a5-5b98-93ab-b74dd4c75a5e.method_for_datation: The Aljafería Palace was constructed under the patronage of Abu Yafar Ahmad al-Muqtadir (r. 437–73 / 1046–81), the second monarch in the Banu Hud dynasty, which governed the Taifa of Saragossa during the years 432–503 / 1040–1110. In the southern portico of the Palace, where this arch belongs, there are two inscriptions that include the title adopted by al-Muqtadir after the conquest of Barbastro in 456 / 1064.
b9121ce3-b4a5-5b98-93ab-b74dd4c75a5e.method_for_provenance: In 1867, before the demolition of the Palace's San Jorge Chapel and the adjacent areas, the recently created Commission of Monuments managed to salvage some architectural elements of the Palace and move them to the National Archaeological Museum in Madrid and the Provincial Museum of Saragossa.
b9121ce3-b4a5-5b98-93ab-b74dd4c75a5e.obtention: The arch was donated to the National Archaeological Museum on 19 August 1869.

b914b3ad-c4ec-5742-a411-fc1720a3eb43.description: This embroidery fragment is decorated with colourful flower arrangements placed in staggered rows on a cream-coloured ground.
keywords: Embroidery; fabric; textile; Ottoman textiles; floral motifs

b9280ed6-19f0-55b4-a602-5d1098d3ab59.name: Dish
b9280ed6-19f0-55b4-a602-5d1098d3ab59.description: Composite-bodied ceramic dish, the centre with a configuration of six circular dense foliated and floriated scrolls and five stylized palmettes, bordered by eight paired Chinese-style cloud devices, the rim with a border of small flowers on thin scrolling stems; exterior with alternations of two types of Chinese-inspired cloud motifs. It was wheel-thrown, covered with white engobe, painted with cobalt blue stain, and transparent colourless glaze.
b9280ed6-19f0-55b4-a602-5d1098d3ab59.dates: Hegira first half of the 9th century / AD 1520–1540
keywords: ?znik ceramics; Floral motifs; blue-and-white; chinese motifs

b9d55563-3221-5150-9626-d1ff8d78bba0.name: Kohl Container
b9d55563-3221-5150-9626-d1ff8d78bba0.description: Cosmetic kits such as this one, comprised of a kohl container and kohl stick, were used by both women and men in many countries to apply eyeliner. The use of kohl was widespread in Egypt from the Pharaonic period onwards, made from burning the saffron plant and combining it with raw copper and lead. Kohl was used to beautify the eyes as well as to medically treat them.  This mid-20th century kohl container is a fine example of use of the predominant Arabesque pattern used in Islamic design.  The Arabesque as a specific decorative element consists of a continuous branching stem with split palmate leaves. The aesthetics of the Arabesque are derived from the imposition of order on the natural world. Arabesque patterns are used extensively in traditional Omani woodwork, plasterwork and metalwork as a means of covering entire surfaces or precise areas within a defined geometric framework.
b9d55563-3221-5150-9626-d1ff8d78bba0.dates: Mid 14th century AH / Mid 20th century AD
b9d55563-3221-5150-9626-d1ff8d78bba0.obtention: Museum of the Ministry of Heritage and Culture
keywords: Kohl Container; Jewellery; Arabesque

ba3d1a83-a184-5e97-ba14-14862bec4cac.name: Man's festive ikat robe
ba3d1a83-a184-5e97-ba14-14862bec4cac.description: In 19th century Turkestan, an expensive Ikat coat represented wealth and dignity. Many specialists were involved in the creation of Ikat textiles, from the breeding of silk worms to the dyeing, weaving and tailoring of the cloth. Ikat silks are luxury articles. They are given as gifts at weddings and other important occasions. Ikat fabrics probably originated in China, from where they were disseminated along the network of the Silk Road throughout Central Asia.
ba3d1a83-a184-5e97-ba14-14862bec4cac.method_for_datation: Entry in the general inventory and archival documents.

ba569c5c-b80f-54e0-98af-3d838677a438.name: Bab Mrissa.
ba569c5c-b80f-54e0-98af-3d838677a438.description:
The fortified port of Salé, which could be used as an arsenal and was linked to the Wadi Bou Regreg by a canal, was built between AH 658 and 668 / AD 1260 and 1270. Boats entered the dock through the arch of an enormous gateway, Bab Mrissa (the Gateway of the Small Port). Built into the adobe wall, the stone façade of the gateway is embellished by beautiful inscribed decorations and sculpted floral knotwork.  
The two 3.50 m-wide oblong towers, projecting by 2.20 m, flank the large pointed horseshoe arch measuring nearly 9 m wide by 9.6 m tall despite the fact that the ground level has risen owing to the silting up and covering of the dock and the canal.  
Its intended function explains why Bab Mrissa has no defensive chicanes.  
The side structures consist of barrel-vaulted rooms below stairways that lead to the wall walk. These stairways are interrupted by landings with loopholes overlooking the vaults. Firing rooms, covered with domes supported on pendentives, were built into the towers. The loopholes are splayed at an angle to provide a line of fire over the canal that linked the dock and the river.
ba569c5c-b80f-54e0-98af-3d838677a438.short_description: Between AH 658 and 668 (AD 1260 and 1270), a harbour connected to the Bou Regreg by a canal was built in Salé. It was accessed through an enormous gateway with a pointed horseshoe arch flanked by two oblong towers. The lower part of the flanking structures contain vaulted rooms and stairways leading to the wall walk. The towers had firing rooms covered with cupolas on pendentives and arrow loops looking out obliquely across the canal. The stone façade is carved with decorative inscriptions and floral interlacing designs. When closed, this gateway protected the harbour and the boats in it.
ba569c5c-b80f-54e0-98af-3d838677a438.address: On the right bank of the Bou Regreg opposite Rabat.
ba569c5c-b80f-54e0-98af-3d838677a438.method_for_datation: *Rawd al-Qirtas*, written by Ibn Abi-Zar in AH 726 / AD 1326, and *History of the Berbers*, written by Ibn Khaldun a quarter of a century later indicate that the construction of the fortified enclosure of Salé was started immediately after the town was plundered by Christian merchants during the festival of the breaking of the fast in AH 658 / AD 1260.

ba7672c4-fed6-5ce8-8f1d-ccd9a7e359e4.name: Marriage document.
ba7672c4-fed6-5ce8-8f1d-ccd9a7e359e4.description:
A document relating to a marriage and a divorce written on the back and the front of the scroll. The document refers to the marriage of a resident of Jerusalem on the front, and on the back, deals with the divorce of this same individual from his wife. Vermin have eaten away at part of the document, making it difficult to read.  
The marriage document occupies seven lines. It begins with a *Basmala* (In the name of Allah, Most Gracious, Most Merciful) on a line by itself, followed by the marriage contract. The contract warrants that Sheikh Sharaf al-Din Ya'qub bin al-Hajj Yusuf bin Ya'qub of Jerusalem gave his first born, a mature, free Muslim woman from Hebron, in marriage; she was said to be free from any legal impediment. It is notable that the name of the bride is not given in the contract; the information is limited to the mention of the place she is associated with, which is Hebron. We know that her name is Fatima from the divorce document, which is written on the back of the scroll. The contract mentions that the *mahr* (dowery), paid in advance was 450 *dirham*s, and that the deferred *mahr* was 150 *dirham*s. The contract also mentions that the representative of the bride in the marriage was Sheikh Qasim bin Musa bin ‘Umar al-Ghazzi. And the contract was completed by the attendance of two witnesses, one of which was al-Sayyid Sharaf al-Din Hamza bin al-Sayyid Abd al-Rahman Ali al-Mughrabi. The name of the second witness is barely legible, but the family name “al-Asti” is readable. At the bottom of the contract is the signature of the witness. And on the left side of the text is written: “her husband, her representative has legally presided, registered by Ahmad bin al-Naqib al-Hanbali”.  
On the back of the scroll are two other documents. Each document is five lines long and at the end of each one are the names of two witnesses. The first document reads: “Praise Be to God, on the 5th of Muharram in the year 795 \[21st November 1392\], to bear witness that the aforementioned Ya'qub divorced his wife, the aforementioned Fatima the day before this date. Then he recanted his divorce and took her back into his protection and marriage contract, a legal revision, attended by witnesses and witnessed on the date above.” The second document on the back of the paper is distinguished by a settlement between the husband and wife on her return to his protection. This was to take place on the condition that he gave her the deferred *mahr*. The document records the confirmation of two witnesses, that he had given the deferred *mahr* on the basis that she would not demand the *mahr* again in the event of another divorce or the death of her husband.
ba7672c4-fed6-5ce8-8f1d-ccd9a7e359e4.short_description: Curiously, this mariage contract from Jerusalem has a document on its reverse relating to the divorce of the same couple. The document bears all the conditions and rights pertaining to marriage or divorce. It contains the names of the married couple, the judge and the witnesses. There is little fundamental difference from a contemporary Islamic marriage contract.
ba7672c4-fed6-5ce8-8f1d-ccd9a7e359e4.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
ba7672c4-fed6-5ce8-8f1d-ccd9a7e359e4.initial_owner: The Islamic Religious Court (al-Mahkama al-Shar’iyya), Jerusalem.
ba7672c4-fed6-5ce8-8f1d-ccd9a7e359e4.method_for_provenance: Jerusalem was narrowed down as the place of issue for this document supported by the text itself.
ba7672c4-fed6-5ce8-8f1d-ccd9a7e359e4.obtention: This document was found in the mid-1970s amongst a collection of Mamluk papers stored in a box at the Islamic Museum. The documents are likely to have been in the archive of one of the Shari'a judges practicing in Jerusalem.
ba7672c4-fed6-5ce8-8f1d-ccd9a7e359e4.bibliography:

ba9c5104-c11e-5d1f-8a1e-ba20fb2ab406.name: Stand.
ba9c5104-c11e-5d1f-8a1e-ba20fb2ab406.description: A rectangular stand with four legs and two holes in the top, made with slabs of moulded clay, decorated in relief and 'lustre-painted'. The relief design on each of the wider sides of the stand comprises pairs of griffons surrounded by swirling arabesques. 'Lustre-painted' pottery was produced in Abbasid Iraq before the technique appeared in Fatimid Egypt and was possibly introduced by migrating craftsmen. After the end of the Fatimid dynasty, the lustre technique sprang up in Ayyubid Syria, again probably brought by craftsmen who moved to areas where they would find the greatest patronage. Lustre painting was one of the most popular decorative techniques of 'Raqqa ware'; a type of pottery produced in AH 6th–7th- / AD 12th–13th-century northern Syria. The original use of objects similar to this stand is not certain although the turned legs on some objects of this type imply that they were adapted from wooden models, making it possible, therefore, that the stand was used as a table and that the holes in the top were used to hold bowls, drinking vessels, oil lamps or ink pots.
ba9c5104-c11e-5d1f-8a1e-ba20fb2ab406.short_description: The exact use of this lustre-painted ceramic stand is unknown. It may have been adapted from a wooden table; the holes at the top could have been used to hold bowls, drinking vessels, oil lamps or ink pots.
ba9c5104-c11e-5d1f-8a1e-ba20fb2ab406.dimensions: Height 19 cm, length 28 cm, width 13.5 cm.
ba9c5104-c11e-5d1f-8a1e-ba20fb2ab406.method_for_datation: A large number of stands like this one survive from the Ayyubid period.
ba9c5104-c11e-5d1f-8a1e-ba20fb2ab406.method_for_provenance: The style and technique correlate with similar ceramic objects produced in Raqqa. Furthermore, this stand was found in Raqqa, Syria.

ba9d80ab-9947-55e8-bd84-8062ba4f2798.name: Sprinkler.
ba9d80ab-9947-55e8-bd84-8062ba4f2798.description:
A small but heavy glass vessel made of dark purple glass, decorated with gilding and with white, red, and pale- blue enamels. The vessel's shape links it to a group of similar vessels referred to as 'spheroconical': the upper section is almost hemispherical, while the lower section tapers to a point at the base. The neck of the vessel is also tapered at its opening. The main decorative motif is a band of white calligraphy which reads, 'Glory to our lord, the sultan, the ruler, al-Ashraf Abu al-Fath ‘Umar, son of the sultan al-Malik al-Muzaffar'. Above the inscription, floral motifs alternate with circular medallions filled with coloured triangles. Below the inscription, similar floral motifs alternate with pointed circles.  
  
Spheroconical vessels, which are more often made of ceramic than of glass, are a bit of a puzzle. Their function is unclear, and suggestions have included hand grenades, loom weights, containers for holy water, and perfume sprinklers; a recent theory has it that they were drinking vessels for a beer-like beverage called fuqqa'. This vessel belongs to a group of about 50 objects made under the Mamluks as gifts for the Rasulid sultans of Yemen, with whom the Mamluks had close diplomatic ties and trade relations. The sultan named in the inscription is al-Malik al-Ashraf ‘Umar II Ibn al-Muzaffar (r. AH 694 / AD 1295–6). The circular medallions enclosing patterns of triangles are thought by some to be a personal emblem of his, and here it is indeed used in place of the usual emblem of the Rasulids, a rosette with five petals.
ba9d80ab-9947-55e8-bd84-8062ba4f2798.short_description: A small glass vessel of ‘spheroconical’ shape and uncertain function, with enamelled decoration including an inscription band naming a certain sultan of Yemen. This is one of a group of wares known to have been made under the Mamluks for export to Yemen, possibly as diplomatic gifts.
ba9d80ab-9947-55e8-bd84-8062ba4f2798.initial_owner: al-Malik al-Ashraf ‘Umar II Ibn al-Muzaffar, Rasulid Sultan of Yemen.
ba9d80ab-9947-55e8-bd84-8062ba4f2798.method_for_datation: The inscription names a Rasulid Sultan of Yemen who only reigned for one year (694 / 1295–6).
ba9d80ab-9947-55e8-bd84-8062ba4f2798.method_for_provenance: Cairo and Damascus were the two most important centres of art production under the Mamluks.

bac9e0ba-15e5-5bf5-a004-180b8c11e31d.name: Astrolabe
bac9e0ba-15e5-5bf5-a004-180b8c11e31d.description: The astrolabe is an astronomical instrument device that Muslims inherited from the Hellenistic world and then passed on to medieval Europe. According to its inscriptions, this handsome gilt brass astrolabe was made in Seville, in southern Spain. Like all such instruments, it was designed to measure the altitude of the stars, sun or moon, and to establish different astronomical and topographical associations without resorting to calculations or formulas. It was especially valuable for timekeeping, as the Muslim times of prayer are astronomically determined. In addition to being functional, the astrolabe was also intended to be beautiful. This example is unusual in that it seems to have been altered nearly 70 years after it was made, possibly in Egypt or Syria; Seville had by that time already fallen to the Christian reconquest.
bac9e0ba-15e5-5bf5-a004-180b8c11e31d.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
bac9e0ba-15e5-5bf5-a004-180b8c11e31d.method_for_datation: According to its inscriptions, the astrolabe was made by Muhammad ibn ‘Abda al-‘Aziz al Khama’iri in Seville in Hegira 624/AD 1226-7, who may have a familial relationship with another Spanish astrolabist also associated with Seville. The rete of the astrolabe was later altered by the astrolabist Ibrahim in Mamluk Egypt or Syria in Hegira 693/AD 1293-4, based on an additional inscription.
bac9e0ba-15e5-5bf5-a004-180b8c11e31d.method_for_provenance: Its Arabic inscriptions indicate it was made in Seville.

baf17501-3d43-54cd-9200-19fc581dd885.name: Almohad Mosque of the Kasbah.
baf17501-3d43-54cd-9200-19fc581dd885.description:
Built on a rectangular plan, the prayer hall is longer than it is wide, unlike the usual model for Ifriqiyan mosques. It is divided into seven naves and nine bays and it is roofed with groined vaults separated by horseshoe arches supported on columns with Hafsid capitals and imposts in long parallelepipeds.  
The *mihrab* is covered with marble panels. Above it hangs a fine dome adorned with plaster stalactites (*muqarnas*) and flanked by colonnettes with finely carved and gilded capitals. At the time the mosque went over to the Hanifite rite, the wooden *minbar* was removed and replaced with a stone *minbar* covered with marble.  
The most important element of the Kasbah Mosque is undeniably its minaret. It borrows its main decorative features from the Kasbah Mosque in Marrakesh, which predates it by 50 years. The decoration is made of stone – not of brick like the usual Moroccan model. This consists of a network of interlocking arches from the base to the top, forming a tracery of diamond shapes which stand out from the ochre stone background. This decoration covers all four sides of the square tower. Two of the diamond shapes on the east face bear an inscription dating the monument.
baf17501-3d43-54cd-9200-19fc581dd885.short_description: This mosque was built at the high-point of the *kasbah*, once defended by strong walls and the site of the palace of the powerful sultan Abu Zakariyya al-Hafsi. Its status was elevated from courtyard oratory to Friday mosque, a status enjoyed only by the Zaytuna Mosque before the conversion, and it was allocated to worship according to Hanafi school after the arrival of the Turks. The most important part of the mosque is its minaret, which borrows decorative elements from the Almohad towers of the mosque of the Marrakesh *kasbah*, the Hassan Tower in Rabat and the Giralda in Seville.
baf17501-3d43-54cd-9200-19fc581dd885.method_for_datation: Inscriptions on the minaret and inside the mosque.

baf17501-3d43-54cd-9200-19fc581dd885.history:
After declaring his independence from the Almohads of Marrakesh, the first Hafsid sovereign, Abu Zakariyya, had a palace built in the *kasbah* (seat of the government). Shortly after this he built this mosque. Starting off as a simple oratory, it went on to attain the status of a Friday mosque. Until then, only the Zaytuna mosque had enjoyed this role.  
With the arrival of the Turks it went over to the Hanefite rite practiced by the new masters of Ifriqiya.

bb0cbae2-4cdc-5b6e-a8ea-7cc05358a8e7.name: Ewer
bb0cbae2-4cdc-5b6e-a8ea-7cc05358a8e7.description: This rock-crystal ewer belongs to a small group that has survived from the Fatimid period. These luxury items were found in large quantities in the Fatimid caliphs’ treasuries in Cairo. The treasuries were plundered in the 1060s, after which the ewers that have been preserved found their way to European churches, used as containers for precious relics.
keywords: Ewer; Fatimid; Crystal

bb16c976-5f77-5e9a-b98f-840ba455f757.name: Silk sash
bb16c976-5f77-5e9a-b98f-840ba455f757.description: This fragment of a sash has its origins in Iran. The city of Kashan was renowned for the production of silk waist sashes. These were folded lengthways, wound around the waist and knotted at the front. Two different patterns can be seen on the same textile along the longitudinal line, so that the wearer had two sashes in one, depending on which side was turned outside. Hence the decoration was oriented on the way the object was worn. In Europe the demand for these sashes in the eighteenth century was so great that workshops were set up in Istanbul, Russia and Poland. In Poland the sashes eventually found their way into the traditional national dress of the aristocracy, which is why they are called Polish sashes (Polish: *kontusz*).
keywords: Silk; Safawid; textile; costume; Poland; vegetal decoration; floral decoration
bb16c976-5f77-5e9a-b98f-840ba455f757.author: Martina Dax

bb43f026-1a65-5250-959c-c4347189231f.name: Wall panel with geometric interlace
bb43f026-1a65-5250-959c-c4347189231f.description: Polychrome marble mosaics adorned the interior walls of both religious institutions and palaces in Egypt and Syria during the Mamluk period. This example, from an unknown building, probably once decorated the lower register of a wall, but similar mosaics also appear on *mihrab*s, spandrels, and even cenotaphs of the period. The interlocking slabs in contrasting colours bordering this mosaic, as well as the rectangular baseboard panels below it, are also characteristic of Mamluk architectural decoration.

bb7952b6-4d91-5465-865c-1ced864ef922.name: Painted wall-hanging: The Day of Judgement (*Ruz-e mahshar*)
bb7952b6-4d91-5465-865c-1ced864ef922.description: A painted wall-hanging depicts the *Day of Judgement* from a Shi'ite perspective in Isfahan. The main theme is the reward given in paradise to the martyrs who fell at Kerbala on 10 October 680, corresponding to the Islamic date 10 Muharram 61, and the agonies of their enemies on Judgement Day. Elements of Christian iconography are present. There is the trumpeting angel who blows into the bugle at the Last Judgement; the receiving of the arisen into heaven; the two angels who attend to the weighing scale of the souls; the chosen ones who await their entry into paradise; the blood witnesses who in advance enjoy the delights of paradise; and finally those of different faiths and traitors, who, already condemned, stand before the infernal ground. There are also new elements: the prophet of Islam is now an established, important figure, and Christ, the judge of the world, assumes the part of a precursor-prophet.

bb98e522-f646-5d72-a9f4-01e1cce27fbd.name: Brooch (Amulet)
bb98e522-f646-5d72-a9f4-01e1cce27fbd.description: Originally a heart-shaped amulet with a longitudinal perforation at the top which allowed it to be strung and hung. It was later set in a gold-and-enamel mount, fitted with a clasp, and served as a brooch. The stone features engraved and gilded Arabic inscriptions in *naskhi* and in *nasta'liq* script; there are also several inscriptions in low relief. The texts along the border reproduce in their entirety four of the last Suras, starting at the top, from right to left, as follows: Sura CIX (*Al Kafirun* / *The Disbelievers*), Sura CXII (*Al Ikhlas* / *Sincerity*), Sura CXIV (*Al Nas* / *Mankind*), and Sura CXIII (*Al Falaq* / *The Daybreak*). Other inscriptions are incorporated into a vegetal design whose large leaves are used as epigraphic cartouches. At the bottom, the invocation ‘*Ya ‘Ali!*’ (‘O ‘Ali!’). The texts are either excerpts from the Qur’an, such as verse 13 from Sura XIII (*Al Ra’d* / *The Thunder*) and verse 13 from Sura LXI (*Al Saff* / *The Ranks*), or formulas exalting the divine power and invocations which include several of the ninety-nine names of Allah. Also inscribed on the stone are the Muslim profession of faith, *shahada* (‘there is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah’), and the invocation ‘*Ya Muhammad!*’ (‘O Muhammad!’).

bba9a6eb-34f8-578b-b58b-ae4a8784d89d.name: Leather binding.
bba9a6eb-34f8-578b-b58b-ae4a8784d89d.description:
Back-board. Italian format. The red-brown dye of the leather has turned black at the edges.  
The panel is covered with wicker-like strap-work tooled with fringe markings enclosing roundels. The central rope is twisted into three knots. The border consists of four linear frames. The second frame is decorated with a twisted rope motif and a fringe with roundels. The leather covers a panel of what appears to be poplar, on the back of which is glued a piece of parchment.  
The decoration applied to this binding follows the style in fashion at the time in Ifriqiya. Twisted rope, plaiting, curled interlacing and chequer-work are all in fact used in the *minbar* (preacher's chair) of the Great Mosque at Kairouan, which bears the stamp of Syrian Umayyad art, with its heritage of Byzantine themes, and which also evokes Abbasid art with its profound Sassanid influences. However, these arguments do not allow us to conclude that the Kairouan bookbinding was influenced by Syria. Several links in the chain are missing. Furthermore, the books bound at Kairouan seem to borrow their decoration from a repertoire that was familiar to the Christians and which the Copts used to extraordinary effect. In fact, it is likely that the binding is one of the acquisitions through which Christian Egypt contributed to the enrichment the Muslim world.
bba9a6eb-34f8-578b-b58b-ae4a8784d89d.short_description: Brown binding from Kairouan separated from the Qur'an to which it belonged. It is decorated with twists, braids, interlacing loops and squares, also found on the pulpit of the Great Mosque of Kairouan, which was strongly influenced by Syrian Umayyad art.
bba9a6eb-34f8-578b-b58b-ae4a8784d89d.dates: Hegira, end of the 3rd–beginning of 4th centuries / AD 9th–10th centuries.
bba9a6eb-34f8-578b-b58b-ae4a8784d89d.dimensions: Length 17.2 cm, width 8 cm, thickness 0.6 cm.
bba9a6eb-34f8-578b-b58b-ae4a8784d89d.method_for_datation: Other identical bindings have been found still glued to the volumes of the Qur'ans to which they had belonged. Palaeographic study of their writing dates them very accurately from the end of the 3rd to the beginning of the 4th century (9th / 10th). Moreover, a Damascene binding definitely dating from the year 270 (883) shows a remarkable resemblance to this Kairouanese binding.
bba9a6eb-34f8-578b-b58b-ae4a8784d89d.method_for_provenance: This binding belonged to the old library of the Great Mosque of Kairouan which was left abandoned in the *maqsura* of the prayer hall. During the 1930s it was re-classified after being discovered by some well-informed visitors. Most of the bindings were separated from the Qur'ans to which they belonged and this one suffered the same fate. This and the other bindings are almost certainly Kairouanese, since the town was a great centre of book production at the time.
bba9a6eb-34f8-578b-b58b-ae4a8784d89d.obtention: After the abolition of the *habus* foundation in Tunisia, this binding board was obtained by the Museum of the Great Mosque of Kairouan in 1963. It has been displayed in the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada since 1986.

bbad2081-7784-53a4-806b-ff1932fc5849.name: Battle axe
bbad2081-7784-53a4-806b-ff1932fc5849.description: This axe is decorated with gilt Arabic letters on both sides. The inscription names the Ottoman Sultans until Muhammad III but only in a cursory and incomplete way. The hammer of the axe features the name of Sultan Muhammad III, suggesting that the weapon was made for a member of his Life Guards. The central medallion contains an appelation to Allah. We do not know how this axe entered the imperial collection.

bbbe8a25-e73d-5418-91ea-dbe154c4effb.name: Remnants of Jakob Eduard Polak's original gravestone
bbbe8a25-e73d-5418-91ea-dbe154c4effb.description:
With the revolution of 1848 and the fall of Metternich, Austria entered a new phase of encounters with the Orient. In 1851, the Bohemian-Jewish doctor Jakob Eduard Polak (1818–1891) accepted an invitation to Persia. He was to instruct surgery in Tehran. Polak stayed for nine years, learned Persian, became the personal physician of the Shah, and studied the land and its people on long journeys. Soon after his return to Vienna, he began to publish extensively. He wished to communicate knowledge between and about both cultures.  
As an epitaph for his gravestone, Polak selected a verse by the 13th century Persian poet Saadi. During the lifetime of Polak, no Persian in Vienna neglected to pay his respects to the former Hakim Bashi (personal physician) of the Shah. Recently, an Iranian doctor replaced the original gravestone in the Vienna Central Cemetery with a new one, as a mark of honour. The remains of the original gravestone found their way to the museum.

bbc8f1e6-fdee-507b-9bb8-8b0201e8ff87.name: Recycled prayer rug
bbc8f1e6-fdee-507b-9bb8-8b0201e8ff87.description: On this recycled Moroccan prayer rug, a prayer niche indicates the direction of prayer towards Mecca. A mosque lamp makes reference to the verse of light in the Qur'an: "God is the light of heaven and of earth. His light [comes] as if from a niche, in which a lamp stands." (Sura 24, Verse 35). Two stylised hands indicate to those praying where their hands should come to rest. Uppermost is the invocation to God: "Allahu akbar" – "God is the greatest". The open hand symbolises the five fundamental obligations of Islam (confession of faith, prayer, charity, fasting, pilgrimage). At the same time, the hand provides protection against negative influences and evoke happiness and fertility.

bbca80c7-2aa6-5a04-9263-603e9e9bc3ff.name: Stirrup
bbca80c7-2aa6-5a04-9263-603e9e9bc3ff.description: This pair of stirrups is made of engraved iron decorated with glass, jade and gilding. The long, wide, curved treads of these forged iron stirrups were particularly suited to the heel-less boots worn by the Ottomans. Their sharp edges served as substitute spurs.

bc013c86-0f26-5f80-ae32-0ad8f6ccb5e5.name: Weighing scales pan.
bc013c86-0f26-5f80-ae32-0ad8f6ccb5e5.description: A shallow circular pan belonging to a set of weighing scales, decorated on the inside only with six six-petalled rosettes arranged below the rim at regular intervals. Below this is a band containing three cusped roundels with composite blazons that incorporate the motifs of napkin, pen case and cup set against a stylised scrolling background. The roundels alternate with three elongated cartouches containing inscriptions in *thuluth* script. These are arranged on a stylised scrolling background with split-palmette and leafy elements incorporated into it. The inscriptions give the honorific titles of an anonymous ruler. The roundels and cartouches are interconnected by roundels with plain borders, filled with six-petalled rosettes. Pointed and cusped split-palmette cartouches further highlight the blazon roundels above and below. In between the latter, six six-petalled rosettes appear placed at regular intervals. The centre of the pan is decorated with an interlaced rosette motif with a central, six-pointed star created from inverted trefoils. The remaining spaces within the interlacing are filled with individual trefoils and scrolling.
bc013c86-0f26-5f80-ae32-0ad8f6ccb5e5.short_description: The style of this scales pan, its layout and the presence of a composite blazon place this object within a late Mamluk context. It may have been made in Damascus or Cairo. Scales pans would have been essential tools in the markets of Mamluk cities throughout the empire.
bc013c86-0f26-5f80-ae32-0ad8f6ccb5e5.method_for_datation: The style of the incised decoration, its layout and the presence of a stylised composite blazon, place this object within the Mamluk period (9th / 15th century).
bc013c86-0f26-5f80-ae32-0ad8f6ccb5e5.method_for_provenance: The style of the incised decoration, its layout and the presence of a stylised, composite blazon, locate this object within a Mamluk context. The major metalworking workshops during the Mamluk period were in Damascus in Syria and Cairo in Egypt.
bc013c86-0f26-5f80-ae32-0ad8f6ccb5e5.obtention: Purchased by NMS from the St Maurice Collection in 1884.

bc0e1083-d95d-5698-ab89-71d2e2154a4d.name: Bowl from Nishapur
bc0e1083-d95d-5698-ab89-71d2e2154a4d.description:
The bowl has a heavy body and a slightly concave base, its centre filled with a grid pattern on which a curved interlacing band forms six circles. They are attached to a central circle that is decorated with a pseudo-*kufic* inscription. The vegetal circles are alternately filled with the same pseudo-*kufic* inscription and a grid pattern with green and yellow dots. The outside walls of the bowl are decorated with black lines.  
The decoration depicted on this bowl relates to a corpus of pottery found in Nishapur where arrangements of the circle-shaped vegetal ornament in black, yellow and green colour are a common motive. Based on the extensive excavations conducted by the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York in Eastern Persia, Nishapur has been a centre of well-designed polychrome pottery made during the Islamic period. However, vessels with this kind of pseudo-*kufic* inscription seem to be rare.
bc0e1083-d95d-5698-ab89-71d2e2154a4d.method_for_datation: By comparison with other objects excavated in Nishapur.

bc2161f5-c0b4-5ed5-b8ea-778bc223c81c.name: Inscription in four languages.
bc2161f5-c0b4-5ed5-b8ea-778bc223c81c.description: Hexagonal marble tombstone in four languages divided into five panels, of which the centre one bears, inscribed within a circle, a Greek cross in polychrome stone inlay with the initials IC XC NI KA, ‘Jesus Christ conquers’. Above the cross there is an inscription in Hebrew, on the lower side an Arabic inscription, on the left a Latin inscription and to the right an inscription in Greek. The inscriptions refer to the death of Anna, mother of Grisanto, a priest of the Norman sovereign Ruggero (Roger), who died in 1148 and was buried in the great *jami* (subsequently Palermo Cathedral) and from there taken by her son to the Church of San Michele Arcangelo and the chapel known as Sant’Anna, built by Grisanto in 1149. The dates in the four versions, each calculated according to the respective calendar, are 1148 Latin, 4904 Hebrew, 6658 Greek and 543 Arabic. There is another tombstone at the Zisa Museum in just three languages (excluding Hebrew) commemorating the death of Drogo, father of the priest Grisanto, also buried in the Chapel of Sant’Anna in 1153. The inscription comes from the Church of San Michele Arcangelo near to the Casa Professa dei Gesuiti, which had many inscriptions, including Latin ones, and is now stored in the municipal library.
bc2161f5-c0b4-5ed5-b8ea-778bc223c81c.short_description: This tombstone, in Arabic, Hebrew, Greek and Latin, commemorates the death of Anna, mother of Grisanto, priest to the Norman King Ruggero (Roger). Each of the dates in the four versions, calculated using the appropriate calendar, corresponds to the Latin year 1148.
bc2161f5-c0b4-5ed5-b8ea-778bc223c81c.provenance: Church of San Michele Arcangelo (de Indulciis), Palermo.

bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.name: Fragment of a pottery bowl.
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.description:
The Raqqa region contains a group of Abbasid palaces that have been labelled with the letters A, B, C and D. This ceramic fragment was found during archaeological excavations carried out in Palace A. The fragment is part of a delicate bowl that was made in a mould and decorated around its girth with Arabic *kufic* script that reads: “from the work of Ibrahim al-Nasrani that has been made in Hira for the Amir Sulayman, son of the Commander of the Faithful." The Commander of the Faithful, or Caliph, in question is the Abbasid Abu Ja'far al-Mansur (r. AH 136–58 / AD 754–75). The text indicates that this piece was made in Hira by Ibrahim al-Nasrani and transported to Raqqa. The name of the craftsperson (al-Nasrani, i.e. the Christian) indicates that he was probably a master craftsman in the Christian ceramic-producing quarter of al-Hira.  
The base of the bowl was stamped with geometric and stylised vegetal motifs including palm trees.
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.short_description: Although this bowl is delicate and fragmented, its moulded band of early *kufic* inscription has mostly survived. It includes the name of the craftsman, Ibrahim al-Nasrani, evidently a Christian, the place of production in Hira and the dedication to Sulayman, '\[son\] of the commander of the faithful'.
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.initial_owner: Prince Sulayman (son of the Abbasid Caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur (r. AH 136–58 / AD 754–75).
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.method_for_datation: The inscription on the fragment associates it with the rule of the Abbasid Caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur (136–58 / 754–75).
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.method_for_provenance: The text inscribed on the vessel fragment specifies Hira, in Mesopotamia (Iraq) as the place of production.
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.provenance: Produced in Hira in southern Mesopotamia (Iraq).
bc31e6e4-7f37-5725-b63d-89472dbadb64.obtention: The fragment was found during an archaeological excavation carried out in 1948 in Palace A by the Syrian General Directorate of Antiquities under the direction of archaeologist Nasib Salibi.

bc369253-62f1-5c62-88c5-9c6d8162b6ca.name: Small glass kohl bottle
bc369253-62f1-5c62-88c5-9c6d8162b6ca.description:
A small glass bottle with a typically cylindrical body, flat base, sloping shoulders, and everted neck. The exterior is decorated with overlapping bands of black and light turquoise chevrons, giving to the flask an overall ‘marbled’ look or marvered finish.  
Marvered glass is created by rolling warm glass over a polished surface to shape and cool. Bands of coloured glass can be added at this stage to create ‘feathered’ patterns. This bottle is made of a dark glass with bands of lighter glass added during the marvering process.

bc3e3c85-1794-58d0-b562-179402fcba26.name: Latin funerary stele (gravestone).
bc3e3c85-1794-58d0-b562-179402fcba26.description:
This epitaph is carved in the most beautiful calligraphy and includes two dates corresponding both to the Christian and Islamic eras. The upper section is broken and the name of the deceased man is missing. But we are assured that he was a Christian and that he was buried in Kairouan. At the end of the epitaph there is a reference to the resurrection ('*resurgat in vits eternal'*) and to the saints ('*cum omnibus sanctis*').  
The inclusion of both the Christian and the Muslim dates in this funeral inscription is quite remarkable. Noteworthy too is the elaborate decorative style of the lettering which, however ancient the graphics and in spite of possible Mozarabic influences, brings to mind the Arab calligraphy of Kairouan.  
Most surprising of all is the designation of Muslims by the words ('*annorum infidelium*'), which, though normal in a Christian community, could possibly  
cause offence in an Islamic capital city.  
From the dates, the content and style of the writing, and from the existence of two similar Christian gravestones in Kairouan, we can form an idea of the prevailing spiritual climate in Kairouan at the time of the Zirid dynasty; one of tolerance and cultural exchange.
bc3e3c85-1794-58d0-b562-179402fcba26.short_description: The inscription on this gravestone relates to the burial of a Christian in Kairouan. The inclusion of both Muslim and Christian dates, the wording and the existence of two similar Christian gravestones in Kairouan are evidence of the climate of tolerance and cultural integration that prevailed in Zirid Kairouan.
bc3e3c85-1794-58d0-b562-179402fcba26.method_for_datation: The epitaph states that the deceased was buried on Monday the 9th ('*luna dies nobe*' according to the text) probably in the month of March in the year 1007 ('*anno domini nostril Ihesu Christi millensimo septimo*'), which corresponds to the hegira year 397.
bc3e3c85-1794-58d0-b562-179402fcba26.method_for_provenance: A chance discovery in 1961 buried in a mound of rubble called Khrayb (ruins) Sidi Saad in the eastern part of Kairouan, the stone was certainly carved in Kairouan itself, whereas the marble is of Italian origin; probably a Roman or Byzantine piece the like of which abounded in the area at the time.
bc3e3c85-1794-58d0-b562-179402fcba26.obtention: After its chance discovery it was kept in store at the National Institute of the Patrimony of Kairouan. It has been on display at the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada since 1986.

bc4ce7a2-a8d5-50c0-b880-c483d4c2dbc7.name: Carpet of floral arabesque type
bc4ce7a2-a8d5-50c0-b880-c483d4c2dbc7.description: This highly sophisticated design of spiral tendrils connecting symmetrically arranged flower blossoms and buds, leaves, palmettes and cloudbanks was popular in Iranian carpet-weaving from the second half of AD 16th through 17th century. Some carpets of this type today are attributed to imperial workshops of Isfahan. The rich and vibrant colour palette of the carpet is based on the deep red tone of the background. Contrasting dark blue ground of the main border renders integrity to the whole composition.
bc4ce7a2-a8d5-50c0-b880-c483d4c2dbc7.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by Leon Guzalian (examination, Hermitage, 1955, date); Hanna Rudyck (Rudyk) (The Khanenko Museum, 2017).

bc55917f-d0f7-5bd8-a131-1a210f5df63d.name: Mosque lamp for the mausoleum of Amir Aydakin al-‘Ala'i al-Bunduqdar
bc55917f-d0f7-5bd8-a131-1a210f5df63d.description: Mamluk amirs adopted emblems, often connected to their ceremonial roles at court, which decorated the objects and buildings they commissioned. Here the two gold crossbows against a red shield indicate that the patron of this lamp held the high-ranking office of *bunduqdar* (keeper of the bow) at the Mamluk court. The inscription states that the lamp was ordered for the mausoleum of Aydakin al-‘Ala’i, who died in Cairo in 1285.
bc55917f-d0f7-5bd8-a131-1a210f5df63d.dates: Shortly after Hegira 686 / shortly after AD 1285

bc585e0e-7651-57e3-a5ba-853d7190ab8d.name: Fragment of an ikat- dyed cotton shawl
bc585e0e-7651-57e3-a5ba-853d7190ab8d.description: This inscribed fabric from Yemen is part of an ikat-dyed cotton shawl dating from the 10th century. It is a typical product of the Yemeni weaving industry with an embroidered white inscription, which quotes a passage from the Fatiha, the first chapter of the Qur’an. The *kufic* inscription displays a unified symmetry and elegance achieved by the impressive triangular endings of the letters and by a number of varied slender arch-like motifs which makes it often difficult to read.

bc9be567-69d3-578d-8754-ec0d34770598.name: Incense Burner
bc9be567-69d3-578d-8754-ec0d34770598.description:
This incense burner is one of two that both belong to a group of similar objects. Within the group a high degree of standardisation is apparent, as the vessels show close similarities. However, two major decorative schemes can be determined. This burner exemplifies one of these schemes, which is a sequence of single split palmette motifs. Other examples of burners with this decoration scheme are held in the Herat National Museum and in a private collection published by Haase et al.  
The artefact is baluster-shaped with a splayed foot. The body of the burner is broadly made up of three different sections. The lowest part is solid with an engraved decoration that ends just above the foot. The middle part consists of openwork which shows a symmetrical design of scrolled leaves around a palmette. This is alternated with a circular ornament, showing the Solomon´s knot. The whole design is mirrored on a horizontal axis. The upper part is solid again, showing an inscription and a pearl-ribbon around the mouth of the burner. Little holes are punched through the inscription, thus indicating a different use at a later time, probably for hanging the vessel somewhere.  
The interpretation as an incense burner is supported by an example of the Linden-Museum Stuttgard, where a similar artefact is stored. There, a small bowl in the middle of the burner is preserved in which the incense was supposedly placed.

bceaff57-522d-535e-a0c3-944479903843.name: *Tughra* of Süleyman the Magnificent
bceaff57-522d-535e-a0c3-944479903843.description: The *tughra* was the personal and official Imperial symbol of the Ottoman sultans. Each Sultan had his own design.
keywords: Manuscript; tughra; calligraphy; Ottoman; Süleyman; tuğra;

bcf9b146-5f0b-5860-b18c-54be05ab62f7.name: Decorative panel.
bcf9b146-5f0b-5860-b18c-54be05ab62f7.description:
It is thought that this panel is part of the decorative woodwork of the Amri Mosque in Qus, and also that it formed part of the covering of the *minbar*’s pulpit. The *minbar* was first mentioned in the 1870s by A. Prisse d’Avennes. Two large forked leaves, with carefully inscribed carvings, are positioned at the centre of the panel. They enclose a central palmette blossom. The tips of both leaves become an almost geometrical pattern of flat stylised tendrils. The main body of both leaves is framed by a ten-pointed star, which connects at the top and the bottom to the panel’s outer frame. Their upper and lower points overlap each other in the form of spiralling tendrils. Vine leaves and small grapes can be seen growing from the tendrils, which are also covered with small hooks and forked leaves. A delicate tendril pattern also covers the surface of the main central forked leaves. The decorative woodwork on panels from the AH 5th / AD 11th century al-Hakim Mosque is similarly well designed, although they are not as finely carved as this piece.  
The town of Qus had developed into one of Egypt’s principal trading towns when the central mosque of Salih Tala’i was built in AH 555 / AD 1160. The famous *minbar* of Qus had been built only a little earlier. Goods traded with central Africa were reloaded at the town of Qus; Qus traded with Yemen and stored merchandise for trading with India. Writing in AH 579 / AD 1183, Ibn Djubair related the town’s rise to the crusades. The town was also a meeting place for pilgrims from Egypt and the Maghreb. Scholars used the *nisba* ‘al-Kusi’ (from Qus), testifying to the town’s significance. In the 19th century, the town was Egypt’s second most important Arabic trading town.
bcf9b146-5f0b-5860-b18c-54be05ab62f7.short_description: Islamic art excels in the ornamental designs often called arabesques. This is a superb example of a composition from Fatimid Egypt. It shows a geometrical star pattern surrounding stylised palmette leaves in the centre enclosed by symmetrical undulating vine scrolls ending in grapes or vine leaves.
bcf9b146-5f0b-5860-b18c-54be05ab62f7.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
bcf9b146-5f0b-5860-b18c-54be05ab62f7.dates: Hegira 6th century / AD 12th century, perhaps around AH 550 / AD 1155.
bcf9b146-5f0b-5860-b18c-54be05ab62f7.method_for_datation: The mosque from which this decorative panel came was built in 550 / 1155, so this panel could be dated to around that time.
bcf9b146-5f0b-5860-b18c-54be05ab62f7.method_for_provenance: The stylistic components of this decorative panel suggest that it could have formed part of a larger wooden decorative piece found in the Amri mosque in Qus in Upper Egypt.

bcfcf3a2-0ee5-5846-b4cf-318fae49e2cf.name: Azraq.
bcfcf3a2-0ee5-5846-b4cf-318fae49e2cf.description:
The Azraq oasis, 120 km northeast of Amman, was renowned for its copious natural springs which have provided a focus for settlement since the Palaeolithic period. A Latin inscription indicates that Azraq may have been called Dasianis or Basianis in Roman times. Today there are two settlements in the oasis, both of which were established by refugees in the early 20th century.  
Azraq North:  
Azraq is strategically located at the northwestern end of Wadi al-Sirhan, a natural depression which stretches some 400 km in a southeasterly direction to al-Jawf (Ancient Duamta) in Saudi Arabia. A chain of Roman fortresses protected the approaches to the oasis: al-Uwaynid, 15 km southwest of Azraq, and 'Usaykhim 15 km to the northeast. A third large fortress was built on a basalt spur just 100 m to the west of a natural spring in Azraq North. The castle (80 m x 72 m) is constructed entirely of local basalt stone. Its salient features consist of semi-projecting towers at the corners and interval towers along the walls. The main gate projects from the south wall and is protected by a projecting machicolation (a projecting window) below which is an Arabic inscription indicating major building works by the Ayyubid governor Izz al-Din Aybak, in AH 634 / AD 1236. The central courtyard contains a small mosque and is surrounded by a range of rooms, apparently once two storeys high. Latin and Greek inscriptions indicate that the castle was occupied from at least the late 3rd–early 4th century AD; aerial photographs from the 1920s show that it was erected within a much larger enclosure. However, the castle has been modified a number of times in its history.  
Azraq South:  
Evidence for early Islamic building activity has been found around the reservoir and marshes at Azraq South. A well-constructed six-sided wall, ranging in length from 200 m to 500 m, was erected around the main spring to create a large reservoir. The walls (2 m–2.25 m thick) were built of rubble core and faced with dressed basalt blocks resting on a foundation of a single course of unshaped basalt stone. Round and triangular buttresses jut out from either side of the walls. Along part of the eastern side the wall widens to form a platform (30.5 m x 6.00 m). Rectangular buttresses occur at each corner of the platform with six additional rectangular buttresses on the exterior and six triangular buttresses on the interior.  
It was in front of this platform that a number of carved basalt stones were recovered in the autumn of 1983 in the course of removing reeds from the reservoir; Claude-Vibert Guigue from the Institut français d'archéologie du Proche-Orient, Amman (IFAPO) discovered additional carved stones in the spring of 2004. The decorative stones include various animals, birds, and fish as well as human figures, floral motifs, and mythical animals such as the Senmurv (a creature part mammal and part bird and a Pegasus (a winged horse). The way the edges of these bas-relief stones are bevelled may indicate that an arched superstructure once stood near the front of the platform.  
An additional buttressed wall (1.30 m–1.55 m thick) extends around the marshland to the south and east. Stretches of this wall can be traced for a length of 3 km before it disappears into the silt and sand dunes of the marches. This long wall with rectangular and triangular buttresses may have once formed a complete circuit of the marshes and reservoir, thus inviting comparison with the large enclosures at Qasr al-Hayr West (Qasr al-Hayr al-Gharbi) and Qasr al-Hayr East (Qasr al-Hayr al-Sharqi) in Syria.  
Lying 1.75 km, to the northeast of the castle at Azraq is a small Umayyad building (17.70 m x 17.80 m) known as Qasr Ayn al-Sil. Abutting the west wall of the *qasr* is a bathhouse with a vestibule and cold, warm and hot rooms all arranged along a north–south line. The walls, 1.40 m thick, are built of two facings of roughly quadrated basalt blocks with a rubble core. A range of seven rooms built against the enclosure walls surround a central courtyard. Excavation and clearance work uncovered two olive presses within two of the rooms, indicating that the building was the homestead of a small agricultural estate adapted for use by a family, rather than that it was attached to a large plantation.
bcfcf3a2-0ee5-5846-b4cf-318fae49e2cf.short_description: The Azraq oasis, 120 km northeast of Amman, has been settled since the Palaeolithic era. A large fortress near a spring in Azraq North was part of a chain of Roman forts. Above its main gate there is a projecting window and an inscription indicating rebuilding by Izz al-Din Aybak in AH 634 / AD 1236. In the marshes of Azraq South, an early Islamic six-sided wall was built around the main spring to form a large reservoir. Along it were found carved basalt stones that belong to an arched superstructure. At 1.75 km to the northeast of the castle, there is the small Umayyad homestead of Qasr Ayn al-Sil.
bcfcf3a2-0ee5-5846-b4cf-318fae49e2cf.method_for_datation: The monument was dated by an Arabic inscription indicating major building works by the Ayyubid governor Izz al-Din Aybak in 634 / 1236.

bd0502e7-8e93-5eae-9634-c4fcfe027590.name: Deir Mar Musa al-Habashi (Monastery of St Moses the Ethiopian).
bd0502e7-8e93-5eae-9634-c4fcfe027590.description:
The monastery grew around an abandoned Byzantine watchtower dating back to the AD 5th or 6th centuries. According to legend, the King of Ethiopia's son arrived to Syria after he rejected royalty to seek out a spiritual existence. After travelling though Egypt and Palestine, attaining his priesthood along the way, he became a monk and settled in the Qalamun Mountains of Syria, living in the caves and the nearby abandoned watchtower and leading a devout life. He was martyred at the hands of Chalcedonian Byzantine soldiers in the early AD 7th century and the monastery was thus named after him.  
The monastery is characterised by a defensive style of architecture. The entrance on the western wall is extremely small, 1 m in height; with arrow loops distributed along the wall. The entrance leads into a dark corridor leading to various small chambers, the church and the terrace overlooking the cliff. The main rooms are distributed along two stories built above the cliff top and three stories dug below. Rain water was collected in reservoirs and stored inside the monastery to be used throughout the rest of the year. In the AH 10th / AD 15th century the monastery facilities were further extended.  
The church is located to the north of the monastery and was built in the year AH 450 / AD 1058. It is square in plan with sides measuring 10 m. This layout is divided into two sections: the Holy of Holies, consisting of the prayer-niche and screen wall, and the prayer hall, composed of three bays separated by two rows of columns. The extensive fresco paintings that cover the church walls have survived as some of the richest examples of regional Christian art. These reveal three different layers of painting, all of which were executed during the period of Seljuq, Atabeg and Ayyubid reigns.  
Due to the flaking of the paint, restorers have been able to examine stylistic and iconographic features of all three layers. Their date inscriptions have survived, written in Arabic, revealing the adoption of the Arabic language by the Christians of the region during the medieval period. The lowest layer, dated AH 466 / AD 1073–4, is the sparsest and has an animated style of painting, a continuity of local Hellenistic Christian art. The second layer, dating just a little later than the former at AH 488 / AD 1095, is similarly expressive and survives most completely on the eastern wall of the central nave, portraying the Baptism of Christ. The third and most visible level, survives as a comprehensive medieval Christian mural, offering a rare opportunity for iconographic analysis. An example is the depiction of the Day of Judgement, located on the wall of the western window, and exactly facing the painting of the Annunciation on the wall of the eastern window. Stylistically, these later paintings reveal a Syriac style, more spontaneous than earlier Byzantine traditions. The date is not very clear; one reading is 1504 in the Seleucid calendar, which corresponds to AH 587–8 / AD 1192. Another reading is AH 604 / AD 1208. Either possibilities place these paintings in the Ayyubid period.
bd0502e7-8e93-5eae-9634-c4fcfe027590.short_description: This monastery is located in the cliffs overlooking the Qalamun mountains, near the route connecting Damascus and Homs. While the oldest part of the monastery is pre-Islamic, an AH 5th- / AD 11th-century church displays *in situ* the most complete survival of medieval Christian mural paintings. The three layers of these distinctive local paintings are dated to the Atabeg and Ayyubid period of Syrian rule. They indicate an artistic renaissance among the Syriac Christian communities, in keeping with the tradition of Islamic tolerance towards communities of different faith, even at the height of political militarism and Crusader warfare.
bd0502e7-8e93-5eae-9634-c4fcfe027590.dates: The oldest part of the monastery (currently serving as the kitchen area) was originally a pre-Islamic Byzantine tower dating back to the AD 5th or 6th century. The monastery’s church dates to AH 450 / AD 1058.
bd0502e7-8e93-5eae-9634-c4fcfe027590.address: Deir Mar Musa al-Habashi is located amidst the rock-cliffs of the Qalmun mountain range 7 km east of Nebek, a city 80 km north of Damascus. The area is vernacularly known as Jebel al-Mudakhan, or “the Smoky Mountain”, due to the misty atmosphere.
bd0502e7-8e93-5eae-9634-c4fcfe027590.method_for_datation: Through excavation, massive dome-shaped constructs in the monastery's foundations were discovered and attributed to the pre-Islamic Byzantine era, dating to the AD 5th or 6th centuries. There is also a manuscript in the British Museum in London attributed to the Deir Mar Musa al-Habashi and dated to AD 575, implying that the monastery was well-established prior to that date. As for the church, a carved inscription dates its construction to 450 / 1058. There is also an inscription above the entrance indicating that renovation works were completed in 902 / 1497.
bd0502e7-8e93-5eae-9634-c4fcfe027590.bibliography:
Cruickshank-Dodd, E., “The Monastery of Mar Musa al-Habashi near Nebek, Syria” *Arte Medievale: periodica internzionale di critica dell 'arte medievale,* 2nd series, 6:1, 1992, pp.61–132.  
Evans, H., *Byzantium: Faith and Power 1261–1557*, New York,2004, p.424.  
Dell'Oglio, P., "Tarikh Deir Mar Musa al-Habashi wa wasf al-Rusumat al-Jidariyya fi Kanisatihi \[The History of the Saint Moses the Ethiopian Monastery and a Description of the Mural Paintings in its Church\]", *Tarmim Deir Mar Musa al-Habashi \[The Restoration of Saint Moses the Ethiopian Monastery*\], Damascus, 1998, pp.11–23.
bd0502e7-8e93-5eae-9634-c4fcfe027590.patrons: Since the AD 6th century the monastery was cared for by the Eastern Christian communities and the residing monks. After much neglect and damage, especially during the 1970s, the task of restoring the monastery was undertaken by Italian Jesuit Paolo dell’Oglio and the Syrian Catholic communities, taking care to maintain the old and indigenous methods of art and architecture.
bd0502e7-8e93-5eae-9634-c4fcfe027590.architects: The architects of the monastery’s church, which was built during the AH 5th / AD 11th century, were called Musa and his brothers (known as the sons of Abu al-Asad) and Mazhlum bin Tuma al-Nebeki. The fresco painter of the topmost layer was Sarkis ibn al-Qassis Ghali bin Barran and the calligrapher was Hunayn.
keywords: Monastery; church; religious architecture; Christian art; fresco; monasticism; Syriac; restoration

bd055ba2-904e-5725-948d-558c018101af.name: Fragment of wall decoration.
bd055ba2-904e-5725-948d-558c018101af.description:
Fragment of wall-cladding made of *timchent* (local plaster) sculpted in the form of floral decoration spread over three registers separated by three frames formed of flat fillets that are themselves separated by a milled edge. In the lower register are four columns surmounted by arches in the form of rose pateras that are composed of nine very geometric palm leaves. The decoration of the second register employs symmetrical trefoil leaves that evoke a spread of vine leaves attached to their stems by large peduncles; the latter are perforated with circular holes forming lower lobes. The stems, linked to the perforated peduncles, recoil into hooks and join back on themselves to form rings.  
Only a small fragment of decoration remains to be seen on the upper register, composed of stylised leaves covering the whole surface.  
This fragment was discovered in three pieces and was then reconstructed.  
The sculpture was executed with the aid of an iron blade acting on the *timchent* while it was still soft. According to H. Saladin, this local plaster derived from limestone peculiar to the region was 'applied onto cob or roughstone walls'.  
This sculpted fragment is only one part of a wall-cladding that ornamented the wall of a room in a palace.
bd055ba2-904e-5725-948d-558c018101af.short_description: Fragment of sculpted wall-cladding with floral decoration divided between three sections separated by flat or granulated lines. In the lower part, four columns support rosette-shaped arches, while in the upper part stylised leaves stretch up to the top section, of which little remains.
bd055ba2-904e-5725-948d-558c018101af.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts
bd055ba2-904e-5725-948d-558c018101af.dimensions: Length 71 cm, width 57 cm, thickness 5.5 cm.
bd055ba2-904e-5725-948d-558c018101af.method_for_datation: From study of the inscription that features on a frieze found in the same palace. According to G. Marçais, the *kufic* characters of this inscription could date back to the '11th century and resemble those in Kairouan', which dates this fragment to the 5th / 11th century.
bd055ba2-904e-5725-948d-558c018101af.method_for_provenance: The fragment was discovered in a palace in Sedrata following the report published in the *Comptes rendus de l'Académie des inscriptions et belles-lettres* in 1952.

bd0ea646-29ee-5137-a641-d80f90e7281f.name: Madrasa al-Shamiyya.
bd0ea646-29ee-5137-a641-d80f90e7281f.alternate_name: Madrasa al-Shamiyya al-Husamiyya after the patron’s son.
bd0ea646-29ee-5137-a641-d80f90e7281f.description:
Madrasa al-Shamiyya al-Husamiyya is one of the grandest *madrasas* to beconstructed in Damascus. Well known for the richness of its *waqf* endowments, and the abundance of its scholars, it was built by the renowned benefactor of the City of Damascus, the great Khatun Sitt al-Sham bint Ayyub – Salah al-Din's (Saladin's) sister. A distinguished patron of education and culture, she also commissioned the construction of a bathhouse (*hammam)*, and a Sufi monastery (*khanqah)*. Shewilled that her private home be converted to become another *madrasa* upon her death.  
Entered from the north, Madrasa al-Shamiyya consists of a rectangular courtyard with a row of alternating black-and-white (*ablaq*)arcs running across it, creating a porch between the courtyard and the subsequent halls. There is a water-basin to the northwest, a funerary hall in the southwest, an oratory that looks into the funerary room in the southeast, and a square-cut minaret to the northeast. It was originally much larger, with rooms for students and dwellings for teachers, but none of them have survived.  
By far the most remarkable feature is the funerary hall. Its entrance consists of a grand central gate flanked by two smaller gates, each surmounted by arched and pierced windows. Unlike other mausoleums found in *madrasa*s, this room is not covered by a dome, but by a slightly pointed cross-vault. There is a *mihrab* on its southern wall. Most astonishing of all is the survival of the painted and pierced stucco work entirely covering the three walls and vaults of the interior. This stucco is applied in symmetrical compartmentalised fields filled with geometric arabesques as well as *naskhi* and *kufic* calligraphic banners. Bracket stucco mouldings accentuate the frames and the vault ribs.  
Three inscribed tombs rest here, still in their original condition and orientation, and very well preserved. The northernmost tomb nearest the entrance, carries Sitt al-Sham (d. AH 616 / AD 1220) and her son Husam al-Din Lagin (d. AH 587 / AD 1191). The middle tomb carries Nasir al-Din b. Shirkuh, ruler of Homs (d. AH 581 / AD 1185-6), who was Sitt al-Sham's first cousin and second husband. The third tomb belongs to her brother, the ruler of Yemen, al-Mu'azzam Turan Shah (d. AH 576 / AD 1180) who was transferred to Damascus for burial in AH 582 / AD 1185. The wealth of attention given to this tomb chamber indicates the important position held by the Lady of Damascus and her family.
bd0ea646-29ee-5137-a641-d80f90e7281f.short_description: A grand *madrasa* complex built by the 'Lady of Damascus', Khatun Sitt al-Sham bint Ayyub. Its layout includes a free-standing minaret in a rectangular courtyard with a water-basin and an arcade in front of the entrance to the tomb chamber. This shows a high degree of flexibility and change from the original *madrasa* layout brought in from Seljuq Iraq and Iran. The impressive cross-vaulted tomb chamber, which holds unique surviving wall-to-wall painted and pierced stucco work, contains three original coffins. They are well preserved and include important inscriptions on the deaths of ruling members of the Ayyubid dynasty buried there.
bd0ea646-29ee-5137-a641-d80f90e7281f.address: The area of present-day Suq Saruja, northwest of the city, outside the city walls.
bd0ea646-29ee-5137-a641-d80f90e7281f.method_for_datation: The monument is dated by the cenotaph inscriptions and by historical records.
